div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Holland's Princess.—For several years the people of Rolland have been waiting for the long looked for heir to the Dutch throne. During all th.t time there has been the fear that the House of Orange might die out, and the throne pass to a German princeling Happily that anxiety is ended, and the little Princess fulfils the hopes of the Dutch people and of their Royal house. For weeks previously the limelight of public interest bad been ttuned en the young Queen quite unnecessarily, but all's well that ends well, and the fact tbat it is a princess, and not a prince, is of no national importance. There is no Solic Law in Holland, a prince or princess being evilly eligible for the succession, and under- this rule Queen Wilhelmina succeeded to the throne in 1590, on her father's death. Should, however, a prince he born, he will supplant his eldest sister, and also his mother on coming of age. He would succeed to the throne' and become King of the Netherlands on his eighteenth birthday, and Queen Wilhelmina, if then living, would become a dowager. The "Baby Book."—Since the arrival ,of the Dutch Princess, there has been a considerable demand for the "Baby Books," many mothers having decided to follow in Queen Wilbelmina's footsteps, in deciding to keep a close and accurate record of their baby's progress. Such items as the baby's weight, height, health, the voming of the first tooth, funny sayings, first lessons, adventures during school days, etc., eta., will be entered and a volume of this description, well-stocked with snapshots, should prove highly interesting and very amusing, especially in later years when the Laby" has grown to man's or woirsn's estate. A" Nest Egg" for Girls.—Another, and much more important point, mothers of baby girls would do well to consider, is, the desirability of at once commencing to "put by " for the little people. If this process merely amounts to a few shillings every month, in the Post Office Savings Bank, the total is very likely to be very acceptable later on for educational purposes, training for some profession, perchance the trousseau, or a permanent "nest egg." Although matters have decidedly improved since the time when everything was spent upon the boys, and notbing on the girls, still much remains to be done for the latter, and one excel- lent procedure is that of setting aside, from the time of their birth, some regular sum for their sole benefit when growing or grown up. A 'Variation to Taxing the Bachelor.—The Budget abounds in fresh burdens, and new principles, but relieves very few. What however, is done in the latter direction, is offered to parents of families with incomes from £l6O to £5OO. The concession takes the form of

a special abatement in the levy for Income Tax of £lO for every child under Iti, and it is practically a varia- tion on the oft suggested "tax on bachelors" Few will be inclined to dispute that this is a just concession to parents who undertake responsibilities-, from which the unmarried are exempt. The exemption is too small to go far to encourage family life, but it may be found possible in course of time to increase the abatement,and make it an appreci- able boon to parents of the professional and middle &asses, who have legitimately to "keep up appearances' and make many sacrifices, in order to provide for their children to the best advantage. No "Picture of the Year."—The Academy, which opened its doors to the shilling public on Monday, is notable for the absence of any dominating "picture of the year." The •4 problem picture" which has been of late years usually expected from the lion. John Collier is conspicuous by its absence. Perhaps the nearest approach to it in pictures of the subject-story kind, is Mr. Michael's "'[he Eleventh Commandment," Ishich appears to suggest the danger of being ,found out. There are portraits innumerable, that of the Earl of Wemyss by Mr. Sargent, being such a striking "speak- ing likeness" that one almost expects to hear the voice. Among others, there are portraits of Mr. Asquith, Mr. Lloyd-George, and Mr. John Burns, but it is generally agreed by the critics that the best contributions in portra; titre, in this year's Academy, come from the brush of Sir William Richardson, although the subjects are less known to the public. Contempt of Dress.—Some people can afford to be negligent of their dress on account of their high social positions, and others on account of their intellectual attainments, but both excuses serve the Duke of Argyle who stated the other day that he had the reputation of being one of the worst dressed men in Loudon. Perhaps the sante night be said of the premier Duke of England the Duke of Norfolk, who is stated to have been occa- sionally mistaken for a workman at Arundel Castle, on account of his negligent attire. The Duke of Argyll is like all his race, fair-haired, well-featured, intellectual, and is a happy combination of poet, author, musician, and man of affairs. To some extent his contempt of dress is shared by Princess Louise, Duchess of Arg3ll, who is not only Vie best looking of Queen Victoria's daughters, but also profoundly cultured, and the King has been heard to say that she is a most entertaining, and the most intellectual woman of his aquaintance. An Economical Device.—A combination in great vogue at the moment is pale mole and Wedgwood blue, which is not only extremely soft and artistic but curiously becoming to almost every girl and woman. To the r ossessor of the unrelastic and small dress allowance, two colours should be the limit. It is wonderful how much can thus be awed in the matter of
Shopland, at the present tune, is nuius ILb the impecunious in this matter, an entire department being frequently set aside for various shades of one colour.

En-tout-cas and Sunshades.—ln choosing an en-tout- cas, or Sunshade, it is well to remember that the plain, flowered or striped greens and browns are the moat desirable for every-day use, while for more dressy roe-colouroccasions, • re-colour is best. Red may be, and undoubtedly is, very artistic upon the river, or at a garden party, but the fact remains that it sends a pale and unbecoming glare on to the face, while with regard to heliotrope and deep blue, no girl or woman with a high colour should ehoose these hues. The craze for fringe has extended to sunshades, and all so finished are carried—when not in use—upside down, that is, the handle is fixed at the top, and the plain stick is in ev dence at the one tine handle end. At the Milliners.- -When milliners have massed more trimming on one Eido than the other, they have invari- ably chosen the left side for this particular attention, but we note a change, and the right side is now the favourite one. For a brief space the conservative among us, will regard the idea with suspicion, but not for long, and after, the new order of things may be quite as universally becoming as the old one, and perhaps even more so. Many Parisian hats show absolutely nothing in the arty of ornamentation save a large cluster of huge blooms, massed closely upon the right side. A Boon to the Homo Worker.—The new linen and cotton "blouse suits," well-cut, well-made, and gener- ally priced considerably under half-a-guinea, will be eagerly snapped up by the stock size girl or woman. They are unlined, but a slip beneath the blouse, and a suitable underskirt, puts this difficulty right. There are many colour-combinations, such as deep butcher- blue "suits," trimmed with crossway bands upon aid and bloue of striped light and deep butcher-blue, the yoke, collar band, and culls being of broderie Anglaise, Lucked net or lace. There are divers selections to be made in heliotrope, pink, green, and the wedgwood blues, and of course there are creams and white.

TO Clean Straw Hats.—To cican atilt° or cream straw bats, take one ounce of oxalic acid, pour upon it a pint of boiling water, dip a stiff brush into the mixture and well scrub the straw. The bat should pre- viously have been soakei for a few minutes in cold water, and should finally be thoroughly rinsed in several waters, shaken, and hung in the sun and wind to dry. MADGE.

div.head: STREET MAKING.
div.p: STREET MAKING.
PROPERTY OWNERS' OBJECTIONS.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr. 11. RoLerts (in the chair) and other magistrates, a number of objections were heard from different property owners in tte town against, apportionments of the cost of street paving. Mr. A. T. Ballaway (deputy town clerk) represented the Corporation, Alderman Tinnion (chairman of tbe Paving Committee), and Mr. T. Longdin (Borough surveyor), were also p:esent. The objections were in respect to the folio aing streets:— Elaine-street, Hale-street, Norris-stn et, Hulme-street. The following were the objectors :—George Sraith,The Limes, Orford ; Richard Hazledine,lB,Brick-street ;John Derbyshire, 125, Padgate-lane ; B. Warburton, 18, Elaine. street • William ;leeks, Albion Hotel, Battersi-y-lane; F. Tailor, 3-1, Or ford Avenue; F. Davies, 113, Lovely- lane ; G. and M. Ashton, Grappenhall ; Mary Alice Jones, Orford Avenue; James A. Heckle, 202, Padgate- lane ; and John Iludsen, 68 and 70, Brick-street. Only Messrs. Darla) shire, Ashton, and B. Warburton appeared. Mr. 11r,rris was called and spoke to serving notices on the above property owners also to advertising the hearing in last Saturday's "Eximiner." Mr. Derbyshire said his first and foremost objection was that the plying of the tack of Elaine-street was entirely unnecessary. It vrTs a street upon which DO other prof erty abutted except the railway line and the present state of the back gave him the opinion that it would not require paving for some time to come. Such paving pressed unduly upon property owners such ati himself and he wished a postponment or adjournment of some kind to he granted. Mr. Roberts : We would be very glad to do that if you could arrange with the Town Clerk: We (the Much) can only try the question of lability to pay. ,If he (Mr. Derbyshire) admitted that, the case vould be settled. The question as to . whether the backs should be paved now or later was a mater in respect of which the Bench had no jurisdiction, but they could very cordially recommend him to the tender mercies of the Corporation with regard to that. At this point Mr. Hallaway and Mr. Tinnion had a conversation v% ith Messrs. Derbyshire, Ashton and Warburton, and at its close Mr. Derbyshire said he was willing to withdraw his objection and leave it to the "tender mercies of the Corporations." . "Ir. Ashton said his objection wes on the same grounds as Mr. Derbyshire's. He could point out many cases not far from that Court where houses had bern built for 25 years, and the front street had not yet been paved. He withdrew his objection but recom- mended a postponment of the paving for another year. Mr. Hallaway said that on behalf of the Corporation he did not press anyone to withdraw their objections. The property owners of the town would be interested to know that at the recent Local Government Board enquiry the Corporation's application received unani- mous support, which was an unprecedented thing. Another point was that Mr. W. Hickman -president of the Property Owners' Association, was present and the venture started with his blessing. The Chairmrn For what it was worth. •(Laughter..

r 3. Mr. Warburton after expressing similar opinions as the other objectors, said he would also withdraw his objections. The.objectors in the above list who did not appear were ordered to pay costs (3s. Gd.

div.head: iPRACTICAL – POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: iPRACTICAL - POULTRY FARMING.
. [By Redcap.] SEASONABLE HINTS.

We have only to look back a few weeks and we are reminded of the extreme difficulty in obtaining :a broody lien. Now I suppose the general objection is, that yon have too many, and a few hints as to how to convert the broody into a layer would be very welcome. S. cloSer.study of practical poultry farming I am glad to say, has done away with many old-fashioned and somewhat inhuman methods of treatment to the broody lien, such as ducking her overhead in water several times daily and shutting her lip in a dark place for two or three -days without food. What a lack of commonsense ! For even if such treatment did serve the purpose it would very materially I.lTect the -condition of the bird, and as a consequence a long time , would elapSe beforeN would commence to lay again.

div.head: ASIATIC
div.p: ASIATIC

or heavy breeds are very much inclined to broodiness at this season of the year, and where such varieties are kept it is often annoying to find half a dozen hens broody at once. Not only so, but from a profit -point of view it is essential that this should not be, and instead of brooding over a pot egg it would be better that they were set- to real work. It is nine- h easier to get such fowls laying again than is often understood. More especially will you find this so, if the following instructions are carefully carried out. Obtain a voop or crate about 3 feet, square, and let the front and bottom be made of laths, nailed on about 1!. inches apart. This admits a constant current of air which keeps the occupants cool, and tends to reduce broodi- ness. IlaiSe the coop about two feet from the ground, fix a trough for food, and one for water at the front, remembering always to feed the broodies because by so doing, that much sooner will they com- mence to lay on their -return from ' " gaol." A crate or coop so constructed will accommodate, at least six or seven fowls. An important point is to place them in such a position that they- have a con- stant view of other birds on the yard or run. It keeps them active and helps-them to forget the inclination to sit. About three or four days at the outside is generally sufficiet to distract them from the natural
propensity ; then you can put them down with the rest of the flock to return to a more profitable employment.
MARKETING EGGS.

However much you may desire that perfect cleanli- ness should exist, you cannot avoid a small percentage of the eggs laid becoming tainted in the nests. It is important that you should know that egg shells are porous and the contents absorb anything which comes into contact with the egg. I mean of course anything bearing with it a strong odour. Thus an undesirable flavour is often prevalent and consumers of such eggs may brand them as foreign .-when such is not the case. This also - sometimes exists as the result of fowls having access to filthy liquid, and if they are neglected as regards a constant supply of freSh drinking water they will partake of such, for they must quench their thirst. Where egg production is the. chief business you cannot be too careful in watching these points. lam reminded when writing of a certain farm where the fowls have a free range, and as a consequence they have also free access to a neighbouring works (a tannery). How they - pick up the offal and seem _to like it ; 'but 1 must say that the flavour of the eggs from that farm is sometimes more than strong. 1 would much prefer a fresh Irish than such a one laid so near home under such conditions. I hope that farmers living near to a town will take the hint and carefully avoid risks of contamination. Then the selection in the size of eggs is important in retain- ing a good class of customers. It is often the case that eggs are collected and simply stored until market day comes- round, without ever a thought of selection. AlWays pick out the smallest and keep for home con- sumption. When you go your daily round it is easy to do this, remembering also to wash any that are tainted. If these few hints on marketing your eggs are carried out you will find cwitomers increase.

SEPARATING TUE SEXES and pushing on the cockerels for an early chicken market is important just now. Early hatches of chickens will have grown to a fair size, and I would advise you, now that they can care for themselves, to separate the cockerels from ,the pullets, for two special 'reasons. Firstly : Where they are allowed to fun together the cockerels quarrel and fight and this stops their growth. It also keeps back the pullets, and as a result whet might have turned out -to be your early layers are checked by not adopting this course. Secondly : Cockerels that are allowed a free range do not feed so quickly and instead of putting on flesh they make muscle—and you know it is the chicken with the Vest breast and not the biggest leg that counts in the market. So I would iecoinmend that you should overlook your flock and if any are to be kept for stock purposes these could be run together in a separate pen. But the ones intended for market should be kept in a roomy shed. They- should also be fed liberally on soft food and. only allowed to run out for about one • hour in the evening. Confinement under proper healthy conditions in young cockerels means flesh-forming, and if you see carefully that they are kept clean and fed well it will 'pay you for the extra trouble. Do not force the pullets., give them all the liberty you can ; by so doing you encourage growth and if fed sufficiently to keep them growing .without forcing them to lay at too early an age, it gives them a good chance of building up a constitution that will stand the strain- of winter egg production. Yever force your pullets until they are full grown. Then you can expect .a good return, and if fed accord- ing to the advice given in last week's column you will have no need to regret having taken a more scientific study of utility poultry fanning.

div.head: LATE 11.tTC11ING.
div.p: LATE 11.tTC11ING.

There are two classes of poultiy that may be still bred from. The Mediteranean or light breeds, and First Crosses for table purposes. I should recommend however, that you get the last batch of chickens off before the end of this month from the light blved,, which are intended of course for egg production. lint table birds may be bred for until well on in the autumn, as the pullets from this variety are usually killed for market as well as the cockerelsb
sriust: CLEANING,

I suppose amid the annual upset of home life one need hardly remind the poultry fancier that he or she too should attend to the lime-washing of coops and poultry houses, and I think I would prefer a bucket and brush in conjunction with an old suit in the poultry runs, than a struggle among furniture of all descriptions for one's hat and stick in the hall. Well ! we have all got troubles of our own in this world, but the trouble I wish to put my readers to is very necessary at this time of the year. Perfect cleanliness is the first essential to success in poultry farming. We are aho having plenty of good strong winds at present and you need have no fear but that after lime-washing your houses will soon dry. If the rills have become somewhat tainted, fork them up and sprinkle over with lime. This will sweeten the earth and add te the continued health of the. stock. Keep a strict eye on vermin and destroy any that you find with insect powder. In conclusion, follow out the details I have mentioned. They are very necessary if you would have a suecessful season in the poultry yard. Next week I shall write on Duck Farming for profit.

div.head: NEW CHOCOLATE.
div.p: A NEW CHOCOLATE.

For many years the name of Messrs. Joseph Epps & Co., Ltd. has been associated with excellence in the manufacture of rocoa. This firm in spite of its age, is keeping well abreast of the times, and is now offering the public a most attractive selection of high grade chocolates. it may safely be conjectured that there will be a ready demand for these, since it seems to have been reserved for this firm to show the ACII3O of perfec- tion in the production of chocolates. One of the principal lines is a Milk Chocolate of particular deliciousness, which is put up in different styles of packing. Another, also in a variety of forms is a very delicate vanilla chocolate, "Solo," which in quality as its name appears to denote "stands alone."

div.head: LORDS AND MOTOR TRAFFIC.
div.p: LORDS AND MOTOR TRAFFIC.

'.:11otorlc-.r vale occupied the Lords during ,Wednes- days siting, Lord Willoughby de Broke moving the second reading of a very drastic Vehicles on Highways Bill. Dust, danger, and drn •tage were the three points agairst motor-cars, he said, and this bill proposed to regulate the speed of cars to ten miles an hour in rural villages or at dangerous points, twenty miles in or near towns, and thirty miles in the open country. All racing competitions on road would be forbidden, hooters were not to be carried, and there were provisions as to fines and so forth. Earl Russell moved a hostile resolution. Lord Allendale raid the Government could not accept either the Bill or the resolution. Leiri Lonsdowne said the Government owed it to the village popnlation to mitigate the inconvenience of the new traffic, and he hoped the Budget scheme would afford considerable relief. After. some remarks by the Earl of Crewe, Earl Russell withdrew his motion, and the second reading was also withdrawn.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
LIVELY SCENES.

A variety of contentious topics appearei on the agenda of the Warrington Town Council meeting on Tuesday, and the members discussed them at such length that the meeting lasted three hours and a half. At times considerable heat was engender d, and there were several lively scenes. The Mayor (Aldermen Forshaw) presided, and there were also present :—Tles Deputy Mayor (Alder.nan Smethurst), Aldernan A. Bennett, W. Bolton, T. Burton, L. Ellisn, John Evans, W. Pierpoint, and D. Tinnion ; Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, T. Barton, 'l'. Birtles, J. 13realhurst, T. Chantler, .J. G. Craik, E. Connington, J. Dickenson, James Evans, J. Holliwell, J. Hawthorn, Dr. Joseph. J. Lord, J. Pemberton, W. Rogers, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, J. Fulton-Smith, 0. Toole, J. Wilkinson, and W. J. Wilson ; Messrs. .1. L. Whittle (town clerk), A. T. Holloway (deputy town cler ), .1. Foil hunt (borough treaaure,), T. Longdin (boaough survey or), .1. Dens (water enginee..), %V. S. Haddock (gas engineer), F. V. L. Mathias (electrical engine,r). J. M. Murray (director of .education), and Dr. J. U. Ilibbert (medical officer). COUNCILLORS' RIGHTS.

THE MAYOR AND COUNCILLOR PENIBERTON. Couneillor PEMBERTON moved: "lbat the Mayor,or Chairman for the time being of the Council, before calling upon the mover of the minutes of any c immittce to reply to the minutes of that 'committee. dr in the event of no reply being necessary, before he calls for the cOnfirmation.of such minutes, shall previously ask if any other member wishes to speak on such minutes." The M A YOR addressing the Councl ad : Before CouncillUr Pemberton proceeds with his motion I wish to make a few obse:vations. This motion is clearly the outcome of the recent conflict between Councillor Pemberton and the chair when he persistently refused to obey my ruling. Councillor Pemberton seems unable to understand the elementary rule that no mem- ber of the Council has the right to spetk more than once on the minutes of a committee, and this motion, if carried, will give him no such right. (Hear, hear.) This motion would interfere with the discretion of the Chairman and trammel his right to conduct the meeting according to recognized rules. (Hear, hear.) If Councillor Pemberton will sttely the Standing Orders instead of propounding new tules which he considers necessary for the cincruct of a meeting he would see lor himself that this motion if quite unnecessary. Every member, as I have previously explained, is entitled to speak once on the minutes of any committee except only when an amendment is proposed when be has the further right of speaking on the amendment. I object to the motion not so much on my own account, but for the protection of the chair, and personelly I sboold refuse to be bound by a rule which interferes with my conduct of the loysiness of this Council. and to leave .my rulings open to be chellengei because I may fail to ask the members whethr they. want to speak when everybods knows that he has the right to do so if he wiste)s. I think it is abut timo that. this Council understood that ,the m,etings aro to be con- ducted from this chair, and not from the lower end of the room. (Hear, hea-.) I object tt the motion. Councillor PEMBERTON said he was sorry that the Mayor had token up the position belied done that night. He contended that the Mayor did not know what he was going to say when he uas ruled out of order. As the matter had been mentiencd, be was tound to mention it also. The right as claimed by the resolution was a right they really had at present, and it was the usual custom for the Mayor to express exactly what he bad stated in his resolution, but there were times in the rush of business when the Mayor might fail to do so. On the occasion mentioned by the Mayor, he rose on a point of order. The MAvon : After the m7nut es had been confirmed.. Councillor PEMBERTON- : It does not matter. The MA.von : You are challenging my rulings. now, end I will not have it, I tell von. Councillor PEMBERTON : lam telling you about an incident that took place. The MAYOR : I have told you it was after the minutes were confirmed. I will not have you disobey my ruling. Councillor PEMBERTON : lam not. I am simply asking for your opinion. (Cries of "Chair.") lam only giving my version of what took place. Alderman BOLTON : W 3 don't want it. The MAYOR We don't want it. You still challenge my ruling. Councillor PEMBERTON 11111 not challenging it. The MAYOR: .You are.

Councillor PENIRERTON : What am I challenging. The MAYOR.: You said you got up to a point of order. You got up after the minutes bad been confirmed. Councillor ...P.E3IIIRRTON said the Mayer was in stall a " temperament " that he could not follow him. He (Councillor Pemberton) was speaking carefully and slowly. and knew perfectly well what he was going to say. On that occasion he rose to a point of order, and neither the Mayor nor any other member of the Council knew what that point of order was. ho MAYOR: You wished to monk on the minutes of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee, and they had been confirmed.

Councillor PEMBERTON : With all due deference, I did not say what I warned to refer to. I rose to a point of order. I don't want t 4 make this a personal question. I bad no idea of doing S 3 ijite I put this motion do3rn. Vito
Alderman SAlrrirunsT appealed to Councillor Pemberton to withdraw the resolution.

Councillor PEMBERTON said it was important that business should be conducted in that Council in the proper way. They must pay a certain amount of respect to the Mayor and his hoped be had never been deficient in proper respect to the chair. There was no man in that Council who bad been placed in more awkward positions than he had been, but ho had always tried to be respectful to the chair. They were, however, all representatives of the ratepayers, and even the Vayor had to obey rules. No mayor was infallible—he was not speaking of any particular mayor, nor did he wish the resolution to apply to the Mayor personally. It how- ever, happened from time to tine, ouing to the rush in which business was being carried through that some member of the Council got up too late and was then ruled out of order. The MAYOR : That is not true at all.

COURCinOr ...PEMBERTON : How many times have gentlemen got on their feet to speak and been ruled out of order? I don't suggest for one moment that it was done purposely, but it simply happens that when the minutes of a number of committees are not dis- cussed they are gone through sometimes almost too rapidly for anyone to have an opportnnity of speaking if he wishes. I simply want the onus to beplaced upon the Mayor to af.k whether anyone wishes to spesk on the minutes of each committee. L want this to be made into a specific rule to be applied before the chairmen of the different committees reply. In doing so I don't wish to cast the slightest reflection upon the Mayor..
At this point Councillor ASHCROFT proteqed against feveral members of the Council speaking to fach other, and he said he hoped the Mayor would keep theni all in order.
Alderman BOLTON : I think it is a disgrace to the Mayor In allow a thing like this to be discussed by the Council.

COBBeinOr PEMBERTON : I ask the Mayor and the Council to accept my assurance that I do' not recom- mend this resolution in any offensive manner. Alderman BOLTON: The Mayor was quite right in whit he did in ruling you out of order. You know the rules and you should obey them. Councillor PEMBErrrox : You are the man who obeys them least of anybody. I want to give an example. The MAYOR : I ant not going to have my conduct discussed like this. I must tell you to keep to your motion.

Councillor PEMBIirtTON : I am keeping to the motion and telling what took place. The MAYort : Which we deny. Councillor PEMBERTON : I was referring to Alder- man Bolton. We are not going to be coerced by one or tao men, it amounts to disfranchising all the other rds of the town.

The MAYOR: It is nothing of the kind. I will not allow you to discuss my conduct ip the chair. Alderman TINNION : 1 think Councillor Pemberton would do his cause more good if he left out the other incident and tiied to prove that his motion is essential to fair and reasonable debate.

Councillor PEMBERTON : The only way you can prove it is by giving an actual cause. The rights of the members must be respected. There are standing orders which the Mayor must obey. A Mayor cannot rule debates here as he likes.
The AI ‘YOR : It has never been suggested. Keep yourselfto the motion, Sir.

Councillor ThotnErtTox : Really, I must protest against so many interruptions. I am not a practised speaker—(laughter)—and I cannot stand them. I will show that the tnoticn is not put down for any personal motives by stating tkat Councillor Lord had a similar motion down a few months ago. Councillor IluoAnnurtsT : Are we going to sit here all night discussing this motion? It is awaste of time. Councillor WILKINSON: If you had let him go on, he would have finished now.

Counciller PEMPERTON repeated that there was nothing in tho resolution rell( cling on the Mayor, and said if it could be proved that there was, he would withdraw it out of respect to the Mayor. What he wanted was that there should be no trickery. The 3fArort : I am not asvare that there . has been any trickery in the conduct of the business of the Council.

Councillor PamßEtrees : I said just now that yeti were not aware of it. Councillor LORD seconded the resolution. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH sqid he hqd not read the resolti- tion until Councillor Pemberton had commenced hl6 speech. Really, however, he could see nothing unreason- able in it.

The MAYOR : I have already indicated that it is tiler practice of this Council and requires no rule at all. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH: If you say tat, I ant, satisfied. If that state of affairs did not exist, I coula not but support the motion as a fair-minded wan. Councillor BROADHURST said they must all admire the courage which Councillor Pemberton displayq• but at the same time he could see no necessity for this motion. He had alwa3s found the Mayor courteous enough to allow any member to speak on any motion before the Council. He considered the present dis- cussion a great motto of time, and it was a disgrtu:e to the town that so much time should he occupied 10 discussing these motions.

Councirlor WILISO-N. ,id he bad been a personal friend of the Mayor from a lad so that it could nit be suggested that there was any personal feeling in his mind in this matter. He had a hand in the framing of the resolution, and he agreed with it because be wished to bare a safeguard in the conducting of the business of the Council. There wets no insult ever thought of. AU they did was to humbly beseech the Mayor to ask a certain question before calling upon the Chairman of N Committees to reply. The MAYOR : I tiltiltyB do it. Councillor WILKINiON In this case you did not. I was one of the sufferers. The TowN CLEftX : This is a distinct interference - with the conduct of the chair.

Alderman Tixetos: thought the resolution not ceil)'" an insult to the clia,r but also to the intelligence of the Council. If they adopted it, it would be a vote of censure on the chair and nothing else. After appeals by Alderm to Smethurst an', Councillor Evans, Councillor Pemberton agreed to withdraw his' motion, but s he would bring it forward again et the annual meeting of the Council whenbembers would be unable to attribute it to feeling against an particular Mayor. SWIMMING FOR GIRLS: _ Councillor WILKINSON moved :—" That the Council' give instructions to the Town hail, Parks and Bathe Committee to grant to the Education Committee the use of tbe ladies' bath for the whole of Wednesday in each week for the teaching of swimming during the times the sehools are open." He pointed out that tho • negotiations between the Education Committee and the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee had extended • over 18 inonths,but matters had get no further owing to" the obstruction of the Town Hall, Parks and Batlre Committee. He thought it was imperative that extended facilities should he given to the girls to learn swimming' There were BJO girls eligible to be taught, aad under - tbe existing arrangements they had only facilities for 60. With regard to the stetement that it would inter- fere with the convenience of lady bathers to grant arry more time, he might say that he had seen the attend-- ance book at the baths and found that there was so' average of only three every Thursday who visited the baths from April to the end of October. Ire thought it was not unreasonable to request those three ladies to attend some other time,becanse by so doing facilities would be provided for 120 girls. The boys who had learnt to swim whilst at school had become got)d customers of the baths on leaving school, and he. thought the-same would apply to the girls. Councillor LoRD seconded. Councillor BROADHURST supported the resolution ,- and remarked that at the first meeting of the Council be- attended, Alderman Bolton promised something shod'd be done in this matter, yet they remained just as theY - were. The speaker complained that this was the onlY department of the Corporation .where he had bee° refused information, and it would appear that the superintendent had had his mouth "tied up." Alderman BOLTON contended that the Town Hail,' Parks and Baths Committee were doing their best fa. the children, with the facilities at present at their (life*" posal, and as soon as further accommodation was; pr°' vided, the present bath could be handed over to the - Education Committee for tb especial use of the scholar.? He contended that from a health point of view it woul" be undesirable to extend the privileges granted under the existing conditions. Councillor BIIITLES said procrastination was the thief of time, and it was procrastination in dealing With the plans for the baths extension which had led to the present discussion. The plans were prepared two years ago and it was about time the buildings were ereeted• If the School Management Committee wpuld give them time, he for- one would do all he could to get tho additional accommodotion provided. Alderman BURTON said that if a complete day WE set apart for the children, another -profeesional teacher would be required. Councillor PEMBERTON considered there would be hardship or inconvenience in giving the children a In day. Alderman TINNION objected to the Council attempting to over-ride the Committee, whose special duty %vas allot the baths to the various users at the times whice were most suitable, convenient and healthy. After further discussion, in which Councillor sON stated that the Education Committee were prepa' to pay £2O for the privileges asked for, the resolution was defeated by 12 votes to 0.

VIC fORIA PARK. The Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee fill resolvedebat the whole of Victoria Park be DOW 161 out fur the benefit of the inhabitants of the borough._ Alderman Bouras in moving the adoption of tr• w' minutes mid that before the construction of the Shir Canal, the townspeople used to enjoy walks on SundaY afternoons through the Arpley fields. He could not see why the Victoria Park estate should not now be put t°- the same use and paths laid so that the people of Wel; rington might have the full advantage of it. The no" footbridge which had been sanctioned would open Ur the park to the inhabitants of the Howley district. _A Alderman Eeetsos, in secondiug, said he was plea"- to know that at last the people were going to have the' full advantage of the park. He had been fighting ff! it for twelve years and he believed it would be tot betterment of the town. Councillor PEMBERTON said he would liken guarantee from the Chairman of the Committee that the held t° s r* be laid out would not include that set apart .0 allotments. The Towel CLERK, on consulting the minute boola, said the Committee's resolution was out of oldie!, because it conflicted with a resolution passed by th Council in October last appropriating certain land fet allotments. ea After some discussion the resolution was appro. with the proviso "Exclusive of those parts which ery. already appropriated for allotments." BOWLING GREENS. At a meeting of the Town Hall, Park's and Baths Coot' mittee, the following report of the Bowling Greeer'' Sub-Committee was read.—" The Committee made to, inspection of the land on the south of the entrance _Le Victoria Park, and selected site for the propes(7.. additional bowling green. It was resolved that th; Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee be recommendo to proceed with the making of the follocc- ing bowling greens in the order mentioned 1, Land, Winwick-road, late Grace's property ; Recreation Ground, Liverpool-road ; 3, Victoria parl;...; and that the Borough Surveyor be instructed t,`; immediately proceed with the necessacy detailed plead' and estimates in order that application may be for sanction to the borrowing of the money with ie,t least possible delay." The committee resolved Its the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare p1,3",_, and estimates of the cost of constructing a bowl'%. green on the land in Winwick-road, formerly the 51' of Grace's Pottery. ' Councillor PEMBERTON said he took it that the ea -- strection of the heeling green would be let out contract. He wanted some guarantee that the celi.t- mittee were not going to do the work themselves. .13 must not be a repetition of the Latchford green, will° was laid on brick bats. (Laughter.) , Alderman BOLTON: Councillor Pemberton has bes. bothering about bowling greens, but he won't let us ge ahead with them. ree Councillor ROGERS asked if the time had not ce, when tennis grounds should he provided for the ladlece Councillor BIRTLES said it would be very to make a bowling green on the sfte of Grace's Pott,eleir nnd the smoky surroundings were not suitable. T' already had brickbats there. Victoria Park would he splendid site for several additional green, id be Councillor Toole: said a bowling green won welcomed in Winwick-road district. Councillor BROADIWRST said one of the finest WI,/ ing greens in the town was to be found near the era Ole chimneys of Bank Quay. Every district should haveblio bowling green. It was not right to ask inn who ,eO. been working all day to go scores of miles to a gr‘ Laughter.) The minutes were approved. PRESENTATION OF THE CUP. MORE ABOUT THE DOUBTFUL DECISION.

Immediately after the match there was a rush to the grand stand where the presentation of the Cup and watches took place. The victory of Rylands' was immensely popular and for several minutes the crowd cheerAd wildiy. When something approaching quiet- ness had been restored,

Alderman TINNION, 'the President of the Warrington Football Club, said the committee of the Warrington F.C. were justly proud of the competition not only for the encouragement it gave to the works or junior clubs of the town but also for the assistance it was the means of , giving to various deserving charities in Warringtcn: He was happy to say that this year the committee hoped to hand over a record sum—(cheers)— folthe sum to be disbursed, including compensation to injured players, was over £BO. (Cheers). They claimed that they were the only Northern Union Club that devoted the whole of the proceeds of the compeCtion, less expenses, to the cause of charity— and charity of a kind that appealed to the hearts of all of them, and particularly of those amongst the workingclasses who might be compelled, in time of accidents or unforeseen circumstancess,to make use of those institutions.(Cheers). They also claimed that as a Clab they had endeavoured to footer the Rugby game in Werringtou, and their Works Competitions were carried out with a fairness and justness which had confidence. (There were many expressions of 'dissent from thls statement.) Probably' the losers might not he able to see quite as fairly, and as justly the decisions that had been given es those who had weighed them calmly and without prejudice, but, it had always been the endeavour of the Committee to carry out the competitions with due fairness to every competing team. (More interruptions.) Ile hoped the 1 result would be that they would be able to promote healthy football in Warrington. He was pleased that Rylands's them had won because if one firm in the town was carrying out the healthy spirit of sport and com- radeship amongst the - workpeople, it was Messrs. Rylands Bros. in the way they catered for their employees. (Cheers). . Alderman TINNION then banded the cup to Brondhurst, capte in of the winning team, and presented gold watches to the members of the team. The runners-up received gun-metal watches. M. W. Peter RYLANDS, in moving a Tote of thanks to Alderman Tinnion and the committee, expressed the pride which he felt in the accomplishment of his own team in having won the cup for a second year. At the same time. he mutt say that it had been a splendid game, and although the winning goal was a magnificent one—(A, Voice "It went over ')—ho could not but feel that it was really a toss-up which side would win. He congratulated the team on the magnificent light they made. (Here there were some iuterroptir ns, and cries of " Whitecross.") A good number of teams had played in the competition and those who had been unsuccessful would have the feeling that next 3 car they would have an opportunity of retrieving the situation. (A Voice : "if they get fair play.") lie naturally looked forward to next year with some hope thet he would be privileged to see his own team take part in the final aga'n, even if they did not achieve the great success of winning the cup for a third time. He con- gratulated the Werrington Football Club upon their splendid organization and also upon the splendid way in which the competition had been carried through. (Some expressions of disapproval greeted this remark). He would like to say a word upon an incid'ent which had ton certain extent detracted from the satisfaction with which they must regard that competition. He knew there was a fet4ing, whether rightly or wrongly, that re decision given in one of the matches was not correct. As sport Met], it was their duty when they played a game to do their best to win and accept the decision of the referee, whether they agreed with it or not. They mu t remember that the referee was trained to the work and did the very best he could, but occasionally mistakes were made in every walk of life, and if by any chance a referee made the mist die they must take it that he acted accerding to his best judgment. He appealed to them to put the incident out of their minds and .accept the decieien of the referee like British sportsmen. He hoped nothing of the kind would ever occur again to mar the sport which they enjoyed in that annual competition and thet there would not be the slightest ill feeling amongst the different clubs in the town. (Cheers). Mr. J. McDeneilo, on behalf of Fletchcre Russell's team, seconded the vote of thanks, and congratulated the winners upon their splendid victory. It bad been a cepital game, a credit alike to those who took pert •in it and to the Warrington works competition. There had been some exhibition of feeling with regard to the decision referred to but he thought everybody would admit that any reflection of that k;nd rested very heavily upon those who had ch•rge of the competition, if it was to be thought that they in any way favoured a certain team. He believed, however, competing teams had frill confidecce in the committee and that the com- petition bad been cart ied through absolutely without ' favour. He could say on behalf. of Fletcher's team, that they had, neither asked for favour ,nor got any. They had fought fairly and squarely and would take their defeat like sportsmen. Ile hoped any feeling would be forgotten and that rext year they would be ready to take part in the competition and do their best to win. (Cheers). The vote having been carried, Alderman TINNION said no one regrinted more than the committee that there had been any cause for friction. (here the interfup- tions again broke out, but Aldermen Tinnion's invitation to one of the disturbers to come and argue the matter out on the stand was not responded to). Any question of fact in the game rested entirely with the referee and the committee had nothing whatever to do with it. They were bound to decide according to the rules that governed them and they lied no choice in the matter. Therefore there was no favouritism. They only hoped that another year it would be pozsible to take precau- tions to prevent anything of the kind occurring again. (cheers).

The Examiner Saturday, May 8, 1909
Intenary of Holy Trinity Church.

Before the commencement of the ordinary business at the Warrington Town Hall meeting on Tuesday the 111ayor, announcei his intention to attend Holy Trinity Church on Whit Sulday, on the occlsion of the bi- centenary of the church. He uidersbod that the 1.41 rd Bishop of Livarpool would be the preacher, and Ord the 111 lie C3at S3hool Band would pay the procession to and from the chnrch. 113 would like as m=ny mem- bers of the Corporation to accompiny him as p Brick-street Independent Methodist Church.

At the above place of worship the Sunday school anniversary was celebrated last Sunday, the preacher being Mr. John Turner of Bolton. A procession was formed in the morning and afternoon headed by the band which headed the streets of the neighbourhood. At the morning service, which was fairly well attended, Mr. Turner preached from the words" For now we see throug:h a glass darkly, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then shall I know even as Ism known." In the afternoon at 2.30 a sacred festival sery ice entitled "A Jewelled Diadem" was rendered by the choir,the chair being taken by Mrs. James Dadds. At the evening service Mr. Turner preiched an eloquent sermon to a large congregation, from the words "For other founda- tion can no mm n lay thin that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." The anthems "I will extol Thee " and Blessed is the man" were sun 5 in a very creditable manner, the solos and quartet being t tken by Misses H. Howell and H. Hill, and Messr,. VV. Barton, junr.. J. Shaw, and Henry Lightfoot. The collections realised £ll Gs. B.ld.

div.head: CRICKET AND BOWLING NOTES.
div.p: CRICKET AND BOWLING NOTES.

Bravo Warrington! If they maintain the tip-top fqrin villich give them the brilliant victory over Broughton Hall on Saturday, the prospects for the season are of the rosiest. The members are full of enthusiasm and a determined effort will be made to secure the West Lancashire 'League Championship. It is time Warrington made a bold bid for the honours and progress in the competition and doubtless gain them a great deal more support than they at,present enjoy. On Saturday,Warrington made no mistake for they tumbled out tits Chestriana for the small tqtal of -17 and then piled on 182 for the less of 8 wickets.

The featnre of the Warrington innings was a dashing display by J. W. Bainbridge, who made an invalnsble 48, his chief hits including one six and sevea fours. B. Si!cock was also in graneform, his 33 being faultlessly compiled, a hilst W. Richardson made 25 by crisp hitting.
Cresswell, the Warrington professional, took a pro- minent part in the summary dismissal of the home eleven, capturing 7 wickets for 18 runs. 11. Callon accounted for two wickets br 6 runs.

Sankey Wire Mills opened their season in promising style on Saturday, when they entertained Widnes White Rose and defeated them by 22. B. Taylor was the top scorer with s splendid 34, and E. Clare pre a fine exhibition for his 31. For the Rose T. Barber captured five wickets for IS runs and T. Hewitt four for 19.

Warrington Secondary School had no difficulty in accounting for Holy Trinity whoso innings wAs notible for a fine display of" ducks." For the winners Evans knocked up 22, whilst Kelly and Ormsby wrought great havcc with the ball.
St. James' scored a creditable victory over St. Paul's ho made a very poor show and were all out for 18. St. James' ran up 59, the most successful batsman being H. Booth (16) and E.Wright (12).

Whitecrcss Recreation tritrnphed over the"Gaurdiati" eleven by 20 runs. It was curious that three players on the winning side—G. Rillton, Lester and Charno..k— each made 15, the best efforts for the home eleven being those of Sankey (10) and Ditchfield (12). Waywell took most of the wickets for Whitecross.
Secretaries of clubs are again reminded that reports of Saturday's matches and comments thereon should reach us not later than Wednesday morning,

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

\ There was a good meeting of this Society on Sunday last presided over hey the Secretary. Mr. E. James, of Latchford, gave the address upon "Repentance." After explaining the meaning of repeatnnce, what it is and what it is rot, he took the illustration of the Prodigal Son as the best exhibition of repentance. The young prodigal was sorry for the position he was found in after feeling his want. He felt that instead of g•iing farther from his fat hsr he must turn back to him. He confessed his sin first against Heaven and then against his fathe^, and showed his genuineness by stating that he would be willing to be a servant to his father and no longer n srm That gave us a true type of repentanes. Mr. G. Colley and Mr. G. Smiley also took part in the meeting. Miss Suton sang" As pants the hart "and "Nearer, my God, to Thee," which were greatly appreciated. Mr. Payton, Mus. Bac., presided at the organ. A free-will offering was taken at the door for the poor fund. The Secretary moved that a vote of syrnpa!hy be sent to the President (the Rey. John Yonge) and Mrs. Yonge, and also to the son of Mr. and Mrs. Yonge, who had lost his wife by death.

div.head: Silver-street Sunday School. Anniversary Services.
div.p: Silver-street Sunday School. Anniversary Services.

For twenty-omoyears in succession the Rev. J. Grange Bennett has visited Warringten in connection with Sunday School Anniversaries. He has been the preacher at the Silver-street anniversary for several years now, and it was a source of great disappointment to him that he could not occupy the pulpit on Sunday morning. However he found a good substitute lathe Rev. E. B. Keeling, who preached to the young men, and Mr. Bennett aldreased a crowded congregation in the even- ing. Mr. T. Armon Jones, R.A.M., gave several solos during the services which included "Nearer, my God to Thee," " Arra, Arm ye Brave," "Lead Kindly Light," 'and "No burdens yonder." The choir rendered the anthem "Come unto Him," (Gounod), acd the singing of the scholars bore t,.stimonY to the excellent training they had received at the halds of Mr. W. Hipkiss. The organist was Mr. T. W. Pearce. MR. C. E. PARKER ON THE TEACHING OF NATURE.

In the afternoon there was a service of song, over which Mr. F. Boston, 'IP., of Runcorn, presided, and Mr. C. E. Patker was the spetker. The CHA IRMAN gave an interesting aidress on the Christian race, mentioning that. they should ell be Christian athletes reagy to withstand the winds and storms that heat around _them on their journey.

Mr. C. E. PARK ER said he bad come from the country to speak a few words to them who live' in the town: In the country this was perhaps the most interesting time of the year; nature was having her anniversary, and just as many children had been getting new clothes so nature was putting on new garments, all plant life was bursting into leaf and Hower, and it msde him sorry that at stieh a time the children who lived in the towns could not be in touch and sympathy with nature. Whatever advantages and interests there were to those who wete older who preferred to live in towns, to the .children it was a great luss that they could not be in .contesct with name's realities. He felt that our civilization had taken a wrong turn in compelling people, and especially children, to live in dull grey streets where there was so little of colour, so little of natural life, and one could not help feeling that the tendency which became more pronounced every year to crowd together in towns was robbing the children of that which was their birthright and natu•al inheritsnce. But one special disadvantage which was pertinent to a gathering of that kind was that the severing of the association of children with country life lessened the ability of the child to understand the Ilible,the Sunday school's text book. The Bible was written by country people for country people, its authors were in the main shepherds, vine-dressers, fishermen, and herds- men. It was true we bad the word " Cities "often used in the Bible hut these cerresponded more with what we understood as villages to-day. The life of the people in the Bible time and indeed in our own country in the past, was the life of the field, the wood, the meadow, and the stream, and it was on the im)gery borrowed from these that the literate° of the Bible and of early England was built and by which all the experiences of life Were interpreted. If they were to take the Bible; both the Old Test amegt and the New, and take rattail those passages in the PSllll39,Prophets, ,and Gospels which were explained and illustrated through the imagery of the country, through natural things, they would find th Et they had very little of the Bible teaching left. The pictorial language of the Bible was becoming with each generation of town dwellers more end more unintelligible. They could realize from this what a disadvantage it was to the teaehets, to the parents and to the children themselves when they had to interpret a book which was full of the imagery of nature to children who were strangers to nature. A child's universe with its tamp of thought could only be made up of the materials that wale at hand, and to many it was limited to paved streets,hrick buildings, a small square tenement called home; in his outlook he saw nothing but houses, streets!, and chimneys. The question therefore suggested itself : Will it not become necessary if we go on congreetating together as we have been doing for the last forty years to compile a now literature, a new set of hymns, in which the concrete images borrowed from the environ- ment of the town will have to be used instead of our Bible and hymn books, which derive colour and intsrest from natural things of which a town child knows little or nothing? Instead therefore'of talking about sweet fields beyond, the swelling flood, of the sower going forth to sow, of the lost sheep upon the mountains and so on, we would have to frame lessons and hymns ' which took their imagery from smoky chimneys, dull streets, noisy tramcar;' corners decorated by public- houses and the like. Not very lovely images, but they would at least be understood by the child bectansa they were the concrete things which go to make his world. He (the speaker) was afraid if such a thing were done as hehad proposed it would mean is great loss, because even in town bred children, if not from their own knowledge yet deep down in their • nature .was an instinct- that attracted them to the world of nature. There was what we might call the "call of the blood" inherited perhaps from their country-bred ancestors. How instinctively children turned their faces and their minds towards natural things if they only had the chance, just in the same way as the plants turned their faces towards the lighc We could see this in their love for those hymns which spoke of nature and the things of nature. Someone noticed in 'a particular loyality how fond children were of Newmon's beautiful hymn "Lead kindly Light." Now the deeper thought in that hymn was quite unintelligible to a child; what was it then made it attractive? It was not merely the simplicity of its Anglo-Saxon diction, although that was one of its charms, but it was due more to its suggestion of mystery linked with the actualities of nature. "Lead kindly light, amid the encircling gloom" —there was the erie picture of being led into the dark- ness and the unknown gloom. Then vvehed this followed up with the conception perhaps all the more fascinating because not clearly unde)stood by many children, that the path they would tes led would be o'er moor and fen, o'er crag and torent, till the night was gone. He did not think we would like seriously to thin% of doing away with the Bible and our hymns becaese the children had lost touch with the nature which gave to the Bible and those hymns their light, colour and feeling. • A far wiser course would be to bring the children back again to nature. How this was to be done 'svas a large question, and ems not appropriate to an occasion of that sort. But in the meantime it was well that by Sunday School work, by the study of the Bible, and the singing of hymns they should as far as it was possible prevent the further severance of childhood and nature. In addition to the deeper lessons which the Bible taught he looked upon it as no small benefit to the child to be brought Sunday after Sundey hack to the things e hich were far more real, pure and natural, than those artificial conditions which went to make up so much of a town child's life. The pres•nce of the Bev. J. GRANGE BENNETT in the pulpit in the evening pleased the large congregation. He took for his text" They returned to Lystra " (Acts xiv. 21), and said St. Paul bad returned to Lystra although he had suffered defeat when there previously. The rev. gentleman maintained that a Christian should be a Christian all, the week, and not a "Sunday
Christian." Als3 tint in the workshop, office, or wherever be was he should bear the marks of Jana. EVANGELISTIC RE lIINISCENCES.

On Mond iv evenings crowded congregation assembled to hear Mr. T. Armors Jones give a summary of his life and sing "Lead, kindly Light "—the piece he rendered before the Kiog and Queen and the late President McKinley, U.S.A. The Rev. J. Grange Bennett—who is,in his own words, "a fair specimen of .Milk v. Beer,"— gave a gr tphic description of his mission work in the British Isles. Mr. W. Roberti, J.P., presided and was supported by the Rev. E. B. Keeling. The eft AIRMAN said be could understand how proud they we-e of their Sunday Sahoel when he heard such beautiful singing. It was an inspiring sight to see a I crowded congregation on Monday evenins. To those who wire engaged in the Sunday School work let him say that it was the most precious of all, for they wore helping to train the Youth and helping then to form good resolutions in their early life. When he heard some people sty that Free Chnithmen believed in a Godless eduoation he would like some of those people to. be with them that night. (Hear, hear). They did not believe in anything of that kind. They believed, as strongly as any Churchman or any,Roman Catholic, that the secret of all education must be the implanting of true religion in the early life. He wished that we in England wstild take a leaf out of the hook of oer Welsh brethren in the matter of Sunday Schools. In .Wales they never gave up going to Sunday School. In this country too many of our young men and women stopped going as soon as they began courting. (Laughter). They could not do better than select a partner from the Sunday School or the Chapel. In Wales even old men and women went to Sunday School. Referring to the teachers, he said that their labour would not be in vain. They should not be dis- couraged. Tkere was everything to encourage them and they might depend upon it, that with unity—and he knew it Prevailed in that place—success would be the result of 'their happy work in the church.' Concluding he sympathised with Mr. Bennett in his bereavement, and paying a fine tribute to .tAst late Mrs. Bennett said that there was no grgater joy to her than waen her son entered the ministry. (Applause). The Rev. J. G. BENNET r said he was glad to have Mr. Roberts as chairman, because he was a Free church- -man—(applause)—and also because he was a product of Sunday School work, and in that work he had been engaged most of his lifetime. The speakar thanked hint forhis kindly reference to his mother. That night he had to give reminiscences of his tour through tha British isles in connection with mission work in the Methodist Church. His journeys had already reached About 150,600 miles. He had been in the far north in the Shetland group, and also in the Channel Islands, where nearly 13 years ag ) he had one of the most successful missions of his life. It was fraught with tremendous issues to himself, for 1:e found his wife there. (Laughter). He knew Sc Aland and Ireland, and Wales , he thought he knew the Pi incipalitv almost better then 11fr. Jones himself. (Laughter). He had been up and down his natice country until he seemsd to know almost eery e tteway on the main lines of the railway. He bad stayed in nearly 600 different Methodist houses and he was never tired of paying a tribute to the kind- ness of the Methodist people ti their ministers (Hear. hear). He had friends everywhere. They could go to the farthest house in Land's End and they would find that the people there knew him. He had the satisfac- tion of bringing cite of the occupants of that home to ' Christ. If they mapped out a tour of the British Isles be could go on that tour and not have to call at a single hotel on the way, for he had so many friends. He did not think there was any other man that conld'do that. They c '•ild mention Thomas Waugh and other big men doing _11! • same class of work as he, but then, they could not ries bicycles. (Laughter). There were only two homes a something like 600 that he had not gone bark te. The first one was not in Lancashire. The othe- one was in his native county. Many years ago be went to preach for Charles Garrett at the Liverpool mission. Is was December sad the cold and fog was simply terrible. His train was two hours late and when he got to Charles Gairett's house, die found he could not stay with bans, bee oise his -two sons were coming home that night. However, arrangements had been made that he should stay at a member of the mission's house. in the slums. / 'He was taken to a room upstairs and looked out upon the street and saw several gin pals-sea. It was there be realised the terrible havock of the drink. He would never forget the sights he saw as he looked out from that window. Into the gin palaces the crude victims went, and he saw something above the door .0 which made him sick to see—" Walker's Warrington Ales." (Shame.) There were the women half-clad marching into the "palaces." As he looked upon the sight he realised for the first time in his life that no language could descrite the horrors of -that damnable drink and in that room he knelt down and nailed his colours to the temperance mast. He promised God so long as he (the speaker) lived and had a voice to speak he would do semethiag to bring before the people of his country and to hasten the day, whieli he believed would come, when the sons and daughters of England should be free from the fetters of that cursed slavery and rise in all the true menhood and womanhood to liberate England. (Loud applause). _ _ .

At this Tioint Mi. Armin. Jones sang "Lead, lindly Light," and pfterwards remarked that he sang that piece many times for thirty au'neas a time, but he had sacri- ficed all that for the glory of God, (Applause).

. . The Rev. E. B. KEELING moved a •o!e of thanks to the Chairman, Rev. .1. G. Bennett, Mr. T. A. Jones, Mr. W. Hipkisq, Mr. T. NV. Pearce and the chair. The collections amounted to the handsome sum of .CSS —a record.

div.head: Holy Trinity Church.
div.p: Holy Trinity Church.

Sermons in aid of the Sunday school funds were preached at Holy Trinity Church on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. G. B. Thurston, in the afternoon by the Vicar, and in the evening by the Rev. F. E. Chadwi(k. The Rev. G. B. Thurston pointed out that the childhood of Jesus was a true pattern of childhood. His physical and mental growth was gra-lual, as in the case of any other child. Tee point in which He differed wss that His spirit was perfect. It was a great mis• take to endow him ssith superhuman ability either of body or mind, because if they did so they would destroy that important belief in His perfect manhood. 1 he rev. gentleman dealt upon the responsibility which rested upon the fathers end mothers, the clergy and Sunday school teachers, to wham God huh given the priceless privilege of helping in the work of training the child's soul. Archdeacon Spooner's Visitation.

div.head: Welsh Disestablishment and Education.
div.p: Welsh Disestablishment and Education.
Archdeacon Spooner held a 'Court at the Warrington PArish Church on Wednesday morning for the porpc-,53 of admitting to office the newly-eleoted churchwardens and sidesmen.

La his charge the Archdeacon referred to the Welsh Disestablishment Bill, which, he said, many regarded as a half-heartel attempt at redeeming a pledge—a temporary tiding over difficulties connected pith a ' small but active and insistent section of the supporters of the preseet Government, and which would probably be withdrawn era it met with the fate it deserved ta the hands of the House of Lords. The probahilities were that when the results of the recent Commission wore made known the whole afpect of the question would be changed. Statistics had been forthcoming from various sonrces quite independent of the Commis- sion, which showed conclusively that in many parts of the Principality the Episcopal Church had gained, and was steadily gain7ng ground, and that if the wave of success centiutied to flow, her opponents would find themselves armed with a weapon which was consider- ably blunted, if not rendered altogether useless inthe face of increased vitality, efficiency and influende. It seemed, therefore, to thinning and rersonahle persons, grossly unjust that the order of proceedines had been the pratnulgation of the Bill to be followed by the report of die Commitioners, rather than as reason and justice would seem to demand the exact reverse. One fact, however, they would do as well RS church- men and patriots to lay seriously to heart, and thst was that the disestablishinent and disendowinent of the Church in Wa'es would inevitably prove the prelude to similar procedure in England. Should the Bill receive the assent of the House of Commons their hope must lie in the House of Lords, but it could not bear, unaided, too severe a tax, and therefore its hands in this matter must be strengthened by the unanimous and definite opinion of Churchmen th-oughout the length and breadth of the country, . clefrly expressed at public meet- inr or through the medium of their newspapers. rhe. edu :asioa problem was still sub Judice : the outlook full of uncertainty. To many the hold of the [Church upon their primary had eeorandary schools and training colleges seemed to be becoming so insecure, that with the exception of a few local instances to the contrary, their laity were declining to risk the expendi- tare of any large amount of money either upon extensire renovation of existing schools, or upon the erection of ! now ones. Thera were one or two grsve facts which ' they were bound to face. Firstly, many of their Church schools were going under and had been or shortly would be cloied entirely,secondly,the number of ' children being trained in their Church schools was steadily increasing, and no provision had yet been made for the instruction of the Church children there in any definite Church doctrine: thirdly, indirectly, it not directly, their Church training colleges were becoming the ohjectires for an insidious and resolute attack, and as it was to them that they looked for the msin supply of their teachers, sech attick must be carefully watched and repellel, with due regard to justice and reason, in the best interests of their Church ; fourthly, unless some solution of the problem was speedily arrived at, though unw:lling to aegniese in it at pres.ent, the country might find itself in the fetters of a purely secular system of primary and secondary education, the results of which would inevitably Se moml corruption, religious decay, and national deterioration and disaster.

div.head: BRITISH WOOL INDUSTRIES.
div.p: THE BRITISH WOOL INDUSTRIES.
THEIR CASE FOR FREE TRADE.

-- Tariff Reformers are -very confident in regard to tile strength of their plea for the Tariff taxation of foreign wool 'manufactures imported into this country These goods, they argue, are mostly in the nature of luxuries totalling (in 1908) about 0,500,000 worth Of yarn, dregs goods, &c., which Seem to them very suitable objects of taxation. The foreign wool workers have longer working hours and lower wages- than ours. Ve admit the foreign goods duty free, whilst our similar goods sent abroad are heavily taxed. To these considerations Free Traders answer that tinder a Tariff Reform policy our wool industries would probably lose much more than they woula gain, because— _

THE CHIEF WOOL MARKET IN THE WORLD. 1. This country is the principal market in. the world for wool, mohair, and alpaca, and also for the " tops," "nods," and other subordinate products of the wool industries. In the year 1908 the United Kingdom exported a total of V 4,300,000 worth of ' -wool, and yarn, and Various wool fabrics. If we enter upon a Tariff war all these masses cf labour-employing produce would be open to retaliation, with proportion- ate injury and loss to capital and labcfur in thi, countiT. 2. Tariff Reformers affirm that they will impose no Tariff duties on wool or. other raw materials, hi fact, however, the nature and magnitude of the duties will depend, not upon what Tariff Reformers promise us now, but -on the political power of the various interests which deal with the Tariffs in Parliament. The Australian and New Zealand people, for example, would have an almost irresistible case in favour of "preference "for their wool, by the imposition of Tariff duties on South American and other foreign -wools. Such "preference," of course, 'would very .sericusly handicap our wool manufactures.

div.head: RAG-WOW...
div.p: RAG-WOW...

3. An important element in the growth of our wool industries, especially as regards cheap fabrics, has been the time of " rag-wool " or shoddy." It is estimated that we consume about 180,000,0001 b. per annum of this material, equal to about one-fourth of the total of wool used in this country. Growers of wool at home and in the Colonies would certainly agitate strongly for Tariff duties on imported foreign rags, which, they could plausibly assert, com- pete unfairly with new wool. Such duties would heavily raise the price of wool clothing, thus reducing consumption and throwing many workers out of employment. The result would be the large substitu- tion of cotton clothing for wool, as has occurred in the United States, where the consumption of wool clothing per head of the population is only about one-half of lvhat it is in this country. YARNS AND DYE WARES.

4. Spinners of wool yarn in this country would reasonably demand Tariff duties upon imported wool yarn. This would naturally provoke retaliatory duties against the much larger quantities of wool yarn which we export. Moreover, the Tariff duties on imported yarn would be seriously injurious to the home manu- facturers who find advantage in the use of these foreign yarns. - 5. British dyemakers would reasonably demand the imposition of Tariff duties upon dye wares imported from abroad. Inasmuch as the German dyemakers, by reason of the superior skill of their working chemists, lead the world in the manufacture of dyes, such Tariff duties would severely chcck our dyeing industry.

div.head: FOREIGN WOOL FABRICS.
div.p: FOREIGN WOOL FABRICS.

C. 'Tariff duties upon the imported dre-:, goods "and other wool products- would, of course. rai,,c,the prices of these commodities, with proportionate injury to the employment of tailors, dressmakers, and others who are even more -numerous than the persons employed in wool spinning and weaving. 7. • The conipetitive .efficiency of our wool industries under Free Trade has been specially demonstrated of late years by the falling off in the quantity and value of foreign wool fabrics imported. Moreover, of the wool fabrics thus imported, about 10 per cent. are re-exported to the Colonies and to foreign countries. 8. The exports of wool manufactures from Con- tinental countries have of late years been stationary or decreasing, whilst our exports of these goods have continuously inereaso--excepting in the one year of eepressiou,

div.head: FOOD TAXATION,
div.p: FOOD TAXATION,

• 9. The gravest feature of Tariff Reform policy, 'however, from the point of view of the wool indus- tries, is the proposal to tax food—a proposal -which is an indispensable feature of that policy. Inquiries into the household expenditure of the average of working people in this country have shewn that workers earning from 20s. to 3.05. per week spend about two-thirds of the total family income on food. They also spend about one-sixth of their income on house rent. This leaves only about one-sixth of die total income for expenditure on cloth- ing and other things. Now, obviously' if half of this small margin is taken away by food taxation, the ‘Vorkers will have so much the less to Spend cm cloth- ing ; and employment in the wool industries will be proportionately reduced. In fact, experience at home and abroad has shown that Tariff duties on food do raise prices by at least the amount of the duty. Also, by reason ot the small scale of the transactions in retail. trade, a 5 per' cent. duty would be practically equivalent.to 8 per cent. or even more. Thus the nominal 5 per cent. on 'food -would be equal to 8 per cent. on two-thirds of the income of the working-class family. This again would be equal to rather more than 5 per cent. on the total incomei-being the equivalett of an Income Tax of is.

in the X. - But if we consider the case of an earned middle- class income of £2OO per annum, we know that the income Tax is only charged at 9d. in the X upon one- lfth of this total income. That-is, 'he actual burden on the earned middle-class income is a fraction under 2d. in the X. Thus we see that the 5 per cent. of food taxation would fall six times as oppressively on the working class as the present Income Tax falls on the earnings vf the middle class. Yet, as everyone is aware, the middle-cleks taxpayer regards the In6ome 'fax as very oppressive indeed. FROM THE MERCHANT'S STANDPOINT.
Lastly, let us take the broadest view, from the

stamlpoint of the merchants of wool goods in Brad- ford and in the West Riding, who employ so many workers as managers, packers, ,warehousemen, clerks, ;agents, and the like. The continued success of the industry depends upon its ability to supply every quality of wool products, in their countless variety, that may be demanded by customers at home or abroad, at the most economical prices possible. The Tariff Reform policy would infallibly increase work- ing expenses in every direction, whilst at the same time reducinc, the purchasing power of the home masses. 'Under Free Trade the industry holds its ,own in every market where the 'conditions are at all fair, and even in markets where the terms are almost }wohibitive. How long should we be able to make the same boast under the policy of Tariff Reform ? "sot for long," is the emphatic opinion of those best qualified to judge.
