div.head: PERJURY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: PERJURY AT ST. HELENS.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice Hamilton, Elizabeth Barrett (34) was charged with committing perjury at St. Helens, on October 2nd, 1968. Mr:Maxwell proeecuted,and Mr. H. Lindon Riley defended.—The prozecution alleged that during the bearing of a charge against prisoner in the St. Helens Police Court, under the Betting Act, she swore that a woman did not give her any money, and that no slips of paper passed between her snd a man or a boy. The defence was that the prisoner made the statements in the police court honestly believing them to to true. —The jury found the prisoner guilty,but recommended her to mercy on account of previous good character.— His Lordship, in sending accused to prison for one month in the second division, said the offence of which . she had teen convicted as not a grave one of its kind.
The Examiner, Saturday May 8, 1909.

div.head: bAN ON ROSTI-lEINE.
div.p: THE bAN ON ROSTI-lEINE.
EI3TINENT FICTURES AND IDANAGRAPHS FOR
THE PUBLIC.
the Mere.
THE MERE.
A fine sheet of water which the visitor is only allowed to view from a distance.
THE MANOR. Lord Egertoa's Ro-itherne _seat, which stands on high ground overlooking

whole of his villagers' profits on tea, cakes, and sandwiches in the form of rent. All he ha 4 to do was just to have raised the tenants' rents by nearly the amount which he calculated they made out of their hospitality. Had he done that he would have been well within his legal rights. No political economist of stand- ing would have dared to have wagged an admonitory finger at him, and some political economists would, on their own principles, have been compelled to render him a tribute of admiration and applause.

But Lord Egerton of Tatton is not that sort of man. He is content to go without the profits upon his villagers' trading so long as he can compel the folk of Manchester to go without their pleasant week-ends and to, keep their distance from his nobilitY.” Not only the people of Manchester, but the people of Warrington, of Runcorn, of Lymm4 of Knutsford, and many other towns feel that they possess rights—or at any rate privileges —in Rostherne which the Lord of the Manor proposes to ruthlessly trample upon. There is no licensed house in the village, and if his

_ lordship had let his prohibition rest here no one would have questioned either his rights or his discretion. But to ban all refreshment for man and woman, whether in the form of ginger-beer or the popular shilling tea, is a direct challenge to the touring,, nature-loving public. And it will certainly be taken up with spirit. Cyclists and picnickers of all descriptions have long looked upon Rostherne as a favourite resort, and if Lord Egerton's mandate is ruthlessly carried out they will practically be debarred from enjoying the rustic beauties of the place: Our own experi- ence of visits to Rostherne affords no evidence of either the rowdyness or vandalism of tourists which would justify the action of his Lordship. The class of visitors to Rostherne is of the opposite type to those whose objective on the half holiday is a country village with the chief essential—a commodious country " pub." It seems difficult to imagine that Lord Egerton has any more justification for his ban on catering than the purely selfish desire to keep Rostherne exclusive and free from the invasion of the common herd, how- ever well shepherded.
selfish view of matters which so closely effect the pleasures and privileges of the public.

Even last Saturday and Sunday the effect of the prohibition was evident in the largely increased number of visitors from all parts of Cheshire and Lancashire. They gathered in groups in various parts of the villages, they congregated in the churchyard, and they cast sour glances at the tree-hidden Manor as they discussed the situation. But there was no attempt at any demonstration such as is probable this week-end. Visitors applied at the cottages for refresh- ment but in vain: the poor tenants were unwilling to risk summary eviction. Only at the Mill Farm was there hospitality of the usual kind, and here the cyclists and others flocked in crowds.

If there is ,any consolation in the fact it is worth knowing that Rostherne is not alone in its inhospitable regulations. , Precisely the same practice obtains on the estate of Lord Chesham at Latimer, in Bucks, where it is an unpardonable sin for any villager to sell so much as a bottle of ginger-beer to a thirsty pedestrian. The unsuspecting traveller, therefore, who brings up at LatiMer on a hot summer afternoon in the expectation of refreshing the inner man has a rude awaken- ing in store for him, and is apt to use exceed- ingly strong language when the position of affairs is explained to him. For it is hardly necessary to add that not only are the cottagers forbidden to supply refreshments, but that there is no other means of obtaining any within miles. RIGHTS—AND OTHERWISE.

Those embittered admirers of Rostherne and its forbidden cottage teas who are threatening to go there in greater numbers than ever and vex Lord Egerton by taking their teas with them and consuming them on the highroad, must not forget, however, that though the public have a right of way over a highway, it belongs to the landowners on either side. If Lord Egerton owns the land on both sides of a Rostherne road, he owns the road too. The public have only the right of passing and re-passing along it; if they use it for any other purpose they are trespassing. Presumably it would not be trespass to halt for a brief space to devour a sandwich or a bun to sustain one on one's way, but neither would it be very enjoyable. A regular picnic might be a different matter, and especially a whole series of picnics obviously meant as a demonstration. But the trouble might develop into comedy if Lord Egerton endeavoured to exercise his rights over the road as well as the village !

There have been some curious trespass cases under this principle that the highway belongs, half and half, to the landowners on each side of it. In one case, tried in 1893. the land on both sides of ' a certain highway belonged to the Duke of Rutland. One day When the' Duke and his friends were shoot- ing over the moors someone, presumably from humanitarian motives, went on the highway for the express purpose of prevent- ing birds that were being driven towards the butts from crossing the highway. The- Duke's keepers- asked him to desist, and when he refused they held him on the ground until the drive was over. He brought an action fol- assault against the Duke and his keepers, but the Court of Appeal held that as he was using the highway for a purpose other than that of passing and repassing he was a trespasser and the assault was justified.
[Photos by .Tonlle, Latchford,

A QUESTION TO BE ASKED IN PARLIAMENT. The rights of the tenants as effected by Lord Egerton's harsh comthands are to be the subject of a 'question in the House of Commons on Monday. Mr. Levy Lever is to ask the President of the Local Government Board whether his attention has been called to a notice issued by the proprietor to the villagers.dh his estates at Rostherne,Ashley, and Mobberley, Cheshire, forbidding any cottagers to receive any person whatsoever in their cottages for the purpose of the sale or consumption of any refreshment under a penalty of instant notice to quit, and if he will consider the advisability of inserting a clause in the Housing Bill to give cottagers some security of tenure. LORD EGERTON INTERVIEWED. A fuller expression of his Lordship's views has been secured by a " Daily News" inter- viewer. To him his Lordship explained: "I have taken this action not without reflec- tion." Indeed, it is the outcome of several years' consideration of all the circumstances: I have taken this step on two grounds, namely, moral and sanitary. I regret it, but I have been forced to do so after warning the people. Not only on Saturdays but on Mondays there is a certain rowdy element in the place, from which the villagers ought to be protected. I have not the slightest desire to stop peaceful, healthy-minded persons from visiting Rostherne or any por- tion of the estate which is open to the public, but from my own observation and that of others it is, I think, time that a certain class of people should be discouraged. "I• speak from experience, and on one occasion Lady Egerton herself was pelted with apples. I find myself in the position of many other landlords in England who have had a similar experience to my own." In the same newspaper of the following day, (Thursday) Lord Egerton writes as follows : Sir,—l have read your paragraph record- ing your representative's interview, and I beg to thank you for the careful manner in which my few remarks have been put in. I was not able to give him many other inci- dents, which could not be put into print, but which if you were aWare of would lead you to agree with me in the course I have been compelled to take. There is an excellent public-house, the Swan, with good. garden, and also the Nag's Head, both within a mile of the village, and a village shop where tem- perance drinks are also sold.—Youre etc., EGERTON OF TATTON. 9, Seamore-place, Mayfair, W., May 5. From the above the conclusion is obvious that Egerton of Tatton has, so far, enter- tained no idea: of recanting. The " Swan " and the ," Nag's Head" may be excellent hostelries but they are not in Rostherne, and moreover most visitors to the village prefer cottage comforts and catering. Having been Warned off they will assuredly come on in greater numbers. The Manor itself would hardly be adequate to accommodate the crowds of tea-demanding tourists whom we can mentally see wending their way to rustic Rostherne in the near future. But being modest we will refrain from asking that the Manor should be devoted to any such utilitarian purpose as long as His Lord- ship deigns to occasionally reside there. Rostherne as a rendezvous and tea for the tourist is the sole -demand of the moment. We give Lord Egerton of Tatton a month in which to discover that the line of least resistance tends to climbing down.
THE VILLAGE POST OFFICE, largely patronised for lemonade and picture post-cards.
THE CHURCH, Wnich commands an extensive view of Mere, Manor and woodland,

div.head: EARL AND HIS EDICT.
div.p: THE EARL AND HIS EDICT.

It is only in the course of the last few years that the gentleman now known and respected as the Earl of Egerton has become in any degree famous, but at present he is enjoying (?) a notoriety which has spread over the length and breadth of the land. To what giddy pinnacle he may eventually climb we will not attempt to prophesy. Briefly stated the milestones in his career,so far as vie know_ it, are as follows. In 1906 as the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton he played an unwilling part in the Tory rout in Cheshire, Mr. A. J. King, M.P. administering the coup de. grace in the Knutsford Division. The Honorable gentleman might have sub- sided quietly after this event, but for a feel- ing that he must explain the defeat to his own satisfaction. He therefore informed the public that "The reasons which have brought about my defeat are Ananias per- vading the whole constituency,and the action of traitors to the Unionist cause." This little speech has become historic and may in course of time be included in the text-books ' for the guidance of Unionist politicians when placed in trying and unhappy circumstances. The next , achievement of the Honorable gentleman was to succeed to the family title of Lord Egerton of Tatton, which we believe he did with the utmost grace and pro- priety. Since then his vaulting .ambitioli has -led him to achieve greatness -without waiting for a possibly unwilling public to thrust it upon him. None but a " great " man, an over-lord typical of the middle ages, would have risen to the height indicated by the notice which his Lordship has recently issued to the tremblingcottagers,ofßostherne, which rustic beauty-spot has the honour to form part of the Egerton estate. The afore- said notice reads as follows : Lord Egerton of 'Eaton will not permit any cottsgers to receive filly person whatever into their cottages for the purpose of the sale or con- sumption Of any refreshment. Any cottager infringing this rule will get instant notice to quit. After reading this notice you will return it signed, as an acknowledgment of your agreeing: —I agree to abide by the regulations contained in this notice. There it is in all its wonder; a document which, let us hope,will be carefully preserved in the British Museum and the Public Libraries for the instruction and interest of future students of Twentieth Century social life in England.

div.head: PUBLIC AND THE BAN.
div.p: THE PUBLIC AND THE BAN.

Though the cottagers of Rostheme are practically helpless and will doubtless have to obey the lordly edict, they are none the less restive and dissatisfied. They stand to lose substantially in those material things which make up the comfort of life, for the providing of teas to Rostherne's many hundred visitors has brought in revenue which, in many cases, has doubled the ordinary weekly income of the household and provided for many a rainy and unprofit- able, winter day. However, the dwellers in Rostherne's rose and ivy-clad cottages ,have orders to forego these legitimate profits or "quit "—as Lord Egerton puts it in his forcible feudal fashion.
" Hubert " of the "Sunday Chronicle" has waxed sarcastic at His Lordship's expense and thus discusses the question :
"Now, if Lord Egerton of Tatton had been merely a needy or a greedy landowner he might have added quite a nice little sum to his income by shaving off nearly the

div.head: PROTECTION AND RETALIATION.
div.p: PROTECTION AND RETALIATION.

The great " 8.F." has no intention, how- ever, of sitting at home and submitting. There will probably be more people in Rostherne to-day—and every succeeding Saturday during the summer—than there ever were before, and they will clamour for reasonable refreshment till they get it, or line the road side with impromptu picnic parties. This will not tend to make Rostherne any more select and we imagine that at no very distant date the status quo ante benzin' will be restored. To-day will see a huge gathering of cyclists and motorists in the village with the object of making a protest—a decent and dignified protest—against the Earl's ban.

"We don't want violence or violent speeches," writes one correspondent, "We want, on the other hand, to show Lord Egerton that a large body of people can be as reasonable and as well-behaved as any of his lordship's friends. We have got to uphold the credit of visitors to Rostherne— that is our business."
We hope Warrington will " send its quota to swell the ranks and help Lord Egerton to take a less narrow and

Sir,—There is ample evidence in Mr. Parker's paper that he desired to continue a social system wherein "competition would be an important factor." But Nfr. Parker seems to have fallen int-) the error of mis- using or confusing terms. The elimination of c ira- petition is an impossibility. What Mr. Parker wants is the retention of, the competitive system. But competition and competitive system are not always synonymous. What Socialis n aims at is the eviction of competing capitals and the associat'ion of competition. When Mr. Parker advocates a system of earnpeting capitals with certain modifying factors, he is simply repeating the position of present-day Liberalism, and exemplifies the distance that Liberalism has travelled from the laissez-faire of the Manche-ter school. As Mr. Parker favours the continuance of the system of the private ownership of capital and would' support the restriction and control of the effects of the competition which this system resu'As in, be has to s'iow how this is to be.effected, unless "the State is to take possession of a surplus and.diatribute t) those in need " ? The inequality in arNalth distribution is Caused by the economic dominance of a class. , This dominance is due t ptivate capitalism. How does Ntr. Parker propose t ) abrogate the power of private capitalism and yet maintain sufficient incentive to the accumulation, of capital by private individuals? Mr. Parker denies that capital is a monopoly, and asserts that it is questionable whether it can ever become -ta monopoly. .It is sufficient, I consider for the pirpose of this diBcu3sion, to show that capital is the monoply of a class. Mr. Chiozza Money asserts as an understatement of the actual facts that one-seventieth part of the popula- tion owns far more than one-half of the-entire wealth public and private of the United Kingdom. He further states that the monopoly of capital is a far more far-reaching thing than the monopoly of land, and it
The Examiner, Saturday, May 8 1909.

capital, whether land or the implements of production, weighed heavily against those who had not and the same applies to-day. The problem facing us is how to equalis3 these inequalities and neutralise the injustices created by these elements. Mr.. Parker. believes in a system that would supply, crutches to the crippled and 1 believe in a system that would eliminate the necessity fur clutches. The. case fir land naturalisation Mr. Parker believes to be unanswerable. With the men poly in land eliminated Mr. Parker would then proceed to build his Utopia. Competition in industry with fairer rules would be the regimio And 1 personally deubt if the conditions of labour would then be improved. Supposing wd had relaxed the :hold of the landlord, would the people generally receive the money previously paid in rent? I trow not. The possessors of the Malts of production control the pi ices we pay for goods produced, and they would soon manipulate prices in order to get tte aforesaid tent. Let us see what Leti teach us. In matters of social legi-lation Germany is far ahead of us. Railways and canals are natiooalised ; they have State forests ; Royalties on minerals are State approptiated ; they have sick and old age pensions ; an income •tax of se. in the psued for incomes over about £l,OOO per year ; a good many municipalities own the land their towns are built upon. All thee things are steps in the right direction and might be what Mr. Parker would term moralizing economic relations. So far as I can judge. with the exception of all the land being collective property, Mr. Parker's progressive legislation Would not extend much farther than these beneficial things. As good as they are they have been insufficient to touch the hinge of Germany's poverty and social problems. At least there is a great volume of opinion tending in that direction, for we have in Germany a party- Of great magnitude which favours the extension of public ownership to all the means of production. What puzzles me is where does Mr. Parker believe public •ownership cemes to .be beneficial and becomes detrimental? Unlimited thought by myself fails to , find the line of demarcation. Ruskin favoured Government, which I prefer to call public or collective, alongside private production. It was his belief it would moralise private production. If collective production is good in some things; then Collective production Should be extended to its maximum possibilities. Ido not doubt the beneficial nature of such legislation as Mr. Parker favours, but what seems to be good in part seems also geed in whole. I • believe in the *hole nseans of production being used for the benefit of all, and do not see the necessity for any modification of that ptinciple. Production for private profit necessarily clashes with the public welfare, and public welfare must necessarily be a second consideration so , long as it exists. We may trust a lot to private enter- prise but we cannot allow it to juggle with society's welfare. If the Warrington people can supply and purify their own water in their works by themselves in their collective capacity, why cannot they do the same with other liquids such as milk and beer? If we can produce our owa gas in our own works why cannot we extend the principle and supply out selves with the coal that gas is extracted from? To say that the absence of competition deadens individual activities is a large statement. Competition has not developed the boat in the individual's activities. It hks develcped the cunning and appealed to the lowest elements in man's nature. It has not given the best and most capable men their rightful positi ins in society. If the•best men should have been thestuccess- ful ones they have not received their prize, that is the honour and tru,t of their fellows. To the mass of the people production for private profit has condemned them to toil and conditions of life which has crushed the individuality out of them. The workers at present are only used to connect one machine with another. Instead of a nation of servile, sycophants Socialism would give us a nation of healthy, independent men and women with a voice as to how their country's affairs shall be managed. I often imagine some of our indi% idualist friends who detest the word Socialism. Tlerey talk about the freedom of the individual and the restriction that Socialism would place upon him I may say here that John Stuart Mill defined liberty as "the libeity to do as you like in so far as you do not interfere with the liberty of others." The indivi- duslist talks about the State doing this and doing that. He imagines the State to be the Muse of Lords and Commons and its officials. What the Socialist call the State is the people. He talks about Socials n to his friends in a condemnatory tone and returns home. As soon as he passes into his house he becomes a Communis:t, a stage further than the Socialistic doctrine. Inside his house the strong take care of the weak. Inside the home each contributes according to his ability and takes according t 3 his need. And which oae of us will say that family life suffers from deadened activities? Socialism would put material care from where it ought never to have risen - under our feet. The people's mieds released from perpetual anxiety would seek new occupations and would revel in those things which have been so long locked away from them, literature, music and att. rts soon as the people become more enlightened a new code of morals would spring into existence. The people understanding the relation of the individual to economics would act in a way t 3 better economic eonditious, and this if we only take into consideration the lowest element in man, self preservation. But whether we call ourselves Socialists or not makes little difference to its progress. .Socialism is a force to be reckoned with. It s an evolutionary force that is irresisti i ble. Public opinion may hasten its progress, but passive disinterest will not stop it. Whether the Liberal or Tory party be in power it will march steadily onwards, as witness the recotn- mondation of a Royal Commission for State afforesta- tion. But whatever our views on economic questions and differences in our ways of achieving better social conditions, do not let us make them into means of mental recreations and opportunities for displaying verbal gymnastics.—Yours, etc., LABOR (AMA. VINCIT.

secures - for a number of people almost as limittivi as the .great landowning • class, a gross profit com- pared with which the S!1111 of British land rents is insignificant. Further, taking Mr. Parker's definition of capital as " labour swed in material things," as , long as there is a p: actical iii nopoly of material things, it inevitably follows that there must be -a ' practical monopoly of the capital. And the trend of industrial development towards greater concentration and wider organisation, will make capital more of a MOnopoly. Mr. Parker raises the question of the right to the whole product of labour. Vandervelde sa3s that to seek the share of ir.dividual labour in a social pro- duct is, in the vast majority of cases, to want to find a needle in a haystack. "Individual labour" said llodbertus." is, in great part, fruitful only by co-operation. How should that -which he has not created be restored to the individual? The collectivity whose united effort alone renders the results useful, has its right to a part of the social product, a part which will not be divided:" The question involves such a number of considerations that 1 contend that it is impracticable to appraise the value of individual labour. It is sufficient to postulate that under Socialism, the workers would receive their share of the product after the preliminary deduction for the purpose of organisation and administration. Mr. Parker's propositions appear to illustrate the difficulty of those reformers who would apply pallia- tives only. Mr. Parker would bring about a better state of things without causing a fundamental change in the structure of society. Socialism on the other hand affirms that short of an organic change, correct- ing the basal error of private ownership of capital, the fruits of this error will largely remain. Mr. Parker says it is for opponents of the present system to prove it to incapable cf providing the conditions out of which the just recompense will naturally be given. I assert that as long as you allow the economic domination of one class by another, by permitting the ivate ownership of capital, so long will you prevent the existence of those conditions. The root evil is private competing capitals engaged in production for moth. The present system is therefore incapable of giving just recompense. Short of nationalising the means of production, what remedy does Mr. Parker propose? How far would be modify the determining factor in our economic relations, the ownership by ' private individuals of industrial capital ? Mr Parker seems to object to the State control of our industrial system. He seems to project the State of to-day to the future, when Collectivism will be es'ablished.

But I suggest tint the Sate will then be different from wliat it is tc-day. The funeti)us of the State are cintinually changing, ,is duties are becoming more varied, extensive and paternal, its intetference in social relations is increasing ; and these will ultimately change its character, until the State will become what the Socialist means it to become, " the organ of the eolleetfre w:11." (Vandervelde). "The aiministrative State will be nothing less than the totality of the functions and organs having as its object to secure the greatest pro- duction and the most just distribution." (Vander-

velde). In conclusion I would repeat what I said in my former letter that the great problem for those social reformers who are opposed to a fundamental change in our industrill relatims is to deal effectively with a state of things involving such antagonism of interests without an organizAtion that would essentially effect the cause of it. _ .

A greater problem seems to bs thei;s than that of Socialism. For, whilst aiming at an adjustment of on: swi 11 relations, so as to eliminate pfiverty and other evils of our present system, they would yet retain that element of competing capitals, which issues in such wide and complex ramifications ; whilst Socialis.n by abolishing competing carita!s, would simplify the problem by removing these complicating facts. DEMOCRAT. Apr:l 25th, 1009.

div.head: Moralization of• Economic Relations. Criticisms cf Mr. Parker's Paper.
div.p: The Moralization of• Economic Relations. Criticisms cf Mr. Parker's Paper.
TO TIIE EDITOR OF TIIE EXAMINER."I

Sir,—l read with interest the paper of which Mr. Parker asked me to give my "candid opinion." The opening portion of it agree with heal tily ; that all the activities, powers, labours and possibilities of a, community of people should be directed t 6 ensure the well-being, development and perpetuation of that people, and, the means employed to that end should be usest with the object of attaining the result desired, All obstacles barring the way should be moved or circumnavigated. Wealth production should not be the end, but only the means to an end, the end being a healthy, happy, contented people; a people with the potentialities viithin them developed to the highest possible state of development; a people whose appearance tells the observer of material comfort, whose actions speak of moral healthiness. Thsse conditions have been the ideals of many of our teachers and thinkers. Ruskin spent his life in trying to inculcate this fact into people's minds,and I think it no contraversion of facts to say the Socialists to-day are reminding us of this much ignored purpose of life. If this be accepted, then, the present mode of procedure in our manner of attaining that end stands condemned by results. The present possibilities to achieve that end were never greater. Look at any sphere of life—animal,vegetable, plant or savage,and compare with conditions obtaining in this country which perhaps is most advanced in the production of things which should have been the medium through which the " dreamer's dreams" should have become realities. If we look at what is paradoxically termed the lowest species of man, the savage, in what way does he differ from the so-called civilised man? ' We have substantial authority that physically he is far ahead of "civilisad" peoples. When this fact is brought to my notice my mind always conjures up an illustration I once saw in a well-known magazine of a piimitive inhabitant of these islands. If this illustra- tion-be correct, anh the object lesson shown typical of the men living then, I wish I bad been fortunate enough to live in those days. He was represented walk ing over reeky ground armed with weapons the appear- ance of which gave me the impression they were used to catch and kill animals required for con- sumption as food. If this man was an example of his type, we are retrogressive and not progressive. Scantily clad he depicted a perfect specimen of physical energy, muscular development and healthy manhood. That this was a true condition of things is supported by the robust physique of some of the tribes who to-day live under prinai ive conditions. And from this picture my mind is switched upon some of the things I see to-day, Where is the robust- ness of the primitive man now? I look around and notice the physique of the people in these "enlightened "days. I have no need to give figures upon this point ; anyone with eyes can see •it for themselves. But if' anyone does doubt the physical degeneracy in our midst I would refer them to the army recruiting returns. A. people not possessing physical soundness is degenerate whatever progress it has made in inventing methods ,of wealth production, and the degree of physical power possessed by a nation is the foundation of its,success or failure. To attain phs sical health certain things are essential. Physical health depends chiefly upon material things obtained and the way they are used. Such things as food, clothing, shelter stc„ being the essentials. The point to be discussed at preient is the way these things are produced and distributed. Food, clothing; &c., are produced by labour power from the land, directly and indirectly. The methods of production have passed through various stages. At one • period we had a state of almost complete individualsm out- side the family. Each family used to produce what was necessary for themselves by themselves. Tshey used to grow their own food stuffs, make their shoes, spin their own cloth &s. By and by this method gradually disappeared and new methods presented themselves.

The power we possess to produce wealth to-day may be judged from the statement made by Mr. Atkinson, a well-known American statistician. Be says that to-day' Four men can produce bread for a thousand. With the best machinery one workman can produce cotton cloth for 250 people, woollen for 300, and boots and shoes for a 1,000 -people." In what I will call the days of. individn dist production the implements of production necessarily belonged to the individuals using them. The land was almost common and Professor Thorold Rogers says they lived in comparative comfort. By the introdustion of motive power, production became collective. But the means of produstion remained individually owned. At first the ownership and managemont was individnal with freedom to compete openly hr the production and supply of the public demands. At present we are living at a time which the future generations might date as the line of demarkation between com- _panies and combines or trusts, and it is admitted on all sides that so far from supplying the material needs of the people our mode of prsduction and distribution is a failure and there is undoubtedly a cinsi•lerable .volume of opinion in favour of a change to obviate the anomalies of great power te produce wealth along- side the great necessity of wealth producers. But there is disagreement as to which is the right course to take. One section favours modificatioa of our present system and another system represents the opinion that a• complete change is necessary and it might be stated that Mr. Parker represents the soction favouring modification and I will take it upon myself to represent the opinion of a complete change. The outssanding feature of our industrial evolution is the tendency to co-operate. From the formation of tribal commumties to the present highly ceatralised state there has been a gradual growth of co-operative effort. Every trile in thegreat morels of evolution has been a stride away from individualism to co-operation and the present power to produce wealth has embodied in it the labour of millions of our ancestors. Present day society has been made by the co-operation of its units. Without co operation our enormous power to produce 99 much would have been impossible. Society is an organism, whether some of us call our selves indivialualis's or not. A stoppage, a shortage, a hitch .of any kind throws out of gear other portions of the whole. A shortige of cotton in India affects Lancashire, a corner of wheat in America affects England in general an iso on. Competition is gradu- ally being eliminated, and whatsoever its purpose has been its services are being cl:spensed with. Com- petition means disorder. Competition may well be illustrated by a scramble for nuts by children. Bringing it down to sterner realism and applying it to industry it is a scramble for bread. Unrestricted. competition has been found to be an impossibility, as admitted by those favouring it in some form. The collective conscience of the people as represented by the Houses of Parliament has been compelled to modify its operations. The advantages of the possessor of

div.head: Temparance and Employmont.
div.p: Temparance and Employmont.

Sir,—My intention in my previous letter was not to aid Mr. Parker, but to give my unprejudiced opinion on the correspondence. As to the expression " help- ing lame friends over stiles " -I was not aware that Socialists were averse to persons helping one another especially, when one is supposed to be lame. I do not think, however,- that Mr. Parker's letters have been lame ones at all, for he has stuck to the question " Temperance and Employment" while " L.Q.V." and " Democrat " have brought another and larger question into the correspondence, thereby hoping to hide their discomfiture.

The fact that J.C.W. has thought I Ares an ally of Mr. Parker's proves what I said m my last letter, that Socialists, while condemning all other schemes for Social Reform, greatly resent even the mildest criti- cism of their own schemes and methods. If J.t .W. had read my last letter closely, he would have had no need for asking his first question, since I stated that Mr. Parker must admit that if the Liquor Traffic were nationalized, such cases as that of Tom "Jones would become rare." A trade which contributes to a large extent the inmates of our prisons-, workhouses and asylums, would be better for being under State control.

His retort that if the Brotherhood were a fact Socialism would be unnecessary, is a conannation of my statement that it would only be practicable when that grate was a fact, as Socialism would have achieved its ultimate aim and would find the "nationalization of everything" practicable but unnecessary.

All Social Reformers see that the problem does not rest at the bottom of a glass of poisoned water, but Socialists would be well advised to encourage and not discourage attempts to eliminate its power for evil. J.C.W. will no doubt be aware that if the Factory and Truck Acts were strictly enforced the insanitary conditions of labour *would greatly disappear. He will also acknowledge that Factory inspectors are, so to speak, nationalised.' Well what I mutt to know is this : If they are under the Govermnent and thus have power to enforce these Acts, why is it that these conditions exist? They are employed by the nation so can have no cause to fear the enmity of unscrupulous employers by enforcing the Acts, and if t overnment employes of to-day neglect their duties to such an extent, what will be the case when the number of such employes is increased by the " nationalization of everything." Socialists say " Abolish the whole system which allows men to oppress their fellows, and establish a system based upon justice instead of injustice, love instead of hate, which is equivalent to saying that employers and their work-People of to-day •hate one another.

If J.C.W. were to visit Port Sunlight or Bournville and tell the residents and employees that they were hated by their employers, they were wage slaves.,' victims of an " unjust system " by which their masters were " grinding them down to the lowest depths in order that they could put their goods on the- markets at a lower price than other • competitors ;'' the workpeople if they did not get indignant would, I fancy take him to be some new type of humorist. Further the "housing question" and "insanitary conditions of labour" are not very prominent in these villages, and the prowerity and trade of the tinns give a direct contradition to the statement that "it is not the man who would act honestly towards his fellows who leads the way under our present social system, but the mean. unscrupulous man and the sweater." _ _ _
The above proves that it is not the system which is at fault since it is possible to have justice awl love even where the Mations of master and workmen exist. —Yours &c. • 11. S.
Penketli, May stli, 19)9.

div.head: MR. M. G. HEARNE'S PROMOTION.
div.p: MR. M. G. HEARNE'S PROMOTION.
Presentation from the Nationalists.

On Tuesday Mr. M. G. Hearne, the leader of the Nationalist Party in the Local 'Parliament was pre— sented by fellow-members of the party with the works of Charle., Dickens in 22 volumes and Morley's Lao of Gladstone in two volumes. The inscription in the: books was as follows:

To M. G. Hearne, Esq. (Kilkenny City) Leader of the Irish Nationalist Party in thee Warrington Parlimentary Debating Society, Session, 1908-1909. From his fellow members of the party as a. token of regard, esteem and friendship and a slight acknowledgement of his able and successfulleadership." Then followed the names and constituencies of du) Loners.

The occasion of the presentation was Mr. Heame's departure from 'Warrington to tale up an important position in the Inland Revenue at Dundalk. Mr. Hearne first came to Warrington in 1895. 600 n after -coming he joined St. Mary's Amateur Drainage Society as secretary, with the one object in view— that of rendering service to local charities. The success of the society and the signal assistance it gave to the Indian Famine Fund, and on various occasions to the Nursing Association was largely dim to the untiring zeal and devotion of Mr. Hearne. Love of Rowers led him to be one of the first members of the Stockton Heath.% Garden Society,and he won the first prize for the best-kept front and back gardens. Kindness to animals was a distinguishing trait in his character, and as an anti-vaccinator he had a share in dispelling some magisterial prejudices on the ques- tion of vaccination. He was one of the most highly respected and valuable members of the Young Men's Catholic Society, and in 1907-08 acted as adjudicator for the debating-team in their contests with various Liverpool societies. For some time he was financial secretary to the Society, and won golden opinions whilst in office. He was also the Catholic representa- tive in the Civic League of Help. During his fourteen years in Warrington Mr. Hearne made a host of *friends by his kindly, sympathetic manner, unfailing courtesy, and absolute sincerity, arid whilst they regret his departure they congratulate him upon his well-earned promotion, and wish him success and happiness in his new sphere of labour.

div.p: Small Holdings Inquiry.

Sir,—A Special Commissioner ha; been appointed under the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries to hold inquiries in districts throughout the country from which applications for Small Holdings have been forth- coming, so as to enable the person concerned to give the Commissioner, in private, information as to their applications. As much dissatisfaction exists in many districts with the administration of the Small Holdings Act, I trust that all persons who have applied for Small Holdings will take advantage of the opportunity offered, and give the Special Commissioner every information regarding their applications. I have ascertained from the Commissioner that he will be willing to interview persons who have not made application hitherto, but desire to do so, and I shall be glad to hear from all who have made or who desire to make application under the Small Holdings Act.—Faithfully yours,

div.head: Church Decline.
div.p: Church Decline.

Sir, The returns presented at the annual Baptist Assembly of church membership etc. do not afford pleasant reading to those concerned. A serious decline is represented all round,and as the Wesleyan body also report a decrease in membership there must be some- thing somewhere which people do not find favour with, in connection with the churches. Years ago a matter of this kind would be viewed with grave misgivings but I suppose nowadays it is taken as a matter of course. The fact has to be faced, willy nilly, that a considerable number of the population do not care a rap for organised religion. An example of the trend of events is found in a suggestion published in a well-known public journal recently by gentleman in the Liverpool district inviting readers' who do not care for Church going nOr Socialist meet- ings on Sundays to join with him in having literary evenings, &c. Another opposition line to the Churches, In the midst of all this Mr. Campbell seems to be going well ride his recent declaration : "The CitY Temple has had a large influx of new life consisting in no small degree of men of culture and independence of character who had given up organised Christianity as hopeless." Where will it all end one wonders ?In our own town of Watirington quite two-thirds of the population are outside the pale of the church. Sunday morning public worship is in a dismal condition. The rising generation do not take kindly to Church attend- ance and this bodes ill for the future, from the church standpoint, it is something in the nature of an " achievement "for the rising generation to attend public worship once in six weeks. Perhaps a remedy may be provided by the churches themselves as they are so very much concerned in the matter.--Yours,&e., PROGRESS,

div.head: "Nonconformity and Politics."
div.p: "Nonconformity and Politics."
A Reply to the Rev. J. E. Rattenbury.

Sir,—l have just read the report of the address of the Rev. J. E. Rattenbury on " Nonconformity and Politics," in the "Examiner " of the 24th ult. It is ; to me an amazing deliverance, and the negation of the spirit and method of Jesus Christ. Political action had no place in the armoury of our Lord. His appeal. was to the reason and conscience, and this, in com- bination with the moral majesty of His personality, His self-immolation and deathful tragedy upon the Cross of Calvary, made his message to men efficacious in winning them to righteousness. It seems to me a pity that if we are unable or unwilling to rise to the height of His *moral grandeur and self-sacrifice, we shotild, ,by implication, drag Him down to our Thvel,- or put into His hand an instrument of which he was entirely independent. It is not a question of using a particular political party to -accomplish.the work of Jesus Christ, but of using any party at all. Mr. Rattenbury says "The Free Church Council would use any party to promote the kingdom of God. This is precisely the point at issue, and it is this that is con- trary to the spirit and genius of the Gospel. Mr. Rattenbury reminds us of the events of the 17th century, and says that " Non- conformity had something. to do with politics in the time of Oliver Cromwell, and that in those days the Church used the political instrument for political ends. .They cut off the head of Charles 1., and it was one of the best things that happened in this country. If the Church of Christ were in earnest to-day it would do away with tyrannies just as it did then." One is almost tempted to conclude that Mr. Rattenbury is speaking in the name of Rome, whose weapon is avowedly that of force in one or other of its forms. But I have always thought that in the furtherance of their objects it has been the proud prerogative of the Free Churches to dispense with the secular power, and strong in their inherent spirituality, allow the Roman Catholic. Church a monopoly of the claim to use the machinery of Government to accomplish her purposes. But it appears that this is not so. But if not, and if we may Claim to use the machinery of Government to accomplish our ends, can we, with any reason, refuse to accord Rome the same privilege? I think not.. And in relying upon political action to do our work for us, we are revealing a moral and spiritual decrepitude which is somewhat ominous. But apart. from this, I am thoroughly convinced that political action is powerless to effect. the ends we have in view as churches. And this is very forcibly pointed out by Mr. J. R. Green in us" Short History of the English People," in which be says : The Restoration brought Charles to Whitehall; and in an instant the whole face of England was changed. All that was noblest and best in Puritanism was whirled away with its pettiness and its tyranny in the current of the nation's hate. Religion had been turned into a system of political and social oppression, and it fell with their fall.

This is a warning to us to-day that in so far as reforms rest on the basis of external authority, and not on the moral consent of the people they will not be of a permanent nature. Men's minds and hearts must first be changed, and when this is done, the House of Lords will oblige Us. But as long as the House of Lords reflects the mind of the people in moral questions, it will remain invulnerable, and all the frothy talk about sweeping away. tyrannies and chopping off the heads of kings, be of no avail. As a contrast to the results of political methods. allow me to quote again from Green's "Short History of the English PeoWe," as illustrative of the results of a purely ethical and spiritual movement. After pointing out the terribly immoral conditions of both the higher and lower classes about the middle of the 18th century he goes on to say, "In 'spite, however, of scenes such as this, England remained at heart religious. In the middle d. classes t htmeh leuondsl i,dat whsPmeausnrwi hns still h,paeritari ihadyrlgai ievnneddai appeared ad saroul eientdiicachl aa as sgoneen .omfot.rae DI see en. and whose power was seen in the disappearance of the profligacy which had disgraced the upper classes and the foulness which had infested litera- ture, ever since the restoration. A yet nobler result of the religious revival was the steady attempt which has never ceased from that day to this, to remedy tbe guilt, the ivorance, the physical suffering, the social degradation of the profligate and the poor. It was not till the Wesleyan impulse bad done its work that this philanthropic impulse began, etc." And what is equally striking is the fact that it was , not until after this religious revival had had time to make itself felt that the civil and religious disabilities under which our forefathers suffered were removed. Here we have first the moral and spiritual dynamic, and then, as the natural outcome of it, the after-math of "all other things." And it is .this moral and spiritual dynamic that we need to-day, not the frantic appeal to the secular power. I am not. disparaging the work of the political reformer, or despising the

div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAY BTH, 1909.
For an adequate appre- TAD T P REFORM ciation of Mr. LLOYD-

AS AN GEORGE'S Budget, it is ALTERNATIVE, necessary to review it steadily as an t alterna- ri\ve to a Tariff Reform Budget. The "I'Pesition critics have studiously turned their heads away from this point of W. There is in .their speeches no of recognition that the new taxes -re the result of circumstances which Would place the same compulsion on a c'uservative Government, to impose fresh taxation. They prefer to talk as if the tq-,°vment was piling up duties for ," mere fun of making people uncom- 412rtable. No one would imagine, to hear the . OPposition Bench speakers now, that i;,".ST a few weeks ago they were denouncing iT,Government for not rushing into blind- expenditure on "Dreadnoughts" without ,-I,`j inquiry whether the type of the new would be obsolete before they were -.43luPleted, or that the amendments of the Age Pension Bill which they pressed Cad°ll a Liberal Chancellor of the Exchequer to be rejected on grounds of economy. ill:lresently there will come a fiscal debate, then We may, as Mr. SYDNEY BUXTON I;ggestel on Monday, hear something of the in which the Next Conservative -7171ment would propose to solve the frrn°l4lem which Mr. LLOYD GEORGE has con- But probably we shall not, for when t;`, wIAM ROBSON began to approach this r LLI ee, evidently an uneasy one for the 'Siti)°,Bition, a futile appeal was made to the draKer to rule it out of order. "We are tiasre,ll;ssing," the Attorney-General said, to the Opposition, "not one Budget, two—your Budget and ours." The to'Aetichnents of the Old Age Pensions Act the I,Nvilieb the Opposition have committed :selves, together with their demands "11 accelerated shipbuilding programme, twe Illd raise the deficit from sixteen to therleight millions at one stroke. But lin- '0 Per cent, duty upon manufactured ctliPorts, Proposed by Tariff Reformers, would taxesodUCe twelve millions, and the food- of d- Itrof Mr. CHAWBERLAIN'S programme „iallirld only Produce eight millions. That e 4.8 a total of twenty millions. From source would the tariff Reformers Pose to obtain the balance? They talk about elasticity of revenue. Would ir food-taxes, the Attorney-General thg_tlired,he elastic? A neater or more deadly ,trust has seldom been made in debate. qrtolle Principles upon which Mr. LLOYD- hasIt constructed his Free Trade ,-tar`t.get, and the principles upon which a ,„11fr Reform Chancellor of the Exchequer ppose eonstr tare diametrically uc his Budget, ing the u* This Budget refrains from touch-, Ileeessaries of life; the Tariff Reform hea_g.et would tax food. This Budget lays the -the vie,st burden on the broadest shoulders; Voilli),°°rer a family, the more grievously ilefc:u it feel the Oppression of the Tariff iivoidrin Budget. This Budget sedulously to 6 the risk of causing any ernbarassment taillii,(l,llstrY and Comm6rce—(if the new Rehht :'."lltY.should appear to interfere with "\ae. transa,ctions in istocks and shares, it cl;(1 )' vithout much loss be modified or 13, PPed, but . is probably more than -the t'u, to the stock, ,t xcharip, by 171ouste,Ine'vl. of the unfair advantage.re- larifi'7,-, tefoenjoYed,..l43` !..,r,riUoket.-shoiss xtditi. , • ..• - Budget, • 'in its taxes up-On

manufactured imports, would sweep into its net the raw materials of many important industries, and work them incalculable injury. This Budget bears plainly on its face the promise of a larger yield in the future from the taxes which it imposes, so much so that the Opposition have been criticising Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE'S estimate of this year's revenue, though he can only obtain during 1909-10 a fraction, and in some cases nothings of the harvest which the new imposts will eventually produce. But a Protectionist Budget imposes taxes the yield of which continually diminishes •as they fulfil the object for which they are primarily imposed—that is, not as the taxes of sound finance, to bring in revenue, but to exclude the commodities which produce that revenue. Stripped of details, and with minor features disregalded, Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE'S Budget is seen to rely mainly upon a revision of the death duties, a super-tax upon very large incomes, the claiming for the State of some share in the unearned increment which ground-landlords enjoy through the expendi- ture of rates that they themselves do not pay, the demand from the owners of licences of a larger contribution to the State in return for the immensely valuable monopoly which has been granted to them for a ridiculously slight consideration, and increased duties upon such luxuries as spirits and tobacco. Any new imposition of taxes is 'felt as a grievance by those upon whom it is placed. Human nature would have to change its character if it were not so. But when the inevitableness of increased taxation has been recognised, is it possible to point to other means which might be employed so as to raise the amount required with greater fairness and less inconvenience to those upon whom the new imposts fall? Lord LANSDOWNE alone of Opposition critics has ventured to indicate the means which he would prefer. He blames the recklessness with which the Government 'last year reduced the sugar duty. It needed a typical aristocrat's sublime indifference to commer- cial interests and social conditions to single out an article so widely used in an infinite number of industrial processes and so integral a factor in the diet of the poor as the most suitable victim. It is true that Tariff Reformers implicitly, by the very nature of their programme, demand the taxation of bread rather than whisky and tobacco, but they dare not explicitly state such a case.
Thanks in the main HOWARD PLACE. to _ the pertinacity of

Alderman Bennett— and to the active support of the press which, as he says so kindly and truly represents freqtently, if not always, the enlightened sense of the community "—Howard Place is saved from the threatened erection of a public convenience in its centre. The Council frequently shows signs of restive- ness when resolutions accepted or rejected at one meeting, bob up again complacently at the next. But there was never more justifi- cation for a return to the attack than in this particular instance. The Sani- tary Committee's insanitary and pre- posterous proposal was only carried by a majority of one vote at the meetng a month ago, and the interval has increased rather than lessened the number and determination of the .objectors. How needful was a reconsideration of the whole question is evidenced by the voting on Tuesday when the Co_uncil decided by 16 votes to 10 to rescind the previous resolution. Next time the Council creates an open space and dedicates it to the use of the public and the memory of some distinguished man, we hope even the Sanitary Committee will have risen to a true appreciation of the eternal fitness of things.

Lord Egerton of THE ROSTHERNE Tatton's ban on BAN. Rostherne continues to be the sensation of the day. Public interest and anger have waxed rather than waned, and if the fine weather lasts over to-day, Rostherne will be the scene this afternoon of a gathering bigger than any since • the days of the Roman occupation of the village. Cyclists are to foregather from far and near and demonstrate against his Lordship's edict that the cottagers shall no longer provide teas or refreshment of any kind to visitors on pain of summary notice to quit. A mass meeting will be held on the land adjoining the Church and speeches of protest be delivered against this run-English—or is it typically English ?—exercise of proprietorial powers. Then the following resolution will be put to the meeting, and doubtless carried without dissent seeing that Lord Egerton does not intend to favour Rostherne with his presence on this occasion : _ _ _

" That this -mass meeting of citizens of Man- chester and surrounding:towns protests emphati- cally against the action of Lord Egerton in issuing an edict to his tenantry prohibiting them from supplying refreshments to visitors, such action being opposed to the best traditions of English liberty. It further calls upon his Lord- ship to withdraw the instructions as early as possible, and so meet the legitimate request of thousands ,of law-abiding and peaceable towns- .people."

Tfie latest interviews with his Lordship indicate that he will persist in his intention to keep undesirables froin the village by barring all and sundry irrespective of class or quality. Public opinion will in the end, we think, prove too strong for him. The next condition of things may very easily be worse than the last. Our readers will find pictures of Rostherne and the Manor, with fuller particulars of the ".ban," on page 4 of this issue.
The wail of the THE BEEROPHONE " I3eerophone" is once AGAIN. more heard in the land.

Since the rejection of the LiCensing Bill by the Lords the • liquor party have rested upon their laurels, but the inclusion of increased licensing duties among the Budget proposals has brought forth the familiar cries of spoliation and robbery. The liquorparty are always assuring us of their loyalty, and patriotism,-but their reception of the Budget strikes us as the reverse of loyal. During the South African war every liquor shop in the country under the pretence of patriotism encouraged " Mafficking " to such an extent that the National Drink Bill of that year was higher than in any :other .year or record either before or since. Soldiers were exploited to such an extent that 'Lord Rbberts and other officers found it nebessary, to appeal to the 'public nofto treat thenLto liqthzt Drunit.en. orgies 'under the gUise'' bf patriottO itaour were coininon eventi.' when a shilling a barrel was put upon beer

to help to pay for the war, the brewers shirked the payment and put it upon the tied-house owner. The liquor people have b6en loud in their cry for Dreadnoughts and increased armaments, but when an extra twelve shillings only is charged for brewing 50,000 barrels of beer, the price to the public is put up a half-penny a pint. The only loyalty, the brewers are'showing is loyalty to their dividends, and Our trade our politics' is the only cry which accords with their propaganda. a

The water supply of OUR WATER the borough has sud- SUPPLY. denly become a pressing question and it is pro- bable that in a short time the Town Council will have before it an extensive scheme which will involve heavy expepditure. The Water Committee have 'felt compelled to take the matter in hand, owing to the increasing demand and the difficulty of meet- ing it with the existing means of distribution. The present 1& nch main from Winwick to Warrington which supplies the whole of the district was laid in 1869 and, with the excep- tion of the high pressure main which serves the higher portions of the locality on the Cheshire side; no additional main has beep laid since that date. The delivery from the 18 inch main is now' much in excess of what was originally contemplated and consequently the Corporation have in certain times of the year found themselves unable to meet all the requirements of the manufacturers. It is now proposed to put down a new main 24 inches in diameter (at an approximate cost of £11,150) which would afford an ample supply for many years to come. The Committee also recommend the provision of additional plant at Delph-lane, as the supply from the new wells depends upon a single engine and if a breakdown occurred the town might be put to great expense and inconvenience. The cost of the new pumping plant is estimated at £9,000. Another scheme which we hear is likely to come forward in the near future is the constructiou of further high level works at an outlay of £lB,OOO. The whole question was discussed in a general way by the General Purposes ;Committee on Monday but the details have not been arranged.
To the strange delusions SIR JOHN which Mr. Balfour BRUNNER'S seems to en,tertain about WHOLESOME the flight bf capital, if CORRECTIVE. it is called upon to pay

its fair share to the cost of administering the affairs of the com- munity, Sir John Brunner's speech should have applied a wholesome corrective. Here was a capitalist who objected most strongly, not to the imposition upon the shoulders able to bear it of the burden of taxation, but to any proposals for "grinding the faces of the poor." Here was a capitalist who laughed at the idea that the present Budget, or any prospective Free Trade Budget, was likely to make Great Britain a plague-infected spot to be avoided by capital_ Here was a capitalist who said that those who clamoured for more "Dreadnoughts "—and it was not the working class—should pay for them cheerfully. And here was a manufacturer who spurned the idea that he should be protected by artificial barriers against foreign competition. If it is said that this is not a typical British capitalist, the more's the pity.

Mr. Lloyd-George's LAND, AND proposals open up a LIQUOR, vista so extensivo that it' is impossible even here to tonal upon many of its features. There is no room to dwell upon the social reforms which it foreshadow. In regard to the taxes upon land withheld from profitable use and upon unearned increment, it must suffice here to point out that if, as has been suggested, the desire of the Chancellor had been to penalise political opponents, there is no reason why he should have exempted agricultural land. Country squires are not suspect of Liberalism. As for the duties upon spirits and the increased taxation of licences, if they will penalise the brewer, the distiller, and the publican, it will be because they bring about a railing-off in the consumption of alcohol. For the brewer, the distiller, and the publican will certainly do their best to hand along the impost to the public. But Mr. Balfour declares that the new taxes are not in the interest of temperance. His dialectical skill is wonderful, and received a deserved tribute from the Chancellor of the Exchequer on Tuesday. But even the Balfourian dialectic would find a difficulty in proving that a decrease in the consumption of alcohol is not in the interest of Temperance. Either the Budget will not affect the "Trade," or it will promote Temperance.

div.head: SUGGESTED VISIT OF THE KING TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: SUGGESTED VISIT OF THE KING TO WARRINGTON.

An effort is being made to induce his Majesty to visit Warrington when he comes to Knowsley, in July, to review the Territorial Forces of the West Lancashire division. The function at Knowsley takes place on July sth and the King will, proceed to Worsley the following day to review the East Lanca- shire Territorials. A suggestion has been put forward that instead of making the journey by train h;s Majesty should motor from Knowsley to Worsley and call at Warrington where a loyal welcome would be sure to await him.

We understand that the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) and Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., visited London on Thursday, and saw Lord Knollys, his Majesty's private secretafy, at Buckingham Palace.. Lord Knollys promised to ask the King to rec.eive an address from the Corporation of Warrington at the Town Hall, but it was understood that if the arrange- ment could be made, his Majesty would not alight from the car and would only stay at the Town Hall for a few minutes.

div.head: OLD LADIES' SOLITARY LIFE.
div.p: OLD LADIES' SOLITARY LIFE.

Sad circumstances were disclosed at an inquest help by Mr.S. Brighouse, county coroner, at the Warrington Police Station, yesterday, touching the death of Elizabeth Fryer, aged 67,wh0 resided at the Old Warps Farm,Latch f ord.—Mr. Herbert. Woods,sol ioi tor,eppea red for the relatives of the deceased.—Robert Fryer, farm labourer, Doe Farm, Penketh, said that deceased was his sister, and she and another sister, Sarah Fryer, aged 60, lived together at the Old Warps, which they rented from the Corporation. They were the sole occupants and did their own domestic wark. About four years ago deceased fell down stairs, and in January of this year she fell off a step ladder. She had suffered very much from bronchitis.—Patrick Collins, farm laboirer, employed at the Old Warps;said he last saw the deceased alive on Tuesday when she was sitting in an arnichair by the fireside. Up to then she had not been medically attended. On Thursday witness was sent for a doctor, but when medical aid arrived deceased was dead. The sisters lived quite happily and comfortably together, in fact they were much attached to each other.—The Coroner read- a letter from Dr.. Collins stating- that when he was called in deceased must luve been dead at least two hours. -The body was very much emaciated.—Mr. T. H Spinks, assistant Town Clerk, said that on April 24th,he saw deceased in town, and she complained of not feeling well. Ile advised her to send for a doctor, but she would not hear of it. On Tuesday, April 27th he went to the farm and was told that deceased had been out the previous day and had got a thorough drenching. ,Ide again went On the 29th,"and she was then ill in bed. He suggested that a doetor should be -ealled in, 'but' Misq Sarah-Fryer said her sister would not hilt; • of, and that she would notllO'sitytbineivitiout'herrl*isfett; Oonsent.—Tbe jury tettlniedifibrdibea:" Matt' riont Natural causes." . ,

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Captain Kincaid-Smith's fight at Stratford did not prove that the cause of compulsory military training has a great following. Out of 8,500 votes he only polled 479, and seeing thathe headed the poll -in 1906 with 4,321 votes he. cannot conkratulatetimself on hav- ing made a change for the better in the flag he has elected to fight under. * * *

Alderman Bolton is not distinguished for that suaviter in modo which was so characteristic a trait of the late father of the Council, Alderman Harrison. On Tuesday he was in His most belligerent mood and kept up a running fire of comments which fre- quently disconcerted the speakers, and led Alderman Bennett to remark cuttingly that "Alderman Bolton was, at times, an awful infliction."

The Methodist Church of Australia has just been presented with a gift which will be peculiarly interesting to, and accepted with gratitude by, that Church as a body. The gift is a chair of historic interest, which was used by John Wesley. The donor is Miss Clifford, whose great-grandfather obtained ,possession of this relic, which had been in the vestry of the Great Queen-street Wesleyan Church, London. The chair is of solid oak, and is in an excellent state of preservation. * *

Our good friend the " Q-uardian " is not often caught tripping in its reportorial capacity, but it has lately made a slip which even "Punch" has found worthy of quotation. In reporting the dinner of the Parliamentary Debating Society recently, the " Guardian ' said "The health of 'The King' was sub- mitted by the Speaker, who occupied the chair, and was cordially drunk?: After all the nice things which were said of Mr. Plinston as Speaker this was indeed an unkind cut.

OG * After watching a young witness sign his name to depositions, Coroner Brighouse, at a St. Helens inquest on Saturday, remarked: "I like to watch children write, and I should like to teach some of our schoolmasters and schoolmistresses how'to hold a pen. They hold it in a most rigid manner, so that they cannot move it." Mr. Brighouse has a most ardent reforming spirit, but unfortunately he is only human and cannot attend personally to .the hundred and one wrongs which he would see righted. A dozen Brighouses might achieve something, but one can only suggest. .

* * * Mr. Birrell is now the fastest speaker in the Hbuset of Commons. When he introduced the Evicted Tenants Bill, which occupied twenty minutes, the Press Gallery agreed on this point. Mr. Haldane's speed in his three hours' performance when he explained the Army Estimates thQyear before last had been regarded as a record; Mr. Bryce in pre- senting the Irish Labourers Bill to the House beat the Secretary for War ; Mr. Birrell outstripped both. In the twenty minutes he poured out about 3,200 words, a speed of 160 words per minute, including stops. The actual average speed was about 200-words a minute. At times it fell to 160 or lower, and at others to well above 200 words a minute. * * *_

Not every Chancellor of the Exchequer has been "quick at figures." A Treasury clerk once put some figures before Lord Randolph Churchill. "I. wish you would put these figures plainly, so that I can understand them," said his lordship. The clerk said he had done his best, and had, he pointed out, reduced them to decimals. "Oh ! " said the Chancellor, "I never could understand what • those d—d dots meant." Charles Pox is credited with having said that he never could understand what Consols were—he only knew that they were things that went up and down in the City; and he was always pleased when they went down, because it so annoyed Pitt.

* * * Wire baskets for waste paper in the streets have been fixed to the tramway poles in a town not far from Manchester. The other Saturday night (says the "Manchester Guardian ") a crowd was attracted round one of these baskets by the sight of a baby safely deposited inside the cage, and there was much discussion of what should be done in the way of rescue. At last a woman who had watched the affair from the window 'of a neighbouring public-house came out and explained to the crowd : " Yo cun mahnd yer own business and goo on; that's ma babby ; it's aw reet ; ah've getten ml eye on it." She had merely been complying with the latest requirements of the law.

* * The biography of Dean Hook recalls a certain minor canon who used to preach at the Cathedral when Hook was a boy, at Winchester School. In one of his sermons there occurred the striking reflection that "What is impossible can never be, and very seldom comes to pass." Another discourse was long remembered for its pathetic' lamentation on the degeneracy of the age: "0 tempora ! 0 mores what times we live in! little boys and girls run about the streets cursing and swearing before they can either walk or talk." But the Church of England has no monopoly of these violent contrasts, for it was at a City Temple meeting not many years ago that a speaker exclaimed: "I find my time is already gone. Therefore I Will keep within it."

* * * If politics are not a congested concatenation of the incarnation of lying . . Miller Maguire. Though disestablishment may be on the lips of agitators, disendowment is in their hearts.—The Bishop of Winchester. statesmen have at last come to recognise that the education of the child is the true preventive of the use of alcohol.—Sir Victor Horsley. People ought not to be penalised because they have been, foolish enough to grow old without being artful enough to get rich.— Mr. Will Crooks, M.P. Americans all think that people work harder in America than anywhere else. They do not. They simply make more noise about it.—The Rev. Dr. Aked.

• * * Councillor Pemberton and the Mayor had another little passage at arms on Tuesday, which, very fortunately, ended amicably. His Worship has one fault, and that is an inclination to be testy and intolerant of criticism. At one time on Tuesday we. feared he was going to refuse Councillor Pemberton a hearing on the question of procedure which the latter raised quite justifiably, but in the end he admitted a full :discussion while protesting against what he considered an interference with the conduct of the Chair. Councillor Pemberton's motion involved no innovation but merely embodied an instruc* tion to the Mayor to ask if any members wished to speak further on the minutes of any Committee be,fore calling upon the proposer to reply • or put" the minutes. The Mayor7o,:eontentiOn la that: such a ,) vractice being already _observed ,the motion , ivas unnecessary. 'As Ifirifift;6l-of fteet tthel 'Oractice now and then falls into disuse when I

routine business is being transacted with rapidity, and consequently members are occasionally shut out from the opportunity of asking a question or making a speech. Councillor Pemberton carried his point and showed discretion in not demanding a vote on the resolution. A word to the wise is sufficient, and the Mayor is not lacking in everyday commonsense. _ .

"Did they live hap-pily together?" was Coroner Brighouse's inquiry with reference to two aged and highly-respectable Warring- ton ladies who were the sole occupants of the Old Warps farmhouse, and one of whom has just died suddenly. " Yes " replied the witness, an Irish farm labourer, I never heard them swear." * * *

An Irish M.P. once declared that of the outrages reported from Ireland, three- quarters were exaggerated and half had no foundation in fact—a statistical computation that reminds one of another Irish M.P. who declared excitedly to a group of fellow- members, "I want to convince you that there isn't any truth in half the lies they are telling about Ireland." * *

There was only a short discussion at the Council meeting on Warrington Bridge, but it produced a curious revelation. Estimates for a 70 feet and 80 feet structure have been deemed necessary, and Councillor Pemberton wished to have a price for a 60 feet bridge included. But no! The Council shied at once. Some members obviously feared that if they got the figures for the smaller structure before them they might be over- come by a sudden attack of economy and adopt 60 feet as the width. So the harmless proposal was put on one side as if it were a thing of sinister import, or a nameless horror. Truly some men are readily frightened by shadows of their own imagining!

Death of an Old Oddfellow. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr. Edward Adams, a well-known Oddfellow, of Morris-court, Church-street, who most regularly attended the lodge meetings up to the time of his illness, and who by his genial disposition won the respect of all with whom he came in contact. The funeral took place on Sunday and the following Brothers assembled to pay him their last tribute of respect :—D.G. G. Wilkinson, P.G. G. Crozier, P.G. H. Jones, P.G. A. Foster, P.G. E. Dower, senior, P.G. A. Condliffe, William Rathmill, P.P.G. W. Pennington, district treasurer' P.P.G. W. Meachin, P.G. W. Perry, district secretary, N,G. Frangleton. Ragged School Treat. At the Warrington Ragged School on Monday even- ing 450 scholars were provided with a grand tea, through the generosity of Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Pan-. After the tea an entertainment was given in the school 'room, and Councillor Skelland presided. Mr. D. Hurrell of Manchester Ragged School addressed the children, and said how pleased he was to be present and also to find that we in Warrington had such kind and generous friends as Mr. and Mrs. Parr. At the conclusion of his speech he said what a boon the Ragged School in Manchester had been to poor children. Solos were rendered by Mr.. J. Jolmson, Mr. H. Wright, Miss Titchard and Miss C. Ashworth, and a recitation was given by Mr. J. Bishop, entitled Little Mercy." The chairman asked the children to give three cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Parr, which the' children did in the heartiest manner.

Warrington Cycling Club. The run to Bollington on Saturday last, took place under rather better we ether conditions than those operating on the previous Saturday runs this season. A fair roister of cyclists turned out from headquarters and the destination reached, bowling was the rule for the afternoon. After tea, the return honi`e 'was made via Knutsfor.d, and some time was spent there by the members interested in the Any Day festivities. An enjoyable afternoon was concluded by a pleasant ride home. The opening Thursday evening ran to Burton- wood and smoking concert at Sankey proved a success- ful event. A large number of members turned out, and from this it is anticipated that this mid-week run will be very popular with the members during tne season. A commencement also of the bowling meet- ings at Sankey was made on Wednesday evening lass and there was a large attendance of bowlers who are making preparations for the forthcoming competitions which start on the 26th inst. Appleton Rifle Club. _ _ _ _ _

-Saturday was the opening day of the Club season. There was a large attendance and althuugh a few show rs fell during the afternonn they were of short duration, the weather on the elole being good shoot- ing. The fact that the club rifles have been thoroughly overhauled by the makers and put into first-class condition for accurate shooting was greatly appreciated. by the members, who are looking forward to making some healthy scores during the season. There were several visitors present, Call ladies' and gentlemen, who all took part in the practice with great interest, one lady scoring a bull's ,eye. There is every promise of a most successful seasoa and the growing interest in rifle shcoting throughuut the country is evidenced in this district, the Club membership being consider- ably increased and applications continuing to come in. Intending members should apply to the Hon. Sedretary, Mr. F. 11.. Cowley, 18, Mitchell-street, Stockton Heath. Matches with other clubs are being arranged, and ,these, together with the usual Monthly Club Com- petitions will provide, a g)oc.l programme for' the season.

Carleton, appears in Holy Trinity Parish Magazine :—The Vicar is sure that the congregation and parishioners will like to know that the above event passed off, very successfully in most delightful weather, and that in the course of the afternoon's reception kind wishes and congratula- tions from Warrington and various other quarters poured in in such numbers that the inspection had to be reserved for the leisure hours of the honeymoon. The happy pair left soon after 4 p.m.' for Paddington Station, on their way to Oxford. Old Warrington friends will perhaps be aware that the bride is a grand-daughter of the Rev. C. The bride- groom has been very much touched by the lovely presents that have reached him from the members of the congregation, and from the mothers belonging to the Parochial Mis4ion in Factory Yard. The latter was presented by Mrs. John White on behalf of the women at the usual Monday meeting, April 19th, the beautiful entre dish and silver vases being garnished with primroses in honour of the day.

In the quiet old churchyard at Lymm, yesterday, the funeral took place of Miss Mary Barratt, Carleton Hall, Holm Rook, Cumberland, a lady who was little known to the present generatien of Warringtonians, but who nevertheless had intimate associations with the town.
