div.head: HOWARD PLACE.
div.p: HOWARD PLACE.
Alderman Bennett Carries His Point.
HEATED DISCUSSION.

At the ordinary monthly meeting on Tuesday the Council devoted considerable time to the dis- cussion of tbo following motion introduced by Alder- man Bennett :—" That the following resolution passed by the Council on the 6th April, 1908, be rescinded: 'Resolved, that a urinal he erected on the centre of Howard-place, in accordance with plan No. 4 prepared by the Borough Surveyor.'" The Alderman pointed out that the resolution was only passed by a majority of one, and at a time when several members of the Council were absent. He admitted that on that occa- sion be waxed rather warm, although he was usually "the mildest mannered man who ever scuttled a ship or cut a throat." (Laughter). This was a matter of importance, and the first thing to consider was the fsel- ing of the residents in the neighbourhood. A petition against the proposal had been signed by every shop- keeper and by practically every property holder in that neighbourhood. Two resolutions against it had been passed by the Beautiful Warrington Society, and that night he had received two resolutions which were quite unsolicited. One was from the Warrington and Dis- trict Property Owners' Association, which represented more than half the ratable value of the town and looked at the matter not from the idealistic but from a hard business point of view. It stated "We heartily support you in this matter, and trust ou will be suc- cessful." The other was from the Guild of the Sacred Heart, who protested on the ground (1), of the unsightli- ness of an erection on a place wh:ch could be made a beauty spot; (21, of its proximity to St. Mary's Church and the Guild room ; and 3, the moral danger to children going to and from school. Father Wilson had also spoken to him on the subject and felt strongly against the site selected. Two arguments bad been used in favour of a convenience. One was that no other site was available. He did not think that could be maintained. He still thought a place could be found at the corner of Dial-street and Fennel-street or near the end of Mersey-street where a scheme of street widening should be carried out. He desired that Howard Place should be one of the beauty spots of the town and he considered it was an ideal place for a statue. Alderman EVANS : Put it on top of this structure. (Laughter.) Alderman BEN:ern: If Alderman Evans would con- sent to be the subject of the sculptor's art, I might agree to that. It would be appropriate that the author of such an ingenious contrivance should have all the glory that could possibly accrue from it for generations to come. (Laughter.) In the course of the discussionit was stated that the Grocers' Association had written pointing out the need for further accommodation of this kind in the town. Dr. Joseph supported Alderman Bennett on sanitary, sthetic and moral grounds. A SCENE. There was a " scene " between Alderman Tinnion and Alderman Bennett. Alderman 'FISSION said a great deal of nonsense had been talkei and much false sentiment, had been voiced. In the course of his reply on the discussion, Alderman BENNETT said that when Alderman Tinnion had a weak case he always became abusive. Ho might well be termed "the champion slanger of Warrington." Alderman TINNION : I never slanged anybody and the expression ought to be withdrawn. Alderman BENNETT: Abuse eserybody else in the Council and when anybody replies, get away—that is what we expect from Alderman Tinnion. Alderman 'FISSION: He charges me nith being the champion slanger of Warrington and I resent it. Alderman BENNETT: If Alderman Tinnion regards it as an offensive expression, I will withdraw it. Alderman TINNION : What else can a gentleman regard it as? Alderman BENNETT: There is not a gentleman in the Council more sensitive than Alderman Tinnion, hut there is no man more prone to jump on those who differ from him. He never spares their feelings in the slightest degree, but hits out right and left. Alderman TINNION : Is this a withdrawal? Alderman BENNETT: It is a withdrawal with reserva- tions. Ido not withdraw the meaning behind it T would like to express it more politely it I could, but, I say when I happen to differ from you, or if any other member of the Council differs from you, you go for him with all the truculence of which you are able. • Alderman TINNION But I don't slang him. Alderman BENNETT: Slanging is a most unfortunate word and I will withdraw it. if you like. If Alderman Tinnion irritates me, he must expect me to retaliate. it is disrespectful of Alderman Tinnion to say we are talking nonsense, but I am not going to follow his weak-kneed esample and ask him to withdraw. div.p: MONKS, HALL AND CO, LTD.

rtosPECTIVE RE-VAIXATIONS.

The Committee instructed the Valuer, in continu- tion of the scheme already inaugurated, to re-value during the ensuing year the whole of the tanneries in Warrington—fourteen or fifteen, it was stated—and also those at Padgate and 'Orford, gas engineers' and foundries, file and toole works, the breweries and distilleries of Messrs. COLLINS GREEN COLLIERY

- The Collins Green Colliery Co. appealed against the assessment of the Collins Green Colliery which stands as follows :—Land, buildings, plant, appurtenances and coal mines, gross £20,000 ; ratable £12,500; water, gross £350; ratable £297 10s. Mr. H. FAlRcr.otdri (managing director) stated that the assessment had been practically doubled, The assessment was quite apart front the Bold Collieries, which were in the Prescot Union.

The CHAIRMAN : Do you seriously protest against the figures? Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : Certainly. If you had assessed us for the Bold and Collins Green collieries combined, you could not have put the figures bigger. The CHAIRMAN : We have no desire to put anything exorbitant in the book but we want, in the most amicable spirit, to arrive at an equitable figure that may give general satisfaction to yourselves and be in the interests of the Union. We know sufficient of the Collins Green Colliery Co. to believe that they have a desire to do their fan- share in maintaining die rates of the Union in which their business is placed. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : All I can say is that if Mr. Meaeock comes over he can have the bbok3 and balance sheets, and he can have my job if he likes. (Laughter). Mr. MATHER : Are there any more of them ? I want a good job. (Laughter). The CHAIRMAN : What do you think would be a fair assessment? Mr. FAIRCIA )UGH : I should divide it by two. It was decided that the Valuer should wait upon the company for further information.

div.head: HAMLET SUBURBAN.
div.p: THE HAMLET SUBURBAN.

A party of German labour leaders paid, a visit to a newly-organised town-village at Hampstead on Wed- nesday, walking over what plomises to be one of the most successful experiments of the kind, inspecting the exteriors and interiors of the picturesque white, red- roofed cottages dotted over the ground with methodical disregard of straight lines, taking tea at the local refreshment rooms, and later on in the evening attending a convereazione in the Institute, at which Mr. Henry Vivian, M.P., who Ivis had a large share in the initiation of the suburban hamlet,presided. An address of welcome to the visitors was read, in which it was pointed out that a debt of gratitude was due to their country for the lead it had taken in town-planning and. suburban-development.
_NGTO. FORGERIES SENTENCE AT THE ASSIZES.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday, Annie Smith (23), married woman, Garibaldi-street, W'arrington, was charged with the forgery of a receipt for £1 purporting to be a receipt from her husband, Joseph Smith, of Warrington, on August 17th, 1907. Mr. 11. L. Riley (instructed by Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co.) prosecuted, and Mr. Madden (instructed by Messrs. Arthur Browne and Co.) defended. Prisoner pleaded "Not guilty." Mr. Riley said the Bank had a deposit fund of over a quarter of a million pounds and the number of annnal transactions was very groat, but only in one case other than the present instance bad the confidence which the bank plactui in its depositors been misplaced. The husband of the prisoner had had an account with the Warrington Savings Bank since May, 1891. On the 17th August, 1907. there was standing to his credlt in that account £177 .ss. 11d. Mrs. Smith went to the bank on that date with her husband's deposit book,a form of receipt to be nsed in connection with a withdrawal of money from the bank, and a letter as follows :—"Kindly give the bearer, Mrs. Smith, £4, as I am not able to come, as lam fast at work." This, however, had not been signed by the husband. An official of the bank. having made a reference to the undoubted signature of Joseph Smith, written seventeen years before, came to the conclusion thst all was right. In addition to that he knew the prisoner as the wife of Joseph Smith. Between that date and the 17th December there bad , been other withdrawals on orders supposed to have bent signed by Joseph Smith, but not actually signed by him. Practically, the whole of the deposits stand- , lug in Smith' e name had been withdrawn, although he had not signed the orders for withdrawal. In cense- quence of the bank becoming suspicious, Smith attended at the bank with his wife on the 17th December. Then all the receipts and letters pur- porting to have been wr:tten by the husband were pro- duced, and Mr. Smith denied that be had authorised or had had anything to do with any of the withdrawals. Prisoner exonerated her husband, and said she had signed them. The question arose as to where the loss was going to fall. L'nder a provision of the Friendly. Societies' Act the matter was referred to the Registrar of the Friendly Societies, who decided that the loss must fall on the bank. The bank, therefore, „had to restore Mr. Smith's account to its old integrity by putting £lB3 back, allowing him the interest that it would have earned. The bank felt it was their duty to prosecute, which they bad done. Before the magistrates prisoner said she thought the arbitrator's decision settled everything. Mr. W. A. Proud, actuary of the bank, g .ve evidence bearing out this statement. In answer to Mr. Madden, he said he asked Joseph Smith if he was going to to prosecute his wife and he replied " No, but I don't want to lose my money." There was no suggestion that Smith and the bank should divide the loss.

Mr. Madden : Didn't you say," Oh, well, you will be all right. It will be settled under the rule. If there is anything to come to you the Registrar will decide." Did you say that ?—No, sir. Didn't you !ply to the husband," If you do nothing the bank will do nothing ? "—No. Robert Hardy, 11, Lloyd-street, and Detective. Sergeant Meacock having given evidence, Mr. Madden addressed the jury for the defence. He said the husband was a hardworking, industrious man, and had saved nearly £2OO before his marriage, three or four years ago. The first two or three years of. their married life were happy, then owing to prisoner's efforts to assist members of her family who came to reside with them, her financial resources were inadequate. Her husband was not aware that she was. not receiving regularly certain weekly payments which were to have been made to her by some members of her family for their maintenance. The husband made her an allow- ance of £1 4s. a week. Unfortunately, prisoner had thus got herself into a financial dilemma, and dared not tell her husband. Thus it was that she was brought to her present unhappy position. Th3re was no i felonious intent whatever n what was done, so far as she was concerned. She bad no notion that she was robbing the bank; she thought she was only taking her husban.i's money. . . _ _

Mr. Riley intimated that he did not suggest that the husband "had any knowledge of it at all.' Accused, upon the advice of counsel, withdrew her plea of "Not guilty," and pleaded "Guilty." Ills Lordship said he would pass sentence the follow- ing morning. Prisoner was brought up for sentence on Wednesday morning. When the case had been called on Mr. Madden put Joseph Smith, the husband, into the witness box. Smith said as far al be could discover his wife had not spent the money upon herself. They were now living happily tnether. There were two children, one seven months old.

Mr. H. Lindon Riley,who conducted the prosecution, was questioning the husband when accused collapsed in a faulting condition in the dock, and had to be removed to the sells below, where she received the attention of Dr. Price, Walton Gaol medical officer. In a few minutes she revived, and was again brought forward for sentence.

In answer to the usu ii rineltion from the Clerk o f Assize as to whether she had anything to say why sentence should not I,e passed upon her, she lisped nut that she only thought sho was taking her husband's money.._

Mr.-Justice Walton said he did not know that be had ever had in its way a more ptinful case before him than that, but he bad his duty to perform to the public. Prisoner hid committed a . long series of forgeries extending from August, 1907, to the latter part of 1908 —a long series of deliberate forgeries. In that way she got a considerable sum of money, about £lBO more or less. He (Mr. Justice Walton) accepted the story that the pressure upon her, at any rate to some extent, was the fact that. she was supporting some members of her own family who did not contribute much to their own support. She Was not taking the money for any personal extravagance, so far as he knew ; but still she was deliberately, week after week, or, at any rate, month after in ,ntb, for many months, committing deliberate frauds and forgeries—forging letters and withdrawal forms, and doing it repeatedly. He had no doubt she thought she was taking her husband's money. When the case was before the justices in the police court she seemed to hive had some sort of idea that. because there had been an arbitration, in which it bad been decided that the bank must bear the loss, that she was relieved of any further responsibility. He could not understand that view at all. It might be that she thought she was taking bet husband's money. Her husband had succeeded in getting the money hack again, so that it was the bank that had to bear tholoes arising from her fraud, and not her husband. She had the money, and he got it back. How that in any way affected the case he (his lord..hip) was at a loss to see. It certainly did not mitigate the case; it seemed to Lim it made no difference. She could not escape because her husband had got the money back; it was deliberate and repeated forgery. She must go to prison for eight montbs in the second division.

div.head: BATCH OF THEFT CASES,
div.p: A BATCH OF THEFT CASES,

Before Mr. Charles White (in the chair) and other magistrates at the Borough Police Court on Thursday, John Melia, carter, 7, James-street, was charged with having been drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Crown-street on Tuesday. and also with baying stolen, between May 3rd and 4th, a piece of pig iron from Messrs. Whyman's works. It appeared that the piece of. pig iron was found in the cart in charge of the prisoner when he was arrested for being drunk, and it transpired that it bad been stolen from Messrs. Whyman's works. Some pieces of lead were also found in the cart, but the police bad not traced ownership. A tine of 40s. and costs (R 3 in all) was imposed. John Allerton, or Nolan, Eldon-street, pleaded guilty to stealing some oranges and bananas from a cart in the market on Wednesday, the propet ty of George Miller. The Chief Constable said the prisoner appeared to be of weak intellect, and was probably not responsible for his actions. The magistrates made an order for the prisoner to be sent to the Workhouse for 14 days, where he will be medically examined.—Hannah Needham, of no settled abode, was sent to gaol for one month for steal- ing £1 from William Jones Lewis. The evidence showed that the woman asked Levis to stand her a drink. They went into a public house and each bad a drink, and whilst there prisoner put her hand into his waistcoat pocket, in which there was a sovereign. Prosecutor got hold of her, but she declined to give up the money. She was taken outside, when she promised to Ore up the money, but eventually denied having the sovereign.

div.head: Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Court.

MOND A V.—Before the Mayor (chairmen), Aldermen Smethorat and Bennett, Councillor Wilkinson, and Messrs. A. T. Pairclough, S. Wright, IT. Roberts, W. Roberts, A. J. Jolley, C. Jackson Holmes, H. Thornton, and G. Pilling. OBSCENE LANG L'AGE.—Annie Turner of School Brow. was charged with using obscene language on School Brow. She was fined 4s. 6d.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLIES.—George Smith, of Sutton-street, and Charles Csmpbel I, of Rose and Crown. street, were each fined ss. and costs (10s. Gd.), for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on Saturday night; William Mariaty, of Mersey-street, 58. and costs (7e. 6d.) ; Mary McLoughley, of Old-road, 58. and costs; William Jackson Lawless, of Crossley-street, ss. and costs; John Platt, Barbauld-street, ss. and costs. BEGGING.—Michael .Monogue, of no settled abode was sentenced to a month's imprisonment for begging in Golden-square on Saturday night:

LICENCi: TRANSFERS.—ihe 'following licences were transferred, outdoor licence on the corner of Kendrick. street and Legh-street, to John Hesketh from Mr. Robinson; transfer of the Golden Lion, Knutsford-

road, from Anne Wilkinson to James Kay; transfor. of the Mersey Hotel, Mersey-street, from William Donworth to John Colne.—Mr. Browne said he had an application to make on behalf of Mrs. Mary Allen, of Mill-lane. Mrs. Allen was desirous of increasing her domestic occupation by adding the next house to it. The extension would be used for nothing else bet domestic purposes. He thought it was a reasonable application. After some deliberation the bench refused the application —Mr. Broane applied on behalf of Messrs. Greenall and Co., for sanction to re-build the Lower Seven Stars in Bridge-street. Messrs. Greenall and Co.. had consented to the -Rose and - Crown Inn, Bridge-street, and the Bird in Rand, Bank-street, licensed premises, referred fur being compensate and if the re-construction of the above be passed.. The buildings would be set back..to come in line of Mr. Blinton's (grocers) shop which was. 'the corporation line of building. Three shops would be built for business purposes. Mr. S. Owen submitted the plans, and after careful perusal by the bench, who afterwards discussed the matter in private, the application was granted: Imrt:DENT STREET OBSTRUCTION.—Edward Nixon, John Forster, Rose and Crown-street, James Barker, Warburton-street, and John Hill, Smith-street, all youths, were charged with obstructing the footpath near the Central Station, on the 22nd April. P.C. Clarke said the defendants held rope across the footpath at the bottom of the station steps, and people had to get off the footpath, and go round the defendants in order to get up the steps. Witness took their names and addresses, and on returning to the spot found the defendants still there.—Hill, who had no previous con- victions was dismissed with a caution. Nixon who had 4 previobs convictions of stealing and house breaking, was ordered to pay ss. and costs or 7 days. Forster, a youth of very small stature and who said he was 19 years of age, ss.and costs or 7 days. Forster had served a period of 4 years on the training ship ra Clio." Barker was lined 2s.
TUESDAV—Before Messrs. 11. Roberts (chairman) Alderman Bolton, Dr. Fox, C. Jackson-Holmes, and Col. Edelsten.

A SOLDIER'S REMARKABLE CAREER.—A soldier's remarkable life story was heard when Thomas Darcy wan charged with making a false attestation when enlisting in the King's South Lancashire Regiment on March .sth.--In answer to the question "Have you served in the army before," prisoner replied in the negative.—Tho Chief Constable stated that the prisoner's military career, although not very creditable was certainly very remarkable. He began by enlisting in the Cheshire itegiment stationed at Chester, in the name of Edward Wilson, on December 15th, 1898. He served in South Africa during the late war, where he was convicted of stealing and pilfering and sentenced to one month's imprisonment. He served in the Cheshires until March 12th, 190?, when he was tried by court-martial at Aldershot for stealing and destroying his kit, etc, for which he was discharged from the Army with ignominy. On January 28th. 1893, he again enlisted in the Liverpool Regiment at Liverpool in the name of Thomas Williams, making a false answer or attestation in doing so. On December 15th of the year he was charged with stealing and was ag tin discharged with ignominy. He, however, again enlisted at Liver- pool on July 14th, 1904, in the South Lancashire Regi- ment (Militia) as Lloyd Roberts. He was tried by court-martial and sentenced to two years' imprisonment for stealing, and discharged from the Army with ignominy. Nothing daunted, prisoner again enlisted for the fourth time in the King's. Liverpool Regiment on the 10th of this month, this time giving his original name, and was given into the custody of the police for making the false attestation.—Prisoner was sentenced to three months' imprisonment.
WEDNESDAY. —Before Mr. Charles White (in the chair), Aldermen Ellison and Smethurst, and Councillor Dr. Joseph. _

"A -Low CLASS THlEF."—Joseph Abraham, Dial- yard, was charged with stealing a shirt from a clothes- line at the rear of the Golden Grove, the property of Joseph Caldwell. A further charge of assaulting Hannah Needhsm was preferred.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner struck the woman in a most brutal fashion, disfiguring her face. He was a confirmed low- class thief and a thorough rascal.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for three months for stealing the shirt and ordered to find sureties of £2O, or six month, for the assault.
FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. Henry Thornton (chairman) and W. Furness.

ALLEGED NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.-117nry Jane Burke, 2, Eldon-street, was charged with neglecting her five children. She pleaded 'not guilty." Mr. Broane prosecuted for the N.S.P.C.C., and said they could not proceed against her husband, because fortunately or unfortunately, he was away serving a term of three months imprisonment. The parties were well known having been before the Court on many occasions. The principal object of the prosecution was to get the children away from the custody of those people. A complaint came to the society s inspector that the children had been begging in Bold-street, telling mos. pitiable tales, 'When' on the investigation of Inspector Cox, were found to be untrue. The woman, whilst her husband was in prison, had to be helped by the guardians, but they had reason to believe that the groceries, which were given to her, were sold in the shop. When Inspector Cox visited the house he found her under the Influence of drink The house was in a dirty condition, and upstairs there were only two beds. The extraordinary thing about it was that the two beds had to serve as sleeping accomrnation for four women and five children.—The magistrates adjourned the case for eight weeks. Three of the children were ordered to be sent to the Workhouse. DESTROYING IllowEns.—Arthur Crossland, 9, Percy- street, and Albert Crossland, Bedford Leigh, were summoned for wilfully destroying flowers in the garden of Joseph Taylor, 295, Wellfleld-street, and fined 10s. And costs each.

div.head: Juyenlle Court.
div.p: Juyenlle Court.

At the Juvenile Court, Herbert Williams, Packet Stsee, pleaded guilty to stealing 3s. Md., the property of Elizabeth Gould. The Chief Constable said the boy was seat by his aunt to pledge a dress. He received a sum of money and went to Liverpool, where he spent it. He returned and was arrested by Detective Clough, when he said he was sorry he came back, as if he had kept away he would not have been caught. The lad told the magistrates that he had been led on by another youth. The case was adjourned for a week in order to see if a reformatory school could be found for him.—Two boys,named James Foster and Percy Eilwell, Liverpool- road, pleaded guilty to stealing 13Abs. of scrap steel, of the value of 24.. 10s., from the yard of -Messrs. Monk's, Hall and Co.'s works, Atherton's-quay. The lads- were seen on Wednesday night at 9.30 by the works watchman near the works. They had a box on wheels, which the watchman found to contain scrap steel, and the boys admitted having taken the scrap, and said they were going to sell it and share the money. Each boy was ordered to receive four strokes with the birch rod.

div.head: Young Man's Serious Injury.
div.p: Young Man's Serious Injury.
COMPENSATION CLAIM FAILS.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.C., Llewellyn Davies, aged 25 years, 11. Wakelield-street, made an application for an award under the Workmen's Compensation Act in respect of injuries alleged to have been received whilst in the employ of the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Co., Ltd. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the applicant and Mr. 0. G. Morris, barrister (instructed by Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.) for the respondents. Mr. Browne said the applicant was formerly in the employ of the respondents as a general labourer and he never worked anywhere else. On February lith,l9oB,he was carrying two buckets of tar to the blacking tanks and had to cross over a railway line. He was wearing clogs, and had got one foot over the • rails when the other foot slipped on the metals and he sprained his ankle. He complained to a workman named Leigh, and rested a short time, but he did not make any complaint to a foreman or manager. A fellow workman gave him some advice, and be bathed the ankle in cold water. On going home he told his father, mother and brother of the accident, and the ankle was again bathed. The following morning it seemed better, and he returned to work, but he again had to bathe the ankle in the afternoon and evening. This continued for a fortnight, the ankle being better in the morning but swollen at night. At the end of a fortnight he received notice of dismissal, owing to slackness of trade, and left work on February 28th. He searched for other employment but did not obtain any, and, the ankle becoming worse' he went to the Infirmary. The ankle having been dressed he was sent home and remained in bed for nine weeks. He was in the house for another month and then went again to the Infirmary, where he remained an in-patient until a week or two ago. No notice of,the accident was given to the firm before January 11th of this year—eleven months after the accident. The Act laid down that notice of claim should be given within six months but• also provided that failure to make the claim in their specified time should not to a bar to proceed- ings if it was found to be occasioped by mistake, absence from the United Kingdom or other reasonable cause. The applicant did not believe at the time be was discharged that the injury would be permanent and during the long time he was confined to bed at home be was not in a fit condition to make a claim. The respondents were not prejudiced by failure to give notice, because the applicant admitted that be did not com Plain to a foreman, but only to a worktian named Leigh who could not now be found. No one was present when the accident occurred. From the sprain tuberculous ankle had been set up, with the result that. the doctors now recommended the applicant to have his leg amputated. He had not .worked a day since the accident, but before it occurred he had never had a day's illness. Applicant gave evidence bearing out this statement and David and Mary Davies, his father and mother, spoke to his complaining about his ankle on returning from work. They could not, however, state definitely when the accident happened and it was admitted that in a letter addressed to the firm on the father's behalf, March was mentioned.
Dr. Manson, who has attended the applicant, stated that that he was now suffering from tuberculous disease of the ankle which had spread to the foot. Witness

and the other surgeons at the Infirmary recommended amputation of the leg. A kick or an ordinary fall in the street might have caused the original injury. He thought the applicant was pre-disposed to tubercular trouble but be was of opinion that the injury would be the prime factor in inducing the disease. Mr. Morris did not call any evidence. He said the very position which the Act intended employers should not be placed in bad arisen in this case:llle onus lay upon the workman to show that the employer had not been prejudiced by the want of notice. Mr. Morris also pointed out that applicant did not report the accident to anyone in authority.

. - 1111 Honour, in gi yin& judgment, said he found that the notice was not given In accordance with the require- ments of the Act of Parliament, and he found that the claim was not made in accordance with the Act of Parliament, No reason bad been proved to his satis- faction to justify or warrant him in dispensing with the requirements of the statute such as he had referred to. Therefore the want of notice and absence of claim were fatal in that case, and his award must be for the respondent with costs on Scale B.

Window Cleaner's Fall UNSUCCESSFUL CLAIM FOIL COMPENSATION. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, IC.C.. John Williamson, 100, Fox-street, brought an application under the Work- men's Compensation Act in respect of injuries alleged to have been sustained whilst employed as a window cleaner by Mr. Edwin Woods, Rock \tilled, Ackers-lane, Latchford, managing director of the Longford Wire Co., Ltd. Mr. Cuthbert Smith, barrister (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel, of Warrington) appeared for the applicant and Mr. Arthur Browne for the respondent. Mr. Cuthbert Smith stated that the case presented a peculiar set of circumstances. For ten years there had been existing between Williamson and the .Longford Wire Co. and Mr. Edwin Woods, concurrent contracts of service. Williamson was ordinarily employed as a la,iourer by the wire company, but be had a contract with Mr. Woods for periodical employment as s window cleaner at Mr. Woods' house. For ton years he had been in the habit of going regularly once a- month, sub- ject to occasional breaks, to clean the windows at the house and he received payment. On December 16th, whilst employed in this way, tho ladder on which he was standing slipped and he fell to the gronnd, injuring his ankle. The man was now unable to follow any employment, as the ankle was very severely sprained. Mr. Woods paid him six weeks compensation and then told him that he could not coutinue the payments as the insurance company would not recognize any liability. Applicant gave evidence in support of this statement. In answer to Mr. Browne, he said be did not clean the windows always once a mAnth, because Mr. Woods was sometimes away. No particular day was arranged for the work.
Mr. Browne: I put it to you that Mr. Woods never arranged with you to go once a month. Applicant: He arranged with me to clean his windows.

r. Browne: Whenever occasion require]? Applicant: Yes. Further questioned, applicant said he knew he could have his old place at Longford again whenever he wanted, but he was unable to do the work ;ha it entailed carrying slates up a ladder on to the roof, using a spade and lifting heavy weights. Dr. Reginald Smith, who examined the applicant on behalf of a Friendly Society, said there was serious injury to the ankle. The bona was enlsrged and caused pain when walking or standing. He was of opinion that the applicant was not capable of doing work which entailed prolonged standing or walking. Mr. Browne said that according to the Act, the term "workman "did not include a person whose employ- ment was of a casual nature and who was employed otherwise than for the purposes of , the employer's trade or businEss. In the present case there was no agreement for permanent or periodic employment. During the last twelve months the applicant was only at the house six times, in one instance twice in One month, and he was not them s at all from August 27th to December 16th. That was not regular but only casual employment. _

Mr. t uthbert Smith submitted that there was a con- tract ten years old between the reirties that the man should go there once a month to clean the windows, that he as to have notice when he would be required to go and in the two years before last year he was there times and eleven times respectively. That was strong evidence in support of the fact that a permanent contract for periodic employment was entered into, which would roughly mean that the work was to be done monthly. _ _

His Honour said the first point be bad to consider was whether there was any agreement between the parties for the purpose referred to in the action. Applicant in his evidence did not use the w.)rd contract or agree- ment, but said there as an arrangement by which he was to clean the windows once a month. His Honour found that there was no agreement; no day or time in the month was fixed and he was only to go when sent for, at times when it suited the employer. He could not complain if the employer sought the assistance of some other uindow cleaner and be could not have brought an action had the employer engaged somebody else. Therefore in his (his Honour's) judg- ment the employment was casual and be felt himself constrained to find for the respondent. Costs were allowed on scale b, together with a quali- fying fee for Dr. Richmond.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. Before Mr. C. White (chairman), and Mr. C. Roger Parr on Wednesday.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. Before Mr. C. White (chairman), and Mr. C. Roger Parr on Wednesday.

_ MOTORISTS INED.—Reginald Bond of Chester, MS charged with driving a motor car, at a speed dangerous to the public along the Liverpool-road on the 22nd April. P.C. Houghton spoke to stopping the car at Sankey. The car was going at a speed considerable over 24 miles per hour.

Mr. A. E. Tickel of Chester, who &fended, said that at this particular spot there was a dip in the road and down this defendant allowed_the car to run' with the gas off. With regard to the speed,they had heard the evidence of the police, and would have to abide by it. It was unfair of the police, to attempt to time motorists down such a hill, in fact it was unfair to do so on any roads of the same description. He hoped the bench would see their way to deal leniently with the case.— Defendint was called and said he had no idea he was exceeding the speed limit.—He was fined lOs. Samuel Ashworth, Chester, was also fined 10s. includ- ing costs for the same offence on the same particular spot.—William Rylance, of St. Helens, was resa fined 10s._ for the same offence.
The Chairman remarked that those particular cases being the first of their kind in that court the Bench wculd deal leniently with them. They were warning cases.

These motorists were caught by police traps, the police having been instructed to watch the roads by the Sankey Parish Church. UNJUST SCALES.—John William Jackson, a green- grocer, of Sankey, was .chareed with using a pair of beam scales used for weighing potatoes that were unjust.—Defendant said they were good scales but the cotter pin had been lost and a naq substituted, this putting the scales out of balance. Defendant was tined ss.—Thomas W. Brough, baker, of Sankey Bridges, was charged with the same offence, the scales being used for weighing bread.—lnepector Kay proved the case, and said be stoppfd defendant's van and examined the scales. They were ft very old pair and were considerably out of balance.—Defendant said they never used the scales only when they were asked to weigh their loaves by customers and that was very seldom.-ss. was the fine.
LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAMBOAT
SERVICE.

From the advertising column it will to seen that the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company are announcing the regular season's .sailings. Com- mencing next Saturday, the 15th, the St. Elvies will leave the Prince's Landing Stage, Liverpool, at 10 45 a.m. for Llandudno, Beaumaris, Bangor, and Mt nai Bridge, duo hack at 7.30 p.m. Special railings are also announced for the Whitsuntide holidags, when La Marguerite takes up the daily service. We understand that last season was a record for season tickets issued, and as the company have still kept to the popular prices, and the contracts being available for Liverpool and Isle of Anglesey trips, there is no doubt the demand will increase. Special low rates are quoted for con- tracts available for any member of a family, or tram- ferable in case contractor desires to take a friend.

div.head: KNUTSFORD DIVISION.
div.p: KNUTSFORD DIVISION.
Address by Mrs A J. King on the
Children's Act.

Under the auspices of the Knutsford Liber:'l Association a public meeting was held in the Ruslo3 Rooms, Drury-lane, Knutsford, on Wednesday eveir ing when Mrs. A. J. King gave an address on "11° Children's Act, 1908."

Mr. A. L. Goodson, J.P., presiding over a g°°ll attendance, said he had great pleasure in taking the, chair that night. He might say without any for contradiction that that he had never taken the chair in his career with so much pleasure as he did tha evening. (Hear, hear.) They had assembled there that night to hear Mrs. King lecture on the Childred4 Act and he knew that she had it all at her fingq ends. As a Borough Magistrate of Knutsfar'-` he could say with authority, and at the still time with pleasure, that since the introduction the Act it was working' out most satisfactor%. Referring to the Budget, the Chairman 03 he should like to congratulate Mr. Lloyd-George 011 tb° excellence of his Budget. It was a Budget which ay?' man_ might .be proud of. It was a strong man: Budget, and it was one which taxed us all round, bu it certainly did tax those who could afford to Pa. . He felt perfectly sure that. the Budget was taxing those things which would eventually-produce in°ll revenue and that those ignorant people who talk about Protection would in a very few years see tin their cause was absolutely hopeless, because money which those new taxes would bring in wonitt enable us to pay for any expenditure that could be incurred. by any Government, whether Liberal or Conservative. (Applause). . Mrs. King gave a detailed review of the Children'T Act, in the course of which she said that a good de"f- .had been said about infant mortality. The subject u, infant mortality was one which would appeal to all them. It was especially to the mothers that should look for the uplifting of our national life. J„ had been said" What the mother is, the children are. They were sometimes told that we were haying to4ll grandmotherly legislation. They could say they liked about that, but it had been recognised dig" the child had rights as well as the parents. (Hear, hear) Twenty-five acts for the benefit of the children had bee° passed during the last three ,years. The last act wet' with the good will of and the co-operation of all partles- - interested in the children lifted it above Parti strife, and as a consequence high hopes were enter- tained for the Working of its provisions. It was the striving to help the future citizens of our count*" that we should be helping the nation. With. suck '3 infant mortality as we • had it was time that the Shit° should intervene and this they had done. We were by no means pioneers in the work of saving tf.__l° children, for Germany was ahead of us. Germany,w spite of her advantage,. in spite of her infant associa; dons had the greatest .mortality except 'Austria a-ga Russia. Continuing, she said some good work in tile way of training the mother was being done in the: towns and villages of England. She knew thg" in. div.head: HOPE OF HOLLAND.
div.p: THE HOPE OF HOLLAND.

Young Holland has played a prominent part in the celebrations in connection with the birth of a Princess to the House of Orange. A holiday was declared in all the schools, and the school children paraded the streets of the Hague all afternoon, singing and waving flags. The birth of a Dutch Ps incess relieve!. Holland of the dread of being ruled by a German Prince, and of being dominated by Germany. .
THE FLYING MA N. MR. WILBUR WRIGHT.
THE AUSTRALIAN CRICKETERS. .

Mr. Wilbur Wright, the flying man, has a.rrived in London, and will now proceed to each us how to fly. Considerable interest aitaches to Mr. Wright's visit from the fact that the War Office interids to purchase one i?f his aeroplanes, and has ..nvited him to fly az this country before its expert advisers.
THE MANAGER OF THE TEAM.

Mr. Frank Laver is again in charge of the Australian cricketers, who hava now arrived in this country, and whose presence will add considerably to the interest taken in our great summer pastime. Mr. Laver declines b prophesy the results of the Test Matches, bat he admits that he is hoping for the best.

div.head: HOPE OF HOLLAND.
div.p: THE HOPE OF HOLLAND.

The birth of an heir to the Dutch Throne was followed by an extraordinary display enthusiasm on the part of the usually staid Hollander. Young and old, rich and poor, tiave rejoiced together, and in palace and in cottage the auspicious occasion has been marked some fashion or other. Even the poorest home had its decorations, and our illustration sunws the children hanging gay garlands on the window of their humble home.
A LOTTERY PROSECUTION.

At the Chester Potty Sessional Court held at Chester Castle, on Saturday before Colonel Evans Lloyd, Judge Moss and Messrs. J. M. Frost, J. Fenna and 11. Whalley, 'l°seeh Friesner, William Friesner and Ellen Friesner, of N\ arrington and Ellesmere Port, were•charged with having on the 20;h April at Ellesmere Port sold chances in a lottery contrary to the Lotteries Act 1823. Mr. 'l'. S. Steel of Warrington, represented the defendants. A Police Sergeant stated that acting upon instructions of Superintendent Sutherland he visited the business premises of the defendants at Ellesmere Port on the elite in question. He theropurchased from the female defendant a picture post card when she handed him a coupon ticket. The ticket was numbered at each end and she tore one part of the ticket off. After waiting' sometime the numbers of the tickets sold wet° placed into a receptacle and a member of the audience was asked to draw one of the tickets. The holder of the winning ticket received a prize.. The moment this was over the female defendant began to sell more postcards and to tech purchaser she gave a ticket. She asked the witness whether he had had any hick in the la-it draw and on his telling her that he had not, she said she hoped he would do batter next time and he purchased another post card and received another ticket but did not win anything on either occasion. Mr. Steel on behalf of the defendants stated that he was not prepared to dispute the facts but the defend- ants pleaded ignorance. Joseph Friener had keen in business for some years and he first saw a similar draw at Barns in Furness. For over seven months he was in busim ss in Warrington where he started draw ing for prizes. His premises at \\Torrington were from time to time v:sited by the police and naturally he thought that the practice was in order. Jtrieph Friesner had at one time held an auctioneers license and he hoped in the future to take out another. The present was the first summons Mr. Friesner bad ever received and he was desirous that there should be no conviction against him as it might jeopardize his future position. The defend- ants through him (Mr. Steel) were prepared to give an undertaking to discontinue the practice and he (Mr. Steel) hoped that under the circumstances the police would'see their way to withdraw the summons on the defendants paying the costs.—ln answer to the chair- men, Superinttnent Sutherland said he could not with- draw the summons.—The magistrates retired and on their return the Chairman said that they were bound to recoil a conviction and the defendants must pay £1 between them and costs which amounted in all to .£1 12s. Gd.

WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
BY-GONE WARRINGTON.

We are able to print for the delectation of our readers some charming glimpses of old Warrington written in autobiographical form by the late Mr. Thomas Letherbrow. Born in Warrington in 1825 Mr. Letherbrow remembered the events of .the early thirties, and not long before his death wrote or began to write an autobio- graphy. We purpose copying in this and our next issue some passages from his manuscript. It is necessary to mention that Mr. Letherbrow was a grandson of Peter Phillips, the apostle of Independent Methodism and total abstinence. Next week we shall quote his .pen-picture of 'the famous chair-maker, and give also. some reference to Thomas Letherbrow himself.

div.head: WARRINGTON IN THE EARLY THIRTIES.
div.p: WARRINGTON IN THE EARLY THIRTIES.

Looking back more than 60 years, how vividly the old town of my childhood War- rington upon the Mersey, returns to me. It was a sleepy old town then, lying upon its broad river, circled round by calm fields and flowery hedgerows, overlooked by the dark crest of Hill Cliff and the heights Of Halton Castle, the Arpley meadow and the broad salt marshes of Cuerdley lying between. Our main street was Bridge-street which ascended from the river to the Market Gate, where the latter merged itself in Buttermarket. Half way up was Friar's Green, where stood the Chapel in which we all assembled on Sundays, and where my grandfather (Peter Phillips) an ardent disciple of Wesley, frequently preached. Here and there were quaint gabled magpie houses of the 17th century. In the midst the famous hostelry of the Red Lion reared its sign aloft, and I used to watch the swift mail coaches dashing up with sounding horns,the guards shining in scarlet and gold. Following these came an endless succession of gigs, post-chaises, vans and waggons, which crowded the highway from Manchester" to Liverpool, furnishing continual interest to the loungers and gossips at the street corners. Not far off stood the stocks, where I occasionally have seen a lusty toper bear the brunt of public derision. We all knew our neighbours,- high and low, by sight and names, and took a kindly and sociable interest in their proceedings. It seems to me as I recall, past incidents that the little town abounded in originals of the most varied type. One the most prominent was a certain so-called Captain Leigh, an old sailor, who often looked in at my grandfather's workshop. He wore a long blue coat with large brass buttons, corduroy knee breeches, white stockings, and was ornamented by a pig-tail which I used to twitch, and then vanish round a corner. Many had been old Leigh's adventures, and some of them had found their way into a contemporary newspaper or magazine and bgan widely read. His most terrible experi- ences were on board a Liverpool ship engaged in the Slave Trade. Leigh lived to a great age, and he had a novel way of celebrating his.birthday. With two or three particular cronies he used to drive in a cart through the principal streets arrayed in his Sunday clothes. His grave stone inscribed with his name was reared up in the cart, a barrel of ale occupied another corner, and he treated his acquaintances to free drinks en route. stopping at intervals_ to sing "Rule Britannia" and various other national ditties.

Such small diversions made a town show. We had no concerts, no penny readings, nor guilds, nor Shakespeare societies, and our dim-fronted,poorly-lighted shops gavesmall promise of the rich Cheshire cheese and „,mood • farmers' hams• and butter to be found within. But then there were no flaring gin vaults, nor hordes of male and female noodlums, dirty and blasphemous; thrift, decency, and restraint pervaded society, and a wholesome reverence for one's "betters."

div.head: DIVERSIONS ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: DIVERSIONS ON THE MERSEY.

The pride and glory of our town, along with its old church and its mail coaches and the red brick houses of the gentry, was the river, the world-renowned Mersey. I used to watch it foaming and trembling under the bridge near which the old quay packet used to start daily for Manchester. Another great source of interest were the loch and weir. In the season we could see the big salmon leaping, and there I once beheld a lordly sturgeon captured. On the river wall near the bridge you would see on most fine days a row of anglers, and on the water's edge I and my eldest brother used to catch " stocking needles" (sniall eels), now and then tumbling in and being carried away. I had once a narrow escape of being drowned under the arch of the bridge, but I soon learned to swim, seeming to take to the water from instinct. Another absorbing delight was to watch the fishermen draw in their nets, all rolling and flashing silver, loaded with sparlingg. There was no end to the
riverside delights of old Warrington sixty- five years ago.

What a place it was for boys! I used to go to school to keep me out of danger, but they gave me very few lessons, the three R's being the limit of instruction. The river and the fields were my school, and the summer skies, then undimmed by the hideous smoke raised from the hundred chimneys of the Warrington of to-day. Great was our excitement when the river was in flood after long rains in the Cheshire and Derbyshire hills. It swept down with resistless force from Wilderspool, past Runcorn, Hale and Frodsham, turning Arpley Meadows and the salt marshes into a vast lake. The seagulls came up in thousands and whitened the muddy shores, rising in clouds when a gun was fired. It was great excitement to punt about in this vast lake, and rather dangerous, but my uncles were the boatmen, and knew hav to avoid the sunk stakes and submerged , hedgerows. Being only a few years older than myself we were like playmates. We did not reach home till dusk, muddy, wet, happy, and hungry, and how sweet was our sleep after a supper of butter" milk and porridge under the roof of our childhood.' _ _

An avenue of noble elms then shaded the way to Arpley Meadows. They have been Icing since poisoned by the fumes of chemical works, and only one or two' skeleton trunks remain. There I used to wander for hours, losing myself among fields of wheat and barley, and now and then coining upon a hidden pool hung by alder trees and willows, where our nurse girl told me dwelt a certain Jenny Greenteeth which would seize me .by the hair and drag me down if Iswent there in the dusk.
And these fair scenes have been defaced or blotted out altogether, and it is many decades since the salmon ceased to ascend the river, and the fishermen to ply their nets.

MY LIFE STORY. _

I was born in the quiet little village of Aston, about one mile from Preston Brook and .three miles from Frodsham, on April 10th, 1840. My _parents were in poor and humble circumstances, my father being an ordinary labouring man in receipt of 10s. per week in winter and 12s. in summer. My mother was of weak constitution, and suffered for many years from asthma, dying when I was twenty years of age. My father afterwards became under-gardener to the late Sir Arthur Aston, G.C.8., of Aston Hall, and later succeeded to the more responsible position of head gardener there. He passed away when I had reached the age of twenty- five, and I had to take out letters of adminis- tration. In the days of my infancy Ido not recollect anything special or extraordinary taking place, but my early instruction was received in a small cottage on Aston Heath, kept by a village dame who attended to her household duties and instructed me and eight or ten other children at the same time, in reading, but not in writing, arithmetic or grammar, which were not thought necessary at that period, especially for a poor cottager's children. At the age of nine I was sent to work at a farm house for a penny a day, the hours being from six in the morning until seven or eight in the evening. It was with feelings of pride and great joy that I took my weekly wages home to my mother on Saturday night, knowing that I had con-. tributed something towards the household expenses. Bread, tea, sugar and other articles of food were about as dear again as they are at the present day. Our family consisted of father, mother, two sons and one daughter, all of them now being dead except my-self. I afterwards went to work with my fathier in the gardens at Aston Hall, at - a higher wage,namely sixpence a day,and later, eightpence. I should at this time be from ten to thirteen years of age 'and when a little over that nge,and after considerable thought, I left home and went to reside and work at Halton, near Runcorn, remaining there for over six years. Here it was that I came under the religious influence and example of a good and truly Christian man—the late Mr. John Woodier—and so beneficial was that influence upon my young mind, as well as the fact of often being in the company of -other good and religious men and women, that I firmly resolved that their company, religion and God should be Aline. These men were members and officials of the Primitive Methodist Church there, and there was also a mission cottage in Halton-lane, Runcorn. My final and decided resolve was made on February 24th, 1857, when I was sixteen years of age. I became a member on trial and a Primitive Methodist, although I had hitherto been accustomed regularly to attend the Sabbath school and services of the Established Church and was taught by and sat under the ministry of a good and faithful minister, the Rev. Edward Marsden, M.A., whom I have always looked upon with the greatest respect and reverence. All those good men mentioned above, who lived in or near Halton, have passed away. When about seventeen years of. age, I and some other youthful converts were called upon to assist in the services of the mission held in Halton- road, and although our efforts were feeble and short, we nevertheless held some good and helpful meetings. On the afternoon of Good Friday, 1857, I and three other young converts, about sixteen or Seventeen years of age, were appointed to conduct our first revival service in s_the.

Primitive Methodist -aim- p—ei in the villagb of Halton. This being noised about, there was a large congregation for the four youths to stand up before. We all attended to our appointment, after great efforts and prepara- tion, and amidst the excitement of the whole village we managed to get through the ser- vice in about three-quarters of an. hour—all 'four of us having taken part. I may mention here that one of the four is the Rev. T. H. Hunt, of Bolton, an ex-president of the Primitive Methodist Connexion, who has been called upon to fill most of the important offices in connection with the denomination. In July next he conies to reside in Runcorn, and to take charge of the churches in the Preston Brook and Runcorn station, and no- one will be more pleased to welcome him than the writer of this brief story, after fifty years service in the church of our youthful choice. At the age of seventeen I became a lay- preacher in the Primitive Methodist Con- nexion,so that over two years ago I celebrated my jubilee as such. During that time I have filled many offices of trust and responsibility. On several occasions I have represented the circuit in its district meetings and once I had the honour of being one of the eight representatives of the Liverpool district in the Conference held at Nottingham. Of the names of lay preachers which appeared on the Warrington, Preston Brook and Runcorn circuits plan when I became a preadier, mine is the only one now remaining. Most of Them have been called to their reward. I have also seen the changing in those circuits of over forty ministers. One of the most significant coincidences in my life was that in my jubilee year as a lay preacher I was one of the appointed representatives of the Connexion at the great centenpxy camp meet- ing held on Mow Cop in 1907. The numbers attending on the Sunday were estimated at 100,000 and they heard The gospel preached from many preaching stands. The gather- ing was supposed to be the largest of its kind ever held in England, if not in the world. I have also often been called upon to give my se,rvices for the benefit of other evangelical churches in the neighbourhood, namely, the Church of England, Congregationalists, Baptists, Presbyterians, Wesleyans, Independent Methodists (in whose church at Lymm I was called upon to preach school sermons on Sunday week', April 25th), and others. In

many of my services I have seen much good done and the churches benefited, and this has often given me encouragement to con- tinue in the work. This story is too short to tell the many and _remarkable incidents which have come under my observation during my lifetime. Whilst at times I have in years past, after walking twelve and fifteen miles to conduct or take part in services, seen large congregations, especially at camp meetings held from thirty to forty years ago , when hundreds and thousands attended, on other occasions I have 'walked similar distances and found only small congregations. For instance, I have walked to the Old-road Chapel in Latchford from Aston, a distance of seven or eight miles, and had a congregation of six or eight in the evening and not so many in the afternoon. It is a source of gratifica- tion to see the largely increased con- gregations at Legh-street Church, War- rington, where. I conducted services on' Sunday last.

I have often been to various churches in the neighbourhood of Delamere Forest and other places equally far, to conduct services and have had to walk home some twelve or fifteen miles after the evening service had concluded at eight o'clock, arriving home at midnight and sometimes early on Monday morning. About forty-five years ago I walked to a village about fifteen miles from Warrington where services were held in the evening in the large kitchen of a farm hose. On my arrival there one very, warm 'after- noon, perspiring and somewhat tired, half-an-hour before the time of the services, the good lady of the house invited me to sit down and rest while she got some refresh- ments ready for me. She soon placed some- thing on the table, with the remark "There now, get those and they will help you to preach to-night." To my astonishment, the refreshments consisted of some large pieces of bread and cheese and a pint of foaming ale in a pint cup. Of course, I thanked her for her kind hospitality. I will leave the reader to guess whether I partook of her bounteous liberality in its entirety or not. On many occasions I have taken food in my pocket when I have been conducting services some distance from home and have partaken of it in the fields or country lanes between the hours of service.

One foggy and frosty Sunday morning in the depth of winter, I had an appointment to preach at Ellesmere Port,near Birkenhead, morning and evening. The roads being unknown to me, I found myself about five miles fro-n my destination at 9.3 o—an hour before th service time—in the midst of a dense fo having then walked some eight or nine mil .8. I began to think I was lost and that I should be compelled to return, but by resolution and perseverance I arrived at Ellesmere Port about twenty-five minutes to eleven. After taking the morning service, one of the officials came to me and said "Yoh have to go to Pooltown and take the service there in the kitchen of a farm- house this afternoon." After some inquiry I found that Pooltown was about two and a half miles away, across some fields. Having walked there, I was sur- prised to find in one corner of the kitchen a pulpit from Which the preacher conducted the service. At the close of- the meeting there, I had to walk back to the evening service at Ellesmere Port. This was a fair sample of local preachers' appointments fifty years ago, and there were no other means of fulfilling them except by walking, railways being almost unknown—not to speak of motor cars. One may imagine the sacrifices many of these good and noble men made. There have been many and great improve- ments since those days, smaller circuits, shorter distances to travel, better roads and ' greater facilities in every respect.

- On more than one oCcasio-n I have been Providentially preserved rom danger and probable death. When about the age of thirteen, I well remember attempting to talc a sparrow's nest a considerable height amongst the ivy which partly covered the walls of Aston Church. Ascending a ladder which I reared against the wall, I found the nest was still out of reach. I climbed on to
the topmost rung, and was holding to the ivy above my head when tlie ladder slipped away and I was left in a perilous position, clinging to the ivy some twelve feet or more

from the ground, expecting every minute that the ivy would 'break away from the wall. However, I managed gradually to lower myself about six feet and then dropped safely to the ground. On another occasion, many years after, I had just passed over Wilderspool Crossings when an express train from Bank Quay station dashed through the gates, which for some reason had not been opened, smashing them to fragments which were flung about in all directions. However, I escaped unhurt. Some thirty years or more ago I was the representative of a business firm in Liver- pool, my duty being to go to many parts of the country in their interests. One Monday morning I received instructions to proceed to Derby by the first express from Central Station, Warrington. The express was due at nine o'clock and I hastened from home at Stockton Heath to catch it, but on arriving at the top of the steps I had the disappointment of seeing the train just leaving the platform. However, I went by another express about two and a half hours later. Stockport was the first regular stopping place, but about a mile outside that town the train came to a standstill and on looking out of the window along the line I was startled to see that the first express, by which I had hoped to travel, had run at full speed into a coal siding, smashing up some trucks of coal. The engine had been. thrown off the line, the carriages were badly damaged, men were engaged iit carrying injured passengers away on stretchers, and the line was blocked. I fell down on my knees in thankfulness for my deliverance from this peril. Once I was conducting an evening service at Wrexham and. had announced as my text "I am a stranger with thee" when, a man in the middle of the chapel called out "Not to me, thou'rt not." This took me by surprise but the service was gone through in an orderly way and concluded quietly. On another occasion whilst holding a mission service outside a public house in a village seven miles from Warrington, some men who had been drinking rather too freely threw open the window and holding out a jug of beer invited me to partake of the beverage. I refused and the men quietened down and afterwards some of them became good mem- bers of our society there. At Penny Ford in Wales a professor was announced to take some anniversary services but being unable to fulfil his engagement, he prevailed upon me-to take his place, without the people knowing anything about the change. They expected some learned and titled professor was coming amongst them and some of the Other places of worship in the neighbourhood were'closed in order that their people might come and hear him. The result was that every seat in the chapel was occupied, the aisles were crowded with people, and many were unable to gain admission. It only then became apparent to me that I had made a great mistake in my promise, for I was only about twenty years of age. However, with much fear and trembling I made my

way through the crowd and reached the pulpit. The people soon found out that I was not the professor, but after an explan- ation I managed to get through a service which I shall never forget in my life-time. It was a lesson and an experience. How- ever, there Was a good collection and that was one consolation under the circumstances.

During the fifty years and more that I have been engaged in the work I have /travelled over 12,000 miles, and preached at or taken part in some 5,000 or 6,000 services. I am moderately active and healthy and still take services in many of the Primitive Methodist and other churches in the district,. It was in 1868 that I came from Higher Walton to Stockton Heath, then an insignifi- cant little village of not more than 500 inhabi- tants.ln the year 1871-2 I became President of the Stockton Heath Band of Hope and took an active part in many of its meetings. I had the privilege, of meeting some of the founders of the Society and it may interest your readers to know that I laboured with one of the worthy pioneers of total abstinence whose name is on the fitting memorial unveiled by Mrs. Dodds last week —William Clarke, senior. I have filled many responsible and important offices in connec- tion with our beautiful suburban and con- stantly improving village. For' many years I have been a member of the Parish Council and Parochial Committee and I also hold the office of chairman of the Lighting Committee, which makes large demands upon one's time. I have been senior overseer for a considerable time and until recently was a member of the Runcorn Rural District Council and Board of Guardians. Over twelve months ago I was unanimously appointed a representative manager of the village day schools where- some 800 scholars are in attendance.
MR. JAMES WHITLEY OF STOCKTON HEATH.

div.head: OUR MISCELLANY.
div.p: OUR MISCELLANY.

The claim made on behalf of Warrington, that it is the birthplace of the Total Abstinence Movement has been widely mentioned in the public press during the past eight or ten days, and we have watched with some curiosity to see whether Preston would make any reply. Up to the present the" seven men" have found no vindicator or even apologist. But some sort of state- ment is certainly due. For years past Mr. William-Livesey, the nonagenarian son of Joseph Livesey, and his friends have plied the press with paragraphs on each anniver- sary of the supposed pledge signing at Preston. During the past six years they and the editors of the Preston newspapers have had placed before them in detail the claims of Warrington and no reply to these has been attempted. We think the time has come when Preston should receive an emphatic invitation to "Speak now or hence- forth for ever, hold her peace."
The famous inscription " Bill Stumps his mark" which so puzzled Mr. Pickwick and his Antiquarian friends is almost equalled by an inscription upon a grave stone in the grave yard at Hill Cliffe.
ELIZABETHS EDDONTHEWIF EOFJOSHUASEDDO N 1672.
It would be difficult to find a stone, lettered with such a splendid disregard for spacing as this memorial to the wife of Joshua Seddon.

It is commonly understood that the old Baptist Chapel at Hill Clae was erected in a place which was so secluded as to be almost a spot of hiding. Those who have visited the neighbourhood during recent months must have bee la struck with the changes that are rapidly taking place. Villadom has pushed its way almost to the front door of the chapel, and the crest of the Hill has been chosen as the site for imposing houses. It would seem that this once-hidden shrine is soon to be the Centre of a villa suburb of Warrington. And remembering the tranquil beauties of the slopes of Hill Cliffe one does not know whether to be glad or sorry. ** * *

A paragraph from a Chester newspaper records a curious fungus growth upon the wall of a cottage in that city. From between the joints of a brick wall there grew a mush- room which measured eight inches in diameter without any apparent rootage save the mortar of the wall. Our readers may be interested to know that such phenomena have been very 'common in Stockton Heath during the past year at two. In a seven- year-old cottage the tiled floor of the kitchen began to7rise and was lifted several inches. The cause was found to be a bed of mush- rooms which had grown underneath. In an adjacent house mushrooms began to grow from a joint in the wall which did not exceed three-eighths of an inch in depth. From this a succession of fungi grew. Two extra- ordinary mushrooms, twelve inch ff in diameter, umbrella shaped, and two-and-a- half inches thick, succeeded each 'other. These were followed by a huge flat-topped mushroom fourteen inches in diameter and two inches thick. The owner, feeling that he had attained sufficient fame as a grower of fungus, destroyed whatever roots existed by an applic4tion of chemicals. The most remarkable aspect of these growths is the apparent absence of any kind of rootage except the bricks and mortar of which the wall is composed.

It is reasonable to take pride in longevity, and a very good thing to leave it as a legacy to others. This very proper pride inspired the veteran Cheshire lady who thus dictated her epitaph: "In memory of Hannah, wife of John Wood, who departed this life June 17th, 1871 in her 98th year. She has left six sons whose united ages are 392." We were able to copy the inscription not long ago from the stone which stands on the north side of Woodford Church.

On the English side Sir George Heron was killed and Sir J. Forster, Sir J. Collingwood, the Earl of Redford's son, and a good many other distinguished Englishmen were taken prisoners, it would seem no account was kept of the number of common Englishmen killed or captured."

• 4, The Walk, Hampstead, London, NAV: • .„ September 28th, 1005. Dear Monsieur 7ilarman,—The inquiries set up for me by the French Consul, of which I spoke to you in a recent letter, appear to have been without fruit. . I am, therefore, craving your kind service once more in my interest .and begging your diligence.

It is known to you wthat I -have married Dlademoiselle Mimi, who cost- us so pretty an adventure at Rainey together; but the cir- cumstance of my marriage and my wife's own solicitude make it more necessary than ever that I should be put in possession of all the facts which inquiry and patience may disclose concerning her birth and parentage. I know no one in Paris to whom I would as soon commit my interests na to you, and I hereby beg of you to accept -the service and to spare no expense to further it. From what the Consul has been so good as to tell me, y•bur inquiries will be best pursued in the neighbourhood of Orleans, and especially at the house of the old woman Marie, if she. be still living and capable of answering any viestions at all. There is another circumstance—so shadowy that I mention it with hesitation, but so fill! .of remote possibility that I. have no right to withheld it. For some days now, I have had the idea that this little house of mine in Lon- don is being watched. • Possibly my .feats are altogether groundless. We have led an eccentric .life in this place and have carried here some of the habits and practiCes with which Paris made us familiar. These may have provoked the curia,ity of the neigh- bours -pr of others who have heard of them by rumour. Be that as it may, my wife has been much alarmed upon more than one occa- sion, and I am not without-, my fears that we are upon the threshold of a greater mys- tery than any which has yet attended her ad-:;enturous life. I may add that there is just one man in Paris who, in my wife's judgment, should have been sought out by us before bnt has escaped our observation and eluded our reckoning. He is a burly ruffian who fre- quents the old Cafe of the Assassins, and he is often to be found there nowadays. They know him by the name of .Jean-le-Mont. a title by which_ you" will readily discover. him.
I commend this man to your" notice as one -sato might be able to help you. Meanwhile. accept the assurance of my profound con• sideration.—And permit me to remain, Yours very faithfully,
HENRY GASTONARD
I enclose a draft for a hundred poundo. You are to draw upon me immediately ft•r any further sums you may require.
CHAPTER XXVI.
[Madame Mimi writes a letter to P:uld!' O'Connell.]
The Hotel Afetropole, Brighton, Sitnclay.

Dear Great Big Mon-sieTt-i'l'acl-dy,—l can- not very much -write the English as now, but I shall have to say to you What is not proper: Why do you tell me the untrue thingi*, about ray husband—that he is the poor man and no more shall have any of tile meneys? Is it, Monsieur Paddy, because the men always 'think they are good when they tell the un- truth to the lady. But I know, and lam angry, very angry with yon. You shall never tell me untrue things again—jamais de ma vie.

I would tell you that we have gone away from the Hampstead to the border of the sea. If Harry had not the moneys he could not have led me here in the big motor-car—so big, Monsieur Paddy, that we could have put you in it as well. And we have come to -the hotel, and I am so frightened of the people and I think I shall run away'. But Harry says no—and I remain, for I could not be, oh, not for a little single hour, away from the place where mon man i dwell. So I stay, but am very sad—dear friend, if you would -understand how sad I am!

Why do the men come ,to my lionise and watch me? I do not say to my husband half the things I know, for that vhall make Mm afraid also. Is it, Monsieur Padd-.-, that someone hates me for being hici Ivife.? Shall Toll think that Madame Lea sends the men? he is not the woman who may forget him— how well I remember it, and how often I' tell it by myself when no one is in the apartment with me. She will not forget--that clever, wicked Madame Lea who love all the men for moneys but not any at all for, the love. _ _ .

It was because I have been afraid that my husband brought mc to the border of the sea. We have put on all our clothes and are very beautiful. I must not sing as I. walk to and fro/and if the music makes me want to dance I must hold myself down upon my bane. All the afternoons the monde goes up and down in a carriage—such gros monsieurs with fur round their. necks, and the English. lady who is so sad aud makes her shoulders bare before -she sits down to dinner.

I like the sun and I like the sea—the great big wild sea, where across so far is my be- loved France. I am very happy w:th my hus- band, but, oh, so much afraid, that I wake in the night and lay my head upon his breast and cry -myself because he is there and I am his wife. Ah, Monsieur- -Paddy, how unhappy to be no one—never to have 'known that you 'were a litt:c child and that you had a home. I am that, and I am ashamed because it has been so—that I am not as the others, and that ray husband shall never be proud of me be- cause of what I was AVINa I left my father's house.

Will you not write to me, my dear Mon- sieur Paddy, and tell me how wrong I am? Do not refuse Mimi the Simpleton. She is very simple still, dear Monsieur Paddy, and she have no right to believe that her happi- ness is not the dreanr tvhich vill pass away. Why did you go from us to your desert country? Why did you leave us? It was not kind, Monsieur—and you be ye been our friend. All the others is gone away the Chevalier, the wicked Monsieur Oleander, the kind Monsieur Barrymore. They have taken my husband's money and gone. away—ah, quel drole du monde! Mais vous,—Well, I shall forgive you, for you will come back to me. And you will write the 'letter to say that I am wicked and that I must not be afraid., And please to tell me that it is not Madame Lea, and that my hus- band will never see her—never as long as we both shall live.—Your devoted, MIMI GASTONARD.
cL.,,
CHAPTER XXV.
