not flatter you at all, but if it's the watching that you're after, come °Arta to this getting country, and you shall have five and fifty men on the first tee to see you off, and as many of the women behind them to declare you'd be pretty if it wasn't for your 9aytures." So have dohe with your nonsense ! I'll be writ- ing Harry this very day and giving him a word of my mind about all that you tell me. He's made strange friends in his days of seedtime, and they're above the -ground now at the harvest. the way we men have 'em, my dear. We sow friendships in our youth and often enough reap thistles in our old age. Harry was wise to take You away, and I hope he'll keep you in the same place. There's nothing like- change, though precious iittle of that same comes the way of Paddy O'Connell. To me the world is all the '.same, my dear—just -a- great grass field with a lot of Band-pits therein, and your Paddy in one of them for a certainty. What d'ye think, the fellows here had the impudence to do this morning? Why, to fol- low me and old Colonel Willis when We were playing a round of the golf. He's a very wicked habit of using bad language, which I have no mind to be listening to, and when I saw a crowd about the first tee, I asked them what they supposed they had come out to see. And what do you 'think they answered me? "Why," says one of *hem, we haven't come here to :ee=we've come here- to listen." Be hanged to their impudence. There's one point in your letter which I haven't spoken of, Mimi, and I speak of it now unwillingly. 'Twould be about the Lea woman. Be sure/that Harry will see- no more of her.. I say it, and Paddy O'Connell makes no mistakes in a matter of this kind. He's done with her—he wi.sited to be done with her a year ago but she. wouldn't let him. And ask yourself this, my -dear—when a -man has got the woman he wants, is he likely to want the woman he hasn't got? Think -no more of it, I say. -Be off with him to all the places where there's music to be heard and bright people to be seen, and let me hear of the brave little girl I used -to know in Paris, and will never forget. So here's my love to you wrapped up in a bit of' a letter and posted in the great Irish country. 'Tis no great spirit I'm writing in, but you'd never understand all the trouble that comes to a man who's taking three on the greens where he ought to take two, and can never hold a hand at the cards without some- body insulting him. To the devil .with them all! They- put two aces of .hearts in the pack of cards I played Bridge with last night, and me not discovering it until the second rubber. Would ye wonder that I walked out of the window and btnged it after .me.. I, write to Harry by this post. If he shouldn't show you the letter, don't pretend to know .what's in it. But its wisdom, env-dear, and that's a rare commodity in these clays.—God bless- you— and,
PADDY O'CONNELL.
CHAPTER XXVIII.
[The Same Author addresses Henry Gaston- rad at the Hotzl Metropole, Brighton.] The Headland Hotel, Portrush, Ireland.
October 2nd; _1905

Dear Harry,—What's all 'this now about your trouble at home and the men that are looking after you? Is it dreams, or is spirits about? I hear from your angel of a wife that some nonsense has come into both your heads. And I haven't the patience to hear it—so- there's .the truth. _ - .

Now, you have got to be up and doing, and acting the man's part. Remember, you have made as odd a marriage—but as wise a one—as any man that ever put a ring in .his waistcoat pocket, and couldn't find it there when the parson asked him. Mimi is a little wild animal that you took from the prairie— as soft as silk, PA gentle to • your band; but, man, with the blood of --the prairie in her veins. Remember this every day you get up from her side—she's the daughter of say: ages, and her birthright will cry out for a hearing sometimes. What are all these fears of hers? Are they not the alarm of the gazelle which sniffs a lion on the sky line, and would be moving? What are the mad outbreaks you speak of—the frenzied desire for change and movement? Are they not born of the same impulse which sends a wild pony scampering through the forest and keeps him at it until he's exhausted? . Be very patient with -her. The man who would keep a- wild bird well should not begrudge the money he spends for a decent cage—and a large one to boot. To be plain with you, Harry, I'd be less troubled about your good little wife if I had a better story to tell of her husband. You say • that you are planning a scheme which will surprise me presently, Did you ever hear tell of the South Sea Bubble where a rogue made a fortune by advertising .a busi- ness "presently to be discicsed? " Paddy O'Connell . is not the • one to be putting his hopes for you in any company like that. Pe up and doing; •do you realise that in a tew months you'll have no more than a bank clerk, and with a power of spending which would shame the Jam of Rorypore ? Did 'I tell you that I had a letter from America which guve me some concern for a few days? A fellow wrote me that he had discovered a gold mine, and, being an old •friend of my father's, had put me down at the beginning for fifty shares. "These," says the man, "arc now worth about a thou- sand apiece, and there is gold banked against your name in New York. to that amount." All that I had to do was to send him a cheque for five hundred and forty pounds, the unpaid call on the shares. Be- dad, I'd have done it but for McCarthy, the solicitor, who's the finest nose in Ireland fcr scenting out a "do," - and was on the rat be- fore he'd .got half way out of. his hole. "Why," says he, "this is the gold brick over again." "What brick?" asks 1, ast onishcd.
"The gold brick," says he; "if you go out there, he'll show you a lump of gold as big as a Kerry flint, and there'll be lead inside of the same."

"You've no trust in humanity," says .1— aII d "Devil a bit " says he—so I'm keeping my money, though I've heard of a little scheme for shipping Irish horses to the gold- fields 'of- Alaska, which should be worth something if worked by honest men. Ay, and that's the rub. Henry, my boy, where do the honest men hide themselves these days? I'd sooner look for an old ball in a bunker full- of stones than try to find one of the same. .

You must be coming to Ireland and bring- ing Mimi with you. We'll show her the wild man's country together, and, perhaps, be teaching her the golf. 'Tis true that neither of us can play, but, my dear boy, the best teachers in the world are those who know. nothing themselves, as you'll observe both in the realms of • art and literature, to say nothing of those of sport. Bring the child over and let's cheer her up awhile, ill warrant there'll be men enough to watch her; but she won't be afraid of them, devil a bit.—Your friend, as ever. PADDY.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIX
div.p: CHAPTER XXIX
[Henry Gastonard makes an urgent appeal to Jules Farman. of the Rue du Quatre Sep- tembre, Parrs.] 4, The Walk, Hampstead. October 11th, 1905. Dear M. Farman,—Your response to .my

div.head: CHAPTER XXVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVII.
[Paddy O'Connell replies to 31lini's letter.] The Headland Hotel, Portrush, Ireland, October 2nd, 11103.

, Dear. Mimi,—Your pretty letter came to me in confidence, my (lewd; or I would have answered you with a telegram. Though, to be sure, 'what a man puts in a telegram is pri- vate enough, neither he nor • anyone. else being able to make head nor tail of it sometimes. What I wanted to say to you was just this— that you are a foolish little girl to write to me as you did; though there's no one I'd sooner hear from, and no One whose letter' i'd be readier to. answer. What's all this nonsense about the men that watch you, Mimi? Don't the men' always watch a pretty woman anyway? I'll

div.head: "He was quite dead."
div.p: "He was quite dead."

nrgent telegram that yon should leave Paris and come to me innuctliately. brings the re- ply that you cannot leave until to-morrow. I am therefor 2 writing you this letter wiAli what composure I can in the face .of this dreadful event, that you may be in possession of all the fkots before you leave Paris, and able to deal with them there, if they are Of service to you. .

It was at nine o'clock last Sunday night that I first diovered the crime which had been committed in my *house. I had been absent, perhaps the best part of an hour, making a call upon a friend who desired to consult me upon a French ,picture he pur- chased recently. We rettirned from Brigh- ton upon the previous afternoon, my wife apparently having overcome those hallucina- tions witich have troubled her for some weeks . past, and being • quite reconciled to the pros- pect of a continued residence at Hampstead. She was in no way unhappy at the thought of being'. alone, nor did I have any scruples about leaving her. My, suspicions were first awakened when I discovered that my friend had not written to me at ell, and that the letter which I. received from him Wa6 a clever but undoubted forgery. You may imagine with what haste I went back to Hampstead. I had left my wife- •at the piano in the sitting-room, where, -the weather being chilly, a -bright fire burned; but I perceived immediately I e.pproeched the house that it was in darkness, although a glimmer upon the blind still spoke of the firelight. This alarmed me greatly. I tried to open the font door with my latchkey, but found that the bolt had been slipped. A loud knock and ring obtained no answer. , I was now seriously alnrmed, as you may suppose; and being determined to obtain instant ad- mittance to the house, I smashed the large pane of glass in the sitting-room, and entered without further delay. -

I have told you that I left my wife in this room, s?ated at the piano in the further cor- ner near the French window by which you pass out to the garden. That she had been called away without warning was proved, by the •fact that One of the 'candles still guttered in its socket, though too faintly to give any light, and that the sheet of music lay upon the floor, indicating that she had been turn- ing the very page when the summons came to her. SaYtt foi the fact that the fire burned low and that the electric light was switched off, there was nothing else in this place to excite suspicion. • I called my wife loudly by name, going to the window and hoping to _find her in the garden.. She did not answer me. I returned to the hall, and immediately discovered the body of the man.

Some of the: ncspaper, I remember. say that he was tt Spaniard. I should pronounce him nothing of the kind, but one of your 0-WTI countrymen who had lived long in the Souin. When I found him he was quite dead, and had fallen forward upon a wicker seat at the foot of the stairs. To this, perhaps, he had staffgered after the. blow wan struck. I could not at the first detect APT mark upon his body, nor did I wish to C)clieve that he Wa3 dead ; but, running out into the 6treet to give the alarm, I 6ent one of my neighbours for the police, another for a doctor. The latter told us the worst immediately. The man had been struck down by a heavy itn;. plement ; skull had been fractured, and he was dt2ad. •

It is not my intention, in such a letter as this, to dwell upon my own state of mind at such a moment, or to relate to you the tri- vial incidents of such a momentous hour. My wife's d.sappearance.. the evidence of a con- flict in .the hall, the. wild tales told by the neighbours, were but the first- fruits of .a tragedy which paralysed my faculties. To all their questions i could , give only the vaguest answers. I told tlmn that I 'know nothing of the wretched man who had been struck down in my house ; I could give them no clue as to the purpose of big visit. I bad never seen him before, did not know him, could not imagine any business which should bring him to my house. To the police I. confessed Madame Mimi's stofy of men ‘vho had watched her and of vague fears which had haunted her. They pressed me for particulars more minute, and I could not answer tlim. Nor did I perceive their drift then as I perceive it now. They bolieve, incredible as the lippc..-iition is. that the murdered man had been one. of my wiCe's lovers in Paris,. that be • visited her secretly. and that for oome reason at present undis- closed she has murdered him.

.1 must tell you the plain truth: I,can keep nothing from you. London speaks Of little else than this appalling crime; nor ein'.l sure that the voice of popular opinion does not agree with the cruel assumptions of those officially in charge of this case. I have, my dear Farman, lyen associated with you in much that concerns my private life, end always in the cause of one dear to me and to whom my happiness is for ever linked. You. will imagine my situation this day in England. I• am alone in my house, and there is a hue and cry in the streets for the woman I love more than anything on earth. . I, can say nothing to which the world will listen in her defence. My letter to, the newspapers is printed by some, by others withheld es indiscreet. The police them- selves but repeat a parrot's tale—" The -man came to the house; he was my wife's lover; he was killed by her, aided, it may be, by some of toe disreputable friends she knew in Paris and who are liow hiding. her for their own_ ends.", _ _ _

Admit, my friend, the preposterous nature of this assumption. You have known the child that the Butte called Mimi La Gediche. Is not her whole story a refutation of this calumny most base? Did iihe not guard her virtue in a circle where the very name • of virtue has long been forgotten? Were not her gentleness, her charity, her forbearance the wonder even of the outcasts among whom. i she was thrown? And this • child s noii charged with a lover and with his murder! Oh, monstrous, I say! most monstrous and damnable, as I will presently prove to them. In a common .way, I have now no right to speak of fortune; but I have. been saving of my resources, and still peas a few thou- sand pounds of my own, every penny of which goes to the purpvie of my wife's vin- dication. If others fail. I will find her. If these vigilant • police cannot track her down. I will do so, going by night and day to my task until the truth is known and justice ac- complished. Be you my friend in this, I beg of you. By all that is of old association and friendship, stand by me now and bring your magnificent resources to my aid. I should tell you that the murdered man was apparently forty years of age, small of stature, With a trimmed black beard and a wealth of black hair slightly speckled with grey. He was very well dres.sdli, apparently a man of the world—but there -is nothing on . . . - Ile was nor any Ono

as yet to. his 3dentity. Cross to London, I beg of you, and help us to identify him. Our work will begin when that is done; it can- not begin before. So I repeat, come without delay to a man whoee friends stand apart from him but who3e faith ia unshaken. HENRY GASTONARD.

div.head: CHAPTER XXX.
div.p: CHAPTER XXX.

[Jules Farman sell& to Henry Gastonard some account of his stewardship.] ~The 7-- Inn, Hampstead, October 16th, 1903. Dear Sir,—l am sending this by a -trusty hand to the New Travellers' Club in Picca- dilly as your eetecmed instructions command me.

I have to-day viewed the body of the mur- dered man and am glad .to tell you that I was immediately able to identify him. Ile is the Count d'Antoine, who had an apartment in the Rue Boissiers at ~Paris, and is far from being unknown to our best , society. I had the honour to be employed by the Count some three years ago upon a mission whose particulars do not concern us. He was of an cld family cf the Antoines, of Picardy, a well-known shot and horseman, and by no means an idle member of the Jockey Club. During recent years his for- tunes have been at a low ebb, but he made friendohips which served him well. particu- larly that of the Marquis de Saint Faur, Who will he desolated to, hear this grifrrous news. I will say at once that I am utterly un- able to imagine any cause of association be- tween Madame Gaatonard and this poor gentleman. He was not a frequenter of the artistic world; had, to my knowledge, no in- terest in books and pictures; had set foot in Montmartre perhaps 'twice in the whole course of his life. This I am able to tell veal because I found it necessary to go into you details of his career somewhat closely when I had the honour to act for him.

I am compelled; .Monsieur; to address you very plainly, and to -speak at this moment as I would hesitate to do at any other. The assumption upon the part of the police in London that Count Antoine bad been at one time the lover of Madame Gastouard is not supported by any evidence, and is to me en- tirely .incredible. I shall refuse to give serious consideration to such a supposition until I am compelled to do so by testimony I cannot refuse. And- I would beg you not to bestow upon it a second thought.. • We are therefore confronted by this per- plexing fact.: That a man, distinguished in French society, but knowing nothing of Lon- don, goes over to England to see a _lady of whom he had no previous 'knowledge; that he visits her in a remote quarter of -the city when she is alone; that he is followed there by ethers and murdered ift her very presence. To this there can be out One explanation. The. Count d'Antoine was the instrument of some secret embassy; he desired to see Madame alone; but hi S purpose was known to others, who followed him, and defeated it at the last moment. Let us analyse toe more material evidence for this. And first, the desire to see Madame alone. Is it possible to believe that the Count's arrival at the moment of your absence Could have been coincidence—especially when your own habits are remembered, and the rare oc- casions when you quit your house , after nightfall? More probable in every way is the assumption that he had watched the house for some days; waited patiently for his opportunity, and availed himself imme- diately of your absence.'

None the less, the fttet is significant—for this is done, observe, not by a low fellow, possibly a blackmailer or a beggar, but by a rt,,nch • gentleman of position, one justly esteemed for his honourable actious, and quite incapable of any dishonour in this pur- pose. Here our difficulties be,rbin • but here FOS() I think .that we begin to see the light. Of this it will be time enough to speak when that light shines a little brighter, and is strong, enough to lead us to some surer ground. My duty at the moment is to piace the evidence before you in its simplest form, and to deduce therefrom such an hypothesis as may be both reasonably possible and no less serviceable to Us. And here .I ask you to observe that the Count rAntoine • would not have approached Madame as he did un- less the disclosure which he had to make must be embarrassing- to her or to others. The alternative is the assumption that he was her .lover—an alternative so grotesque that I do not permit it so much as to appear in my reckoning. • No, Monsieur; ,the case is not one of those elementary studies of human folly or of human passion, with which tha police of France are so often called upon to deal. It is the story of a man who carried a secret from France to London. who was followed thither by others who shared that secret with him, and determined either to—prevent its disclosure or themselves to profit .by it. Such unknown men shadowed the Count—it is .possible that , they watched the house as he watched it, and were themselves about to do what he would have done but for this tragic interruption. The question remains: Was their object that ,of blackmail, or did they act for some unknown persons who had determined to guard at any cost this imagined secret?
(To be Continued.)
KNUTSFORD MAY FESTIVAL.

Knutsford's floral May festival on Saturday was a lilliant and most successful affair, and was witnessed by many theusands of people, large numbers coming in from Menchester, Liverpool, Warrington, Crewe, and other places in Cheshire and Lancashire. Unfortu- nately, the weather was bad, and the thousands on the heath suffered much discomfort and inconvenience. The sun was shininc, when the processgon startsd out from the Town Hall, but black clouds gathered later, and as the Queen was 'entertaining the enclosure, rain, hail,bnd sleet began to coma down, and a stiff cold wind swept acrcss the open land. Notwith- standing this, the stands were packed, and although the rebt of the afternoon was showery and terribly cold, the • seats remained occupied. The Knutsford May ceremonies have been held for many years, and the festival is now looked urea as one of, the most attractive and elaborate affairs of the lend in the country. A few years ago the present King and Queen witnessed the interesting procession, and since then the Executive has Lem permitted to call it the " Royal festival." There was no lack of colour or variety in the moving picture, and the tbousmds of people who lined the quaint, narrow streets of the ancient town were delighted. Her mimic Majesty, Mies Shaw. of King-street, looted 'charming in her Royal robes. Her pretty dress was much admired, and was, perhaps, ens of the most elaborate yet sees at the Knutsford crowning. The Queen was attended by maids of honour, heralds sword-bearers, soldiers and sailors. Almost every character one could think of was in the parade, and the Morris dancers were, of course, in evidence. Many bands took part, and altogether the walk and the crowning were very successful, despite the weather.

div.head: GOSPEL OF OPPORTUNITY.
div.p: THE GOSPEL OF OPPORTUNITY.
EARLY WIRE WEAVING IN
WARRINGTON.
By Edward Owen Greening.

In considering the question of the huge overcharges which our Government make on patents, it is important to see the full effect of our national policy in the matter. We have only to carry the enquiry a step furthet and by analysis of Government expenditure see where the bulk of the money goes, and we arrive at startling conclusions. We tax inventive industries to support non- productive departments. This does -not niean to say that the non-productive depart- ments are necessary or useless. That is quite another question. But this is clear. If we penalise progress to maintain non- progressive sections we must not be sur- prised if we have to go to America for self- binding reaper inventions for our farmers. Mr. Lloyd-George recently made a remark upon this point which was sufficiently amazing to come from so acute a thinker. He declared the cost of a patent to be a matter of little importance. Did he ever hear of Connecticut? In that state it is a maxim that no intelligent mechanic considers himself respectable if he has not at least one patent for an invention of his own. Can Mr. Lloyd-George tell us what proportion of the mechanics of our country ever own a patent? A statistical enquiry into the status of those who are customers at the Patent Office would be a revelation to him. The number of working men who complete their patents in Great Britain and carry their inventions into use is sadly few. Our penalising of progress effects its natural result. The mass of workers whose experience should enable them to give us the most useful inven- tions do not, in our countrSr, use their thoughts and minds in that direction. - I can give a very remarkable illustration of the way in which the cost of a patent operates disastrously for the public. My grandfather, the late Nathaniel Greening, of Warrington, carried into that town the business which is now its staple industry. He was a wire manufacturer, but little above a working man in wealth. At first he found the helpful co-operation of a partner with money in Alderman Rylands, whose son, Mr. Peter Rylands, was afterwards a well- known M.P. They continued working- together as "Rylands and Greening" until the luck came to both of them of having sons ripe for business, when the firm split into two, one ' becoming "Rylands and Sons," and the other "N. Greening and Sons." I need not say that these are to- day well-known and flourishing firms in the hands of the third generations.

The immediate effect of the dissolution of partnership upon my grandfather was to leave him with plenty of ideas and practical knowledge, but no money worth speaking of. He soon invented the power-loom for making woven wire, thus introducing into this business what had already been successfully carried out in cotton manufacture. The idea upon which my giandfather had hit was so apparently simple that it was dangerous to make it known to any one. Yet it solved a problem which had baffled the leading members in the trade throughout the country for a long time. They had, in fact, been trying to weave wire by power in the same way that cotton yarn is woven into cloth. My grandfather hit upon the exact difference required in dealing with the two materials. He was then faced, with the problem of protecting his invention. A patent at that time for Great Britain alone cost £350, and to obtain piotection for other civilised countries raised this cost to a very large sum indeed. He and his sons decided as a more advantageous alternative to expending so much of their small capital in patents that they would keep the idea entirely to 'themselves. They fitted up a, room at the top of the little mill in War- rington and carried power by shafting from the engine below. In this little room the sons shut themselves up and produced rolls of woven wire. Of course they were able to undersell the trade everywhere, while still maintaining very high prices. The business grew rapidly upon them, and it became neces- sary for them to increase their plant and number of workers. It was also necessary to protect the secret more thoroughly from being stolen by competitors. They chose a few trusted old employs and gave them phenomenal payment per week each to work additional looms, binding them, of course, to secrecy. The room itself was enlarged and iron-cased against burglars. I can remember as a child playing in the ground floor of the mill and watching with interest the opening of the trap doors in the ceiling to let down the rolls of woven .wire which came like magic from above.

Curious to relate, this monopoly was thus secured in the hands of a few persons for a long term of years—l believe for over a quarter of a century. The whole world was rendered poorer in the result so far as this industry was concerned. My grandfather's firm was established and enriched, but the public paid far more than double what they need have done had a reasonable charge for a patpnt enabled him to obtain one for four- teen years. The moral of this incident is, I think, obvious. It does not pay the public to charge more for a patent than the actual cost of it, in the fallacious belief that they are thus making a profit and adding to the revenue of the State. On the other hand, an absolute monopoly by patent should not be granted at all. What the public should grant to the patentee is an assured revenue. Each applicant for a patent should have his idea carefully examined for him by skilled government experts. It the idea is old or woaAhless the patent should not be granted at all. If it has merit or novelty, it should be granted for a nominal fee and for an adequate term of years. But the one import- ant condition that the public should make with the inventor is to require that he fixes a royalty, upon payment of which the invention can be worked by anybody. The inventor would manufacture his own inven- tion upon advantageous terms, as he would have in his favour the royalties payable to him and his own exemption from them.— From the " Agricultural Economist" for April.

div.head: "DUMMY COCOANUTS."

FUN AT BRIDGE FOOT.

Mr. Ben Tillett, secretary of the Dockers' Union, addressed a Socialist meeting at Bridge Foot on day evening. life is a picturesque personality with touch .of the theatrical, and speaks with gre3l enthusiasm and a wealth of gesture. Mr. Tillett claimed that the Socialist movement represented 10,000,000 of men and women in varioat4, parts of the world and was the most pow-et:fat organization ever known to man. There was nothoecf to excuse poverty and there was only one explanatioa of it-.--somebody had been -thieving. " Who are the. . . thieves " ? asked Mr. Tillett. " Not 'you. Wig' you steal a shilling you get a month for it. Ihit you . stole a million pounds they would make von lord and you would go to Ascot with King Edwaro and have a real good time." (This prompted a listener to interject " You are getting good wages.'? " I am getting very good wages and I ought to hoc more ".retorted Mr. Tillett " I have added to the 'Work' men's wages in my thirty years of agitator's life 13tP millions of money and I haven't more than I stand imp ii? to-day. I. have been working for this poor. muddle- headed friend of ours for years. I have fought the thieves. If I had been a robber like the reSt of then' I would have been a millionaire, but instead of that I have fought for my side." Continuing, he said thot' not "es-en the economist or the Chancellor of tbe' Exchequer -could- furnish them with a reason poverty. It rxisted because one section of the coni- munity owned all the means of life and all OW property. There were heaps of workmen who thought. it was capital that did the business. The capital Or this country did not represent one-thousandth part 0' a farthing in the pound of actual value. There Arel.c!. only 150 millions of money in this country in actaat gold currency. The .workmen got paid out of ahour 50 millions of money every weekc and .the same rio millions did the round for the fifty-two weeks in the,. year. (At this stage the interrupter above nientiono ' repeatedly tried' to address the crowd. On beinp; remonstrated with he indifmantly declared that 11" was a citizen.) "Don't be a fool, if you are citizen," was Mr. Tillett's rejoinder. Mr. Viet proceeded to attack the wealthy capitalist and lal" owning classes whom he described as patasites living upon the labour of others. Their greatest boast was that they never worked, their greatest desire yea that they never should work, and their hope was that' none of their children would ever work. So long other people could work for them, they did rot neea to work at all. Socialism said : We want to producT, on a Co-operative basis. The forms of local mg' national government already existing could be scientifically revolutionised and turned into use. ire already had vast machinery in our loell government and Poor Laws which if properly ad uinistered coal begin at once to revolutionise in an economic serrie the conditions, industrially, socially, mentally, morsiT and nationally, of our people. "We (Io not ant to rob anybody," declared Mr. Tillett, " because you er.l robbed enough. These other fialk have' pinched' every thing you have got." (Liughter). Never was there lie mare patent or obvious than the statement that Socialists wanted to destroy the home. There store a million mothers and fathers and three million children' . that very night without a home. They had nothing t:T. rob. " I went round some of your slums to-day, seid Mr. Tillett, "and I could see the mark of the monster in some of the wretched tone- . ments. An Englishman's home is his castle. WO! a rotten lot of castles there must be around ! Titer' are 14 millions of your fellow human beings in this country without proper comforts in life. They el"' only live half the number of yenrs the well-to-do live' and their children have not a chance to live half th'' time that the childreo of the rich do." Continuing; Mr. Tillett said Liberalism did not know where it csa'' Nobody could define what Liberalism or Conservatism uas, unless it was a faetion fiiht between confederate thieves. Socialists, however, had a definition of ther. • own policy and they said that chit already existed if} ~ principle might be so developed that the revolutior' might take Place by which the poor should he placed on the same footing as the rich were to-day. Socialisnr . was the abolition of private property in the means eital - instruments of production, distribution and excite:4e' e Whatever the future might bring forth, to-day evert economist,every scientifll brain, every great philosopher • and every cultured person knew very well that labour was more than capable of producing more than it needed- In conclusion. Mr. Tillet disclaimed any intention ots the part of Socialists to divide all the money in the Kingdom. It would, he said, only amount to about a head. They were only concerned with the things °L life, the machinery of productton. He urged his hearers, not to interest themselves in Libe,ralism or TorvisalZ Tariff Reform or Free Trade, until the unemployed ara''' riches and poverty problems were solved. CIIRESTIANHY ON A POUND A WEEK.... During his speech Mr. Tillett was frequently inter- rupted by an elderly man wh ) incurred the anger of the crowd by attamnting to address them on his o,re account-. When he had finished speaking, Mr. Tillett made a dash for the interrupter, and drngeed him on ff. the platform. Although he looked somewhat snrpris"- the man was not at a loss for words, and put a few quee- tions which Mr. Tillett answered. Other questions were asked, one being as to whether it was possible for a men to be a Christirn on £1 a week; Mr. Tillett replied in the negative, in fact he did ne'' think that under caeit anybody could be a Chrii• tian. Ile hardly thought they could attempt t 0 be a Chtistinn under VON a yeir' and he did ne'' think they could be honest with less than that emo'int' Although some manufacturers might be chute; hwardevs and deacons, they put a bit of" shoddy " in if the r could. As for being a Christian, he thought it was impo 851 h e in this coontry,—he meant from the standpoint of tlme9 Nazarene. He did not think a parson could be ' Christian because capitaliem did not give the, man,el2. fair chance. SWINBURNE'S SCHOLARLY HABIT. • Swinburne left the University without a degree, but he took with him the warm friendship of Benjata;n Jowett, and 119 acquired what was better still, the- scholarly habit. We have had no such scholar among our poets since Milton, though a few may have bee',' even more widely read. In Mr. Swinburne's cadent' essays the reader is often astonished at the apparflis recklessness of the language, but it is only in the rares.. cases that ho is able to point out any slip in matters °` fact.—Dr. Rotertson Nicoll, in the May "10° temporary."

BOLTOIS:.-At St. Thomas' Church, on Monday, the funeral took place of Mr. Charles Henry Bolton, for many years known in War- rington in connection with the District Bank, to the Liverpool branch of which he was removed some time ago. div.head: LIGIITING
div.p: LIGIITING

Mr. Whitley said that he Irid re.uoived a letter from Mr. George Ashton, their clerk, stating thht be had made enquiries about the clockwork lighting of the lamps, and the cost would t.e 30s. each for immediate payment and 355. for payment extending over three years. There would be a great advantage, for if they wanted the lamps to be turned out at 12 o'clock, this could be done automatically and there would be a" great deal of raving in the gas bill. It would take a wan two days of each week to attend to the lamps. The Clerk said the Frodsham Gas Company had adopted this system of lighting the lamps, and they bad found it to their advantage. It saved gas and saved the payment of a lamp lighter. Mr. Brown : I do not think you ought to consider tbo question until we know what we will get as a rebate. Wbat will we get for a saving of labour? Mr. 11. J. Westbrook: Why should we incur £120? It is very expensive. Mr. Whitley said that the question had arisen out of the uncertain time in which they got the lamps lit. Sometimes it was fully an hour after dark. Mr. Westbrook moved that it be referred to the Lighting Committee for further_ consideration.

Tr. M—vnekyme seconded and it was decided upon. Mr. Whitley said he had received a letter from the Clerk of the Sankey Parish Council stating that at a meeting of their Council it was resolved that the Clerk write to the Councils of the townships of the Warring- ton district about public lighting. His Council had previously communicated with the Corporation Gas Committee relative to the reduction which had been made in the price of gas, and respectfully said that a reduction ought to be made. The Gas Committee had declined to make any reduction in any way, and his Council ventured to say that the question was one that the Stockton Heath Parish Council might be disposed to consider. They should be pleased so hear whether that Council was prepared to entertain the idea of a joint conference with a view to a deputation being formed to wait upon the Gas Committee. They decided to take no action in t e matter. rinE AND APPLIANCE CO3IIVIITTEE.

Mr. Mclntyre said that the Fire Appliance Committee were very anxious that the ratepayers of Stockton Heath should know that there was a Fire Brigade in the Parish and they were endeavouring to put it into a state of thorough efficiency. He had the folio% log recommen- dations to submit. 1. The present apparatus be thoroughly ovnhauled and put in good working condition ? 2. That a bell be provided to be used as a signal in case of fire and that this be fixed on the police building in Victoria Square, if permission can be obtained from the county authorities. The estimated cost of this is £4. 3. Two lamps to he purchased for the .use of the Brigade. .4. 'I he present stock of hosepipe is sufficient to reach buildings in the Parish with a single hose, but in case of a serious outbreak of tire a double length of hosepipe should be required to f ixable the committee to render help. For such an emergency as this they recommend that two new lengths be purchased. 5. Th it a ladder be pnrehased for the use of the Brigade, estimated cost £3 10s. Od. That the Brigade con,ist of ten members, one of (ham to be appointed superintendent or fore- man, and that four practices be fixed. The following remuneration to be paid, to the foreman 2s. 6d., each practice, others at `the rate of Is. per hour • the foremen to keep a record of the men's timeand they ha paid accerdingly ; that .no practice shall exceed two hours; the men to keep the apparatus clean and in good Working order without. extra pay: the committee to find the materials for the men to clean the apparatus with. 7. That a list of the hydrints in the Parish be supplied to each fireman with full pr.:ticulars as to their exact positions, also stating which are high and which are low pressure mains. 8. That. the Fire Station have a skirtirg board put near the ground floor to prevent the dust • and paper from blowing into the building, and that it be painted over one coat. of red paint and lettered in large white letters "Fire Station." 9 That a code of rules aragensral instruction be drawn up for the men to work to and a copy supplied to ,each man. We also suggest that enamelled plates be fixed over the doors of the houses where the members of the Fire Brigade live, marked "Fireman," estimated cost ss. each. The question of the remuneration of the men in cass of fire is being considered by the Committee. The total cost would be £26 4s. which included £0 $B. a year. Tills was adopted by the Ciluncg. Grappenhall. SALE OF WORK.

A sale of work which is expected to turn out success. fully was opened in the Independent Methodist Church, Chester-road, by the Mayoress of Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman.W. J. Porshaw, J.P.) presided, and was supported by Mr. R. ffenshall and the Mayoress. The Chairman said he was very pleased to be present that afternoon. lie had come at great sacrifice, and for a time during the morning he did not know whether he would be able to come or not, but, his wife told him that if he did not come, she would not. (Laughter). He was always interested in work of that character and be knew that they were making great efforts at Grappenhall to provide accomoiation fir the growing population in the neighbourhood. They had his sympathic interest and he wished the sale every possible success: (Applause,. Before declaring the sale open the Mayoress expressed her delight at being present. As bhe looked around the room she saw bow tastefully decorated it was, and it was evident that a great deal of labour had been entailed. She hoped the venture would be very suc- cessful and that they would realise all thekhad set out to get. Councillor Burton proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor and Mayoress. Mr. R. -Henshall in seconding expressed his gladness at seeing the Major with them. His pre§ence showed his catholic spirit. He had been born and bred a good Churchman, but he had the good sense to get a Methodist as his wife. To him and his wife they extended a hearty welcome. (Applause.) immediately the motion had been carried one had a chance to look round on the various stalls, and enquire the reason why such a step as a sale of work had been taken. It transpired that a sum of about £BO is required to pay off the debt on the Church, and by the sale the promoters of it expect to realise that amount.

Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., speaking at a right-to-work demonstration in Manchester, on ::aturday, said that the problem of unemployment was a serious problem, and they could not solve it by shouting about it. They could only get something done by working in the proper way' The resolution demanded the right to work, and he was there to support that demand. Mr. Maddison had told them that to claim the right to work was just as sensible as to claim the right to fly. Mr. Maddison had, forgotten that, even unddr the Poor Law, when a man reached destitution he had a right to be kept at the expense of the community. The Poor Law was the most demoralising, the most brutal, and the most heart- less machinery for dealing with poverty ever devised, and it ooght to be broken down. Bat he was not there to advise acts of violence. If they wanted to break the Poor Law down, instead of-demonstrating in the streets they should present themselves at the workhouse door and demand admittance. If the twenty- thousand men Who were out of work ,in Manchester did this on Monday morning, the Poor Law system would break down immediately. The denfocracy should learn to recognise and use its power. It was no use dealing with .the Liberal or the Tory party. The 'people must work out their own salvation, and they could work it out through the ballot-box.----(Cheers).
EARLESTOWN CHILDREN NEGLECTED.- PARENTS SENT TO GAOL.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed nesday, before Messrs. C. White and Roger Parr, James Hutchings and Ann Jane jolliffe, of Grafton-street, Earlestown, were charged with neglecting their two children in a way likely to cause them unnecessary suffer- ing and injury to health.—Both prisoners pleaded" Not guilty."—lnspector Carr' of the Earlestown Police, said he visited the house and found it in a filthy state from the front to the back door and from the floor to the ceiling.—The children were also filthy and verminous and were not properly fed. There was also nn awful stench in the house. The female prisoner was drunk at the time. On getting outside the female prisoner began to shout and witness was compelled to take her into custody. She was brought up next day and fined ss. and costs. Witness afterwards visaed the house again with P.C. Rirnmer and found the house in exactly the same state. They found the two children (boy and girl lying on a bed upstairs. There was only a few dirty clothes on the bed, the mattress being rotten. There was no food in the house.—P.C.Ritnmer corroborated.— Medical evidence was called to prove that the boy had Lad his growth stunted by neglect and also bore sores. The girl was in the same state.—lnspector Cox also gave evidence as to the neglect of the children.—The female prisoner said her husband was alive and was -a sailor. Ile was somewhere on the ocean but she knew not where. They were each sentenced to 3 months imprisonment. The male prisoner to the ehairm "Thank you sir."

FUNERAL OF MRS. J. 0. SWIFT.

The funeral took place at St. Helens Cemetery, on Monday, of Mrs. Swift, widow of the late Mr. ,J. 0. Swift, solicitor, who died within a week of Mr. Swift's funeral. The deceased lady after the death of her husband was taken ill with pnenmcnia, the malady which caused Mr. Swift's death, and she died on Friday last, at Streatham Hill, London, leaving four young children. The funeral service as conducted by the , Rev. .1. H. Watts. The mourners were Miss Swift (Liverpool), Master Fred T. Swift (Eon), Messrs. E. W. Swift, Harold Swift., Philo (Norwich), Williams (Wake- field), Roe (Loudon), and I'. Garnes. DEATII OF A ST. HELENS DOCTOR.-Dr. Edward Casey, who had practised in the district of Sutton, St. Helens, for about twenty-eight years past, died on Sunday shortly afternoon at the age of sixty-four Dr. Casey had for the past twelve years been in partner- ship with Dr. O'Keefe, and he was Poor Law medical officer and vaccination officer for the district. Deceased Was a native of North Tyrone. Ho was never married, and aas always kindly and charitable towsrds the poor, by whom he was universally beloved. About fifteen months ago he had a somewhat acute attack of influenza, which left him weak. Heart trcuble began to appear, but, against the wishes of his partner and other advisers, he continued to work and would not take the rest that was so necessary. Ile worked on until a few days ago, when he was obliged to lay down his task, and the end quickly came.

The local branch of the Tariff Reform League eritered upon an open-air campaign on Thursday evening, when a meeting was held at Bridge-foot. Mr. Tom Smith, of Burnley, wits the principal speaker. Alderman BENNETT, who presided, said that only that day be beard a gentleman who was somewhat sympathetically disposed towards tariff reform say that the Budget had killed tariff reform. He (Alderman Bennett) entirely differed from him, and he thought they would very easily be able to show thati the Budget bad done nothing of the kind. He did not propose to discuss the Budget that night. One might easily find a lot of fault with it and there were lots of things in it that one might praise. He thought tariff reform would be a better way of raising these large sums. It would, however, he folly to pretend that tro only possible way of raising revenue that was necessary for the needs of the country was by tariff reform. That was a very foolish and short-sighted thing to say and he had never taken that ground himself. It was obvious that in a rich country like ours with such tremendous resources, there must be ways of raising the wind and he would be very sorry to think we were so poor, and in such sad -straits that even a Free Trade Government was unable to find the money to carry on the government of the country. However, he thought the tariff reformers' method was a better one. The fact that, the Liberals had been able to introduce a Budget to raise £16,000,000 was not by any means enough to kill tariff reform and had really very little to do with tariff reform, Advanc- ing the familiar arguments for tariff reform, Alderman Bennett said, it would prevent the competition of the sweated labour on the Continent which was so unfai r to the industries of this country. Occasionally some tariff reformers appeared to get "inebriated with the exuberance of their own verbosity" and promised more than they bad the right to'promise.He(the speaker)would never be so foolish as to promise that if they got tariff reform they would abolish the unemployed. It was impossible to expect that, and many other measures would have to be adopted before they could say that every ran in this country who wanted work could get it at a reasonable wage. Under tariff reform, however, there would be more employment and at better wages than at present. (Applause). Mr. Tom SMITH', a cheery-faced gentleman with a resonant voice and confident manner, sought to prove that tariff reform would not increase the cost of living to the British working man by "a brass lathing." We were paying food taxes in Great Britain on a greater MOO than they were paying them in Germany and the United States. Free Trade England, so-called, raised £13,500,000 every year on the breakfast table in taxes. Before the Free Trader charged the tariff reformer with desiring to tax the food of the people, the Free Trade Governmont now in office would be far better employed in first untaxing the food of the people. Tariff reformers wanted to take the /taxes off every article that we wanted and could not make, and supply the revenue for the deficiency thus, created by placing a duty upon the £143,000,000 worth of fully manufactured goods which came into the country last sear. displaced our labour, and produced the chronic state of unemployment which baffled our present Free Trade legislators to solve. Mr. Chamberlain declared that be proposed to raise 51 millions of new taxation on food, but in order that the British workingmen should run no risk of loss, he proposed to take 7,4 millions off the already existing taxation on food. Dealing with the Free Trade contention that prices would be increased by tariff reform, Mr. Smith said only one of two things could possibly happen, either their employment would be increased and their capacity for tax-paying increase accordingly, or their taxes would be reduced in propor- tion to the amount the foreigner paid to use our market. Referring to the leather trade and speaking "as a practical leather man" who had worked for twenty years at the bench and knew something of the trade as buyer, user, and seller, Mr. Smith said that thirty-five years ago we in Great Britain controlled the hide and leather market of the world. Last year we exported more hides from Great Britain than the United States exported to us. Where did we get them from? The hides came off the backs of the very beasts that came from New York to Liverpool. In 1905-6 the bide of every beast that came to Birkenhead Lairage to he slaughtered for meat was stripped off and sent back to America to be tanned, dressed an d finished there, and then they made; us pay through the nose for the finished leather. ' The English tanner who went to Liverpool to buy hides was met with the . American agent whose purpose was to buy up all the bides and send them back to America. By doing that he found emplosment and wages for the tanners and other workers in America, and made John Bull pay through the In se for the finished leather. Tai HY reformers said ; that if BIWA industries were to le left to the mercy of Government I ounty-fed and subsidised competition, no industry could stand against such overwbehning odds. No county stood to gain more than Lancashire , by tariff reform. Nigeria &One, en the evidence of Sir, Alfred Jones, would be capable within twenty years of producing every ounce of cotton required for the mills of Lancashire. Canada alone was capable of producing every ear of corn required for this country. (Applause.) uncillor BROADEUILST, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Smith, referred to the progress of the chemical industry in Germany rind its decline in Warringtoo. Mr. G. If. W. STEEL seconded, mud tie vote vas accorded.

is generally sane and trustworthy. It is only on really insignifi- cant and unimportant matters that the sense of the community is ever at fault. div.head: MR, W. PETER RYLANDS AND THE BUDGET.
div.p: MR, W. PETER RYLANDS AND THE BUDGET.

Mr. T. Peter Rylands is the chairman and the lead- _ ing " star ' of the Tory party in Warrington. From the position he thus occupies and from his aspirations ne would expect that any utterance of his or any statement under or over his name, would have some reasonable bases of fact. Judging from his notes on • the Budget, which appeared in a prominent column in a contemporary of Saturday last, there is hardly a line, if we except the first, which is strictly accurate, or worthy, of a man who poses as a local representative eader of one of the parties in the State. • In his first line Mr. Rylands says the Budget can only be described as "staggering," and so it is to the Trade, to the Tariff Reformer, to the great ground landlords, and to the very wealthy and luxurious * classes ! It " staggers" because it " touches the spot," because it shews that at last the burdens are to be borne by those best able to bear them, and because, in its incidence, its absolute fairness to every class

eanaot be gainsaid. And after a week's exposure to tt he Olereest fire of its opponents it absolutely and holl "oldsdie field." Mr. Rylands next says the Budget "is full of the Socialist policy of seeking to kill the goose that lays the golden egg." The Budget, of course, is nothing of the kind ; whatever else it may be, it certainly is not Socialism. If our would-be philosopher would only think. clearly and accurately, and would only recollect that Socialism is a proposal to abolish the private ownership of the means of production, and to vest that ownership in the community, he would see that towards that ideal the Budget does not take a single step. In dealing with land it touches nothing which is to-day the landlord's property. What it does is to lay down the principle that any value added to this property, irrespective of its ownership, and solely by the industry of its owner's tenants or by the • growth of the community shall be taxed, as it is now taxed in Germany! Logically the whole of this unearned increment could be demanded by the State. It demands only a fifth! But even if the State demanded the whole increment, the pf oposal would not be Socialism, it would leave the landlord still the owner and the master of his land. , Mr. Rylands, having shewn his utter ignorance of -what Socialism is, proceeds to say that "if any argu- ment is still required to support the contention that the time has come when some change in our fiscal policy is necessary, nothing more conclusive could be adduced than this Budget, with its amazing concentra- tion of the burdens upon certdin sections of the com- munity." Exactly ! Some change in our fiscal policy," whereby our relatively over-taxed workers may have their food and necessaries taxed in order that as they grow poorer, their rich manu- facturing employers and the landlords may get richer and richer ; whereby the wealthy may revel in untold luxuries and wastefulness at the cost of the tears and the life-blood of the struggling poor. Lord Beaconsfield might well say "Protection is damned," and so it ought to be but there will be those who will hanker after it, those who value not human lives, who see by it a quick way to affluence,' and who allow nothing to stand between them and their end. If Mr. Rylands would look at the fiscal experience of Germany, possibly even he might " tak' a thought an' mend." In a leading London weekly of fast Saturday,we read that to-day in Germany under Protection "the gap between the expenditure and revenue of the German Empire for the coming year will be nearer thirty than twenty millions, and the financial position is more likely to lead to ruin and bankruptcy than to threaten or endanger its neigh- bours, also that the latest statistics of unemployment show that unemployment is worse than ever, whereas here in England things are gradually improving." The Income Tax does not, as Mr.Rylands says,range from is. 2d. to is. Bd. in the I—as a matter of fact a very large proportion of payers will pay 9d. or less in the £. For instance, a ran with £3OO a year of unearned income is only required to pay tax on £l4O of his income •, equal to 541. in the lon his £3OO a year. Again if a man with £3OO a year earns it he is only required to pay 140 ninepences or less than 4.1 d. in the I—and a man with £2OO a year, if he has four children gets off altogether! While at the other end, no one however rich, has to pay the full is. Bd., us the first £3,000 of his income is not charged upon. It is indeed refreshing to have a Tory complaining about " taxation being raised in a time of peace to a -war footing," knowing as we all do that the official ame,ndments of his party in respect of Old Age pensions, would have, if carried, increased their cost by five millions last year, and that his party did all they could to foment a war scare which might easily-have involved us in another unnecessary and wicked war with finftncial disasters impossible to conceive. The Tory Boer war, criminal and wholly unnecessary, cost us two hundred and sixty • millions, besides thousands of lives. The increased taxation, says Mr. Rylands, "leaves no margin of resource for the inevitable day of conflict with some foreign nation." Is it not criminal that such stuff should be written.? Do the vast majority of the people of any nation look upon war as "inevitable." Surely it ought not to be so,if there is anything in our religious beliefs. That we must maintain our relative naval superiority everyone agrees, and the truth is that Lloyd George, in enacting his great Budget, Ineets not merely the financial exigencies of the moment, but provides for the needs of the future. The " Yorkshire Post" of yesterday has mn article almost suggesting that the yield of taxation from the Budget is " deliberately under-estimated." Such are the possibilities of our sysein o'f Free Imports.

Perhaps the " coolest ".thing in Mr. Rylands' comment is the allusion to the "economic unsound- ness" of one feature a the Budget, immediately fob lowing upon a glaring piece of economic unsoundness of his own, viz.--that taxing wealthy men will take from the workers their wages. It may displace an infinitesimal amount . of unproductive labour temporarily, but accurately speaking, it cannot interfere with the wages of the workers, which are simply the return to 'them in the form of money of the wealth they have already produced by their labour. Suppose we vary the illustration and extend it. Mr. Richman is taxed to pay old age pensions. He has to sell one of his race-horses, and can now manage with a stable-boy less. What a loss to the community! Is there any compensating gain? What does the oldage pensioner do with his ss. a week? Hoard it? No,he spends it; and in the spending of many such pensions, there is more.goes to the worker as wages than in the spending of an equivalent amount by Mr. Richman. But will Mr. Richman spend less after the Budget? Speaking generally, he Will not. He will save and leave less, and so his heirs will have to pay less in Death Duties, which will of course please them ! It is interesting to hear Mr. Rylands' admission that the workers pay all direct taxation eventually. Does he mean to imply that they don't pay indirect taxation? As a matter of fact, with our present system of taxation, the working man is the most heavily taxed man in the country, taking direct amid indirect taxation into accounvand if the Budget does something to equnlise the burden by taking a larger share from the wealthy man than he has hitherto paie, the latter should not " squeal" because he is 'asked to pay something nearer his fair share at Last.
It is imposible, in reasonable space, to deal with all the numerous error,: and mi,istatements of Mr. Ilylands. Surely -so many were never before con- tained in so short a communication !,

div.head: CRUSHED TO DEATH.
div.p: CRUSHED TO DEATH.
Railway Fatality at Warrington

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the Police Station last evening concerning the death of Ruben Darbyshire, aged 27, who resided in Longshaw-lane, Warrington, and was killed on the London ar..d North-western Railway, on Tuesday night.—Mr. Bland represented the' Rail- way Company. The evidence of Thomas Jefferson Potter,shed turner, in the employ of the London and North-western Rail- way Company showed that deceased was also employed as a shed tnrner at the Folly-lane works of the Railway Company. He FS f. 13 a man of excellent character, a Sunday school teacher and highly respected. Last Tuesday evening Potter went to the coal hots to bring two engines into the shed, and finding that there was not sufficient steam in the engines to drive them, he proceeded to get another engine from the shed to draw the other two engines in. When the moving engine had got within two yards of the stationary engines, Potter stopped it and the deceased went to couple them up. A moment or two later he shouted to Potter to "ease up" and Potter " tuffered" his engine to the other two. He shouted to Darbyshire, if he was ready, but got no reply. On getting off the engine he found that it had not been coupled, and the deceased Was lying in the "four foot," having been crushed. between the buffers. How the accident happened could not be explained. Fred William Barton, storekeeper in the employ of the Company, rendered first aid and the deceased was taken to the Infirmary, but died before reaching the Institution. _ '
A verdict of "Accidental death " ivas returned.

div.head: BUDGET DEBATE. Mr. Crosfield Describes Speakers and Speeches
div.p: THE BUDGET DEBATE. Mr. Crosfield Describes Speakers and Speeches

[To TIM EDITOR OF TIIE "EXAMINEItI.. Sir,-11e first round of the great battle of the ession is finished, and as the parliamentary pugilists who took part in it pause to get their wind one may take a brief glance at some of them, and recall a few of the incidents of what has certainly been a meraorable de4ate. It .began of course with Mr. BALFOUR'S spe6ch on Monday, a speech which lasted if I remember right, fully two hours, but _which held and riveted the attention of the whole House from the first sentence to the last word. In intellectual eminence and debating skill Mr. BALFOUR is of course head and shoulders above any member of the Opposi- tion, and no one in the House can surpass him in polished sarcasm or in his brilliant gifts cf refined irony. The half implied but none the less undeniable admission in his speech of
THE PRINCIPLE OF GRADEATION

as applied to taxation was both signiticlnt and important. On the other hand he contended that no distinction between landed property and other forms of wealth should be made in any scheme of taxation. That I venture to suggest is the fundamental fallacy which underlay a speech in other respects a master- piece of criticism—one that well deserved the high compliment paid to it by Mr. Lloyd-George when he said that the ability of the Leader of the Opposition was not only the admiration but the wonder of his political opponents. The POSTMASTER-GENERAL; who followed, was, I thought, scarcely in 4.s happy a vein as when ,we had the pleasnre of hearing him in Warrington not so long since ; but WINSTOS Ontalcuit.r, made an extremely able and conclusive speech in reply the same evening, and if one is to make any selection I should say these two speeches best represent the different principles which in matters of taxation. guide the tfro great parties of the State. - In his Budget speech Mr. Lloyd-George had perforce to follow pretty closely, and frequently to read verbatim, a very large quantity of typewritten note,: and memoranda in expounding what it Is quite true was not only a .budget but also soinething like a manifesto of policy to the country as well. The Chancellor was naturally a little handicapped by the weight of all this vast mass of material while, as Hazleton wittily put it from the Irish benches, "beating seven the Secretary of State for War in the LONG DISTANCE PARLIAMENTARY MARATHON." _

The contrast of Mr. Lloyd-George's speech on Tuesday when unhampered by more than a very few notes was striking. It was a speech which in point of debating skill and ability was not inferior even to Mr. Balfour's remarkable speech the day before. Like the Leader of the Opposition, too, Mr. Lloyd-George has a wonderful gift of irony—irony of a wonderfully rare and delicate shade, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer can combine, as no one else in the House can combine with this, wit and humour as well._

. with Your readers will all be familiar the exquisitely funny bit of chaff to which Mr. Austen Chamberlain laid himself open by his most unlucky interruption. At the end of that little passage of arms when Mr. Lloyd-George had occasion to refer again for a moment to German politics, he mentioned the Conservative party; and added "I hope I may be allowed to refer to the Conservative party,"—after that a moment's pause —" it used not to be a term of reproach!" The inflection of the voice as he said this, the slight note of mingled regret and mournful remonstrance, together with an inimitable gravity of manner and expression were simply irresistible, and everyone in the House felt this and fairly shook with laughter. Besides Mr. Lloyd-George's reference to the speech by the Leader of the Opposition—a reference in which he certainly gave expression to the opinion of every one in the House—the Chancellor of the Exchequer also paid very proper tribute to an admirable speech earlier in the debate by Mr. Younger. The latter is

merry gips'es, troupes of dancers—all were there—and when they had ranged themselves on the platform the scene was one probably unsurpassed at the Parr Hall. Last of all came the retiring queen .(May Isherwood), with her attendants, and when "her Majesty" was enthroned the stirring hymn "Stand up for Jesus" was heartily sung. After prayer and a short address by the President, the coronation preliminaries were entered upon. For the nonce the stage was supposed to be transformed into a village green, and King Winter (G. Arthur Whitfield), a benevolent looking gentleman resembling Father Christmas, who had dared to intrude in May, was promptly banished at the behest of lairy Spring (Flossie Adams) who by a wave of her magic wand caused fairy flowers to spring up and dance gaily in a ring. After a spirited and amusing encounter between rival sweeps (J. Pearse and A. Wareing) and bakers (H. Bibby and A. Appleton), the choir joined in the effective chorus "Gladly we hail." Than a couple of merry minstrels (A Weir and J. J.,nes) and Jack in the Green (Clifford Jores) tripped on to the stage and the minstrels joined in a tuneful duet. A troupe of boys and girls, trained by Mr. W. Aldred, next danced the old-fashioned Morris dance in really charming style, the effect being considerably enhanced by the constantly changing colours of the limelight. A capital action song "The merry milkmaids" was given by senior girls. A bugle having sounded, Temperance (Miss Elsie Hewitt) the Queen-elect, accompanied by her maids of honour, appeared on the stage and was greeted with enthusiasm. At the foot of the throne, she was met by the retiring Queen, and they joined in a pretty duet composed b Mr. A. Spruce, which was tastefully sung and afforded much pleasure. With charming simplicity the retiring Queen then placed a floral crown on the head of the new Queen and also invested her with the robe and sceptre, the dutiful subjects cheering lustily. Ins neat little address" her Majesty " exhorted her hearers to "rally round our statesmen in their endeavours to keep the Temperance flag unfurled and to support our legislators in making laws that will safe- guard and protect the children from :the ravages of intemperance and vice." 'The Queen, who comported herself with befit•ing grace and dignity, then proceeded to the throne which wad beautifully illuminated with electric lights. The chorus "All hail the Queen of

have to take it back," for he betrayed no nervousness and his gestures were irresistibly amusing. A long programme was brought to a close with the action song "White sails,' by the full choir, and it speaks volumes for the excellence of the entertainment that the interest of the audience had never tugged during the full three hours which it occupied. On_ the

contrary, enthusiasm was strongly manifest and there was a consensus of opinion that the festival was better than any of its predecessors, which is saying a great deal. Too much praise cannot be accorded to Mr. A. Spruce, the conductor, whose whole-hearted interest in the work is a household word. He must have been proud with the way in which the children acquitted themselves under his leadership. Mr. A. W. Clatworthy presided at the organ with taste and skill, and the pianoforte accompaniments were shared by Misses Oakley, Lomas, Spruce and Plinston, Mr. R. Wilson, and Mr. J. Forster. It maybe mentioned that Mr. Forster is not one of the regular workers of the Union but he willingly volunteered his help and his accompaniments of the choruses were helpful and effective. The Union is fortunate in possessing a splendid band of officials who did their utmost to ensure the success of the festival. They are : Committee, Messrs. T. Dale, R. P. Williams, G. Whit- field, J. P. Jackson, J. Thorniley, A. Spruce, J. Muir A. Clatworthy, J. Hamblen, J. Bradley, J. Dunabin, E. Taylor, J. Howell, W. Aldre d, Mesdames Whitmore, Hamblen, Davenport, Shaw, and Misses Whalley, Ellison and Plinston ; trainers of coronation ceremony and May-day revels, Mrs. Shaw, Misses Whalley, Ellison, and Mr. G. Whitfield : platform manager and director of elocution, Mr. G. Whitfield ; marshal of procession, Mr. J. Thorniley ; assistant marshal, Mr. J. Hamblen ; advertisement committee, Messrs. G. Whitfield, C. S. Fellows, R. P. Williams. and J. Hamblen ; lion. secre- tary, Mr. F. Gandy ; hon. assistant secretaries, Messrs. Henry Woolley and C. S. Fellows: procession com- mittee, Messrs. G. Whitfield, R. P. Williams. J. Hsmblett, T. Muir, and J. Thorailey ; programme steward, Mr. J. P. Jackson.
Special acknowledgment must be made of the untiring work of Mr. F. Gandy. as hon. secretary. ,-SPEECH BY MRS. DODDS.

Mrs. Dodds, President of the Band of Ho pe Union presided over the festival and in the earrer part of the proceedings was accompanied on the platfokm by the Rev. T. Miller, Mrs. Owen (President, local British Women's Temperance Association), Mr. F. Gandy (secretary of the Union), Mr. T. Dale (member of the Committee), Messrs. Harry Woolley and C. S. Fellows (assistant secretaries).

Mrs. DODDS said that, was the third time she had hid the privilege and honour of presiding over their festival, and although she thought it would perhaps have been wiser to have chosen someone else for that occasion she felt very sensible of the honour they had con- ferred upon her. That was the childrrn's night and if there were any strangers present she was proud to think that they would see what very bonny children we had in Warrington. As they looked at their bright, happy faces, they thought of the hundreds and thousands of children who had not a chince. But there were others since the days of Mrs. Browning who had heard the cry of the children and they were going to have a chance. (Applause.) A great deal had been dent for the children lately, and more was going to be done. Per- haps someone would ask: "What is the Band of Hope doing ?" She could best answer that by repeating what a friend said to her a short time ago. They were talk- about temperance work in general and he said: "There is a great deal of talk nowadays about environment. The says a man is what his environment makes hint. If that is so, I ought to be a drunkard. Instrad of that I am a life-long abstainer,—a feet due entirely to the Band of Hope." (Applause.) , That was the work the Band of Hope was doing—it was fighting heredity and helping boys and girls and 3oung people to be stronger than their environment. Evert in homes which had been almost ruined by drink and amidst the most dreadful surroundings, it was enabling -thlm to live honest, sober, clean lives. It was her great privilege last Sep- tember to attend that unique and marvellous meeting in the Free Trade Hall, and as she heard such men as Lord Russell, Mr. David Shackleton, M.P., and a host of others, some of whom sat in the high places in our land, get tip and say what the Band of Hope had done for them, and that they were proud even yet to call themselves Band of Hope b'oys, she felt that if it had done nothing more but send into the world a band of men like those, the move- ment had justified its existence. (Applause.) Since they last. met at. their festival, they had received march- ing orders and they were to go forward. They all knew that no forward or aggressive work could be done without funds and so there was to be a big bazaar in , the Free Trade Hall next October, by which it was ' hoped to raise £6,000. That looked a !sur*e amount, but it must be remembered that we spent every year in I strong drink over .£160,000,000. The £6,000 was wanted for the children and she believed they would get it. (Applause.) Then they would get to work to fight the drink, and it would be a fierce battle. There would, however, be no bloodshed and they would not need a single Dreadnought. (Laughter.) They would want sothething far better—men and women, young men and maidens,to whom much had been givensto come:forward with their help and sympathy, to assist those who were powerless to help themselves, for the sake of Him who said "It is not the Will of the Father in Heaven that one of these little ones should perish." (Applause). • Mrs. OWHN said she had been asked by the committee of the British Women's Temperance Association to present a bouquet to the retiring queen and she would, on her own account, like to present a Bible to the Queen-elect. (Applause). Mrs. Owen appealed to the ladies present to lend all the support they could to the temperance movement. It was a dreadful thing that although drunkenness was decreasing amongst men it was increasing t 3 an alarming degree amongst women. She had been a Band of Hope girl since 1854, and it was sad to think that such a state of things prevailed after 60 years' Band of Hope work. In conclusion, Mrs. Owen expressed the hope that the retiring queen and queen-elect would always strive to imitate the late
Waring, Pattie Barton. Percy Bowers, Polly Richardson, 31 illicent Percival, if ilda Wainwright, Eva Alcock and Ben Farrar.

Mr. B. FEw said that as an old Band of Hope boy he had great pleasure in moving that that audience give to their chairman, Mr. Smith, a most hearty vote of thanks. Mr. Smith had come under great difficulty. He was told that he had twenty other engagements that week, and he gave preference to the one at Warringt w. The motion was heartily endorsed.

div.head: SPECIALIST ON THE LIQUOR QUESTION,
div.p: A SPECIALIST ON THE LIQUOR QUESTION,

and a debater who is equally cogent and fair minded. His main argument is that taxation of licensed premises should be in proportion to the quantity of liquor sold in each ; and so far as this principle is capable of practical application it seems to be the fairest and best way of dealing with the question. It is impossible within the limits of these notes to go into detail, but I venture to draw attention to Mr. Youngtes able speech ;s and to another speech of equal ability from his own point of view with which the Debate was opened on the Opposition side last Tues- day by Mr. Pretyman.

On Wednesday the first man at the Table was the ever popular.and ever youthful Mr. Chaplin. With his portly presence and sonorous phrase he represents a good old-fashioned—l had almost said "old crusted "—style of orator, and when he thunders out his denunciations of modern politics there are no half measures about him. He stands uncompromisingly' for Protection, and a sort of fine full flavoured Toryism of days gone by. Later in the afternoon the Prime Minister opened his speech with a graceful reference to this doughty old Parliamentarian. and then, borrow- ing an illustration which Mr. Chaplin himself quoted, treated the House to about
THE BEST BIT OF FUS

it has had for years. Reminding the House that Mr. Chaplin's quotation carried them back to the days of Peel and Disraeli, he pictured Mr. Chaplin bathing in the still (!), cool (!) waters of Tariff Reform-; the Chancellor hard by on a bank-L-" probably on a bird nesting expedition "—.--and led by his predatory instincfs to make off with Mr.. Chaplin's clothes. Pursuing- the subject with a sort of semi-judicial and incomparable 'gravity, Mr. Asquith said it:might-be assumed that m the privacy of his home he tried the garments on—(loud laughter)—and that he then came down in them to introduce his Budget. (More laughter). Glancing at the majestic presence' and ample chest of the Chairman of the Agricultural Committee of the Tariff Commission and atlithe slim .form of the Chancellor of the Exchequer beside him, Mr. Asquith put it to the Chairman of Committee and to the House whether there could possibly be a stronger argument for the Development Grant.. The roars- of laughter from every side Of the House only increased as members had time to appreciate the full flavour . of this delightful episode. -And yet some people have tried to make out that Mr. Asquith is deficient in humour.

Later on in his speech Mr. Asquith spoke with great frankness and -with all that weight and influence which, when one is listening to him often reminds me of Emerson's remark as to -the amount of" coiled force ". there is latent in Englishmen—or at any rate some of them. After exposing

THE ABSVIID FALLACY THAT CAPITAL WILL TAKE WINGS to itself and leave thescountry, he, towards the close of a really powerful speech, put the alternative plainly tri the Opposition.Cri tic ism is easy wliere no one relishes additional taxes. But still the money has to be raised and the Government have boldly stated their plan for getting it. If that plan were rejected what alter- native scheme is open to us? That is the question put with deliberation and emphasis to the crowded benches opposite him. There is a moment's pause ; and a momeM too of very dramatic silence. Not one syllable of reply came from either the • leader of the Opposition of any of his followers, and then .the whole of the Liberal Party heartily cheered a state- ment which from their point of view of 'course, puts the whole position in a manner that is subqtantially unanswerable. And Mr. Asquith followed this up, because he reminded the House that after all the answer to his question lad already been sgiven in Glasgow in 1893, the alternative plan of taxing corn, and meat and dairy produce—the prime necessaries of life for the very poorest part of the nation, was to be adopted, and that was the alternative—a statement again heartily cheered on the Government's side of the House.

Mr. Austen Chamberlain is not as a rule a very effective speaker in debate, and for the first ten minutes of his speech there was a rather forced and laboured note in what he said, but afterwards this dtsappeared. He developed Mr. Pretyman's argument from the landowner's point of view and, certainly came out in his best form in his criticism of
THE TAX ON UNEARNED INCREMENT.

But I noticed that he steered clear of any direct challenge of what Mr. Asquith had said in defence of the principle of taxation of unearned increment, while on the other hand there was not a syllable of response to the challenge thrown out by the Primi Minister to• which I have just alluded.—Yours, etc., A. 11. CROSFIELD,
House. of Commons, May Gtb, 19W
