div.head: Examiner, Saturday May 8, 1909.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday May 8, 1909.
TEMPERANCE QUEEN.
PICTURESQUE FESTIVAL AT THE PARR HALL. -

The " merrie month" of May, always linked in imagination with old-time revels and picturesque pageantry, is fittingly chosen by the Warrington Band of Hope Union for the annual children's festival. It was a happy thought that prompted the • arrangement and from the outset public appreciation has been so enthusiastic and the little folk have entered into the rejoicings with such delight, that the festival is now firnily established as one of the most pleasurable events of the year. The Parr Hall was crowded on Wednesday and Thursday evenings when, with truly regal pomp and splendour, the Temperance Queen was again crowned amid the joyous acclaims of loyal subjects,and presided over merry-makings which were pleasing alike to the little ones and to the "children of a larger growth" who watched them. The platform with its gay and vane-coloured streamers and flower-bedecked throne presented a pretty picture and whea the 350 children in character cos- tumes had taken their places the scene was a brilliant one. First of all, to the martial strains of the organ, there as a procession round the hall, and as the children passed by in gorgeous array, the variety and richness of colour and the general animation presented a s?ectacle beautiful and almost kaleidoscopic. Per- sonalities famous in ramery rhyme, representatives of seasons and nationalities, historical notabilities, diminutive and mild-looking policemen, gallant soldiers,
ROYAL ROBES.

div.head: QUEEN AND HER ATTENDANTS,
div.p: THE QUEEN AND HER ATTENDANTS,

Nifty " having been sung in admirable style, a group of lasses, who had been traiged by Mrs: Whitmore, danced the ever-popular Maypole dance very cleverly. The action song" The Japanese Fan "was then taste- fully given by picturesquely-costumed girls of the Buckley-street Band of Hope, who, it will be remem- bered, won the local prize at the Warrington,Musical Festival. They bad been trained by Misses 11. Kindon and N. Whitby and Mr. A. Taylor. The •Irish dance by girls who had .been instructed by Miss E. Spinks was , a very attractive feature, Oa youthful performers acquittiog themselves right well. An action song "Kilkenny Cats" by a contingent of boys trained by Bert Spruce was highly amusing, the young- sters indulging in quaint actions supposed to be typical of the feline tribe. The "make-up" was striking, although in two cases the skin bore a great resemblance to the leopard's, and there wa3 a roar of merriment when one of the "cats" lost his head in the fray. Quite an Italian touch was given. to the ravels by the castanet dance given with delightful .grace and skill by boys and girls (trained by Mr. Aldred). Williani T. Wilkinson earned rounds of applause by his sweet interpretation of "Make your record clean." A troupe of little gipsy girls (trained. by Mrs. Davenport) sang "We'll tell yon your • fortune" With delightful self-confidence and engaged in a rustic dance. A novel and interesting feature was the Grecian drill, Which was .splendidly executed by a contingent of girls and reflected the greatest credit on Miss E. , Spinks, .vlto had trained them. The voices of a select choir ,blended well in the " Gipsies' laughing trio "—an item piquantly rendered and appreciatively received. The greatest hit of the evening from the comic standpoint was the action song " Susie's Sousa mad," in which boys trained by Bert Spruce figured in military ,uniforms but manceuvred with a complete disregard of soldierly precision, and extracted weird music (?) from a variety of wonderful instruments. Master B. Farrar, as the impersonator of tha renowned Sousa, was a conspicuous success, his eccentric mode of "conducting" convulsing the audience, and although it was understood that encoreswere barred, a repetition.of this item had to be conceded. A duet" I heard a brooklet guShing " was artistically sting by Minnie Mounfleld and Hilda Spruce. Ada Hamer, a tiny dot, quite captivated the audience by the simple yet appealing way in which she sang "In my little coktage and she was rewarded With a eat outburs,, of applause. The Scotch dance by a troupe of girls was remarkably well done, Miss E. Spinks being the lest rue-tress, audit is due to all cOtt. cerned to state iliat the Whole.of.the dances on the pro- gramme were altogether admirable and revealed surpris- ing apt Uncle on the part of the children as well as the tact and skill of those who had so etßiently trained them. Charlie Hamblett, a budding humorist, in grotesque attire, created great glee by his little song "You'll

div.head: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

On Thursday evening the Hall was again filled in every part. Mr. F. H. Smith of Lymm Hall, who pre- sided,said he did not think he had heard better singing in all his life. Continuing he said no one knew the value of a little child. They-bad in a society of which be was proud to be connected, some of tbe evidence of what people would do for little children. Slung on one nail was a poker which had been bent across the back of an innocent English child. (" Shame.") There was also a brass studged bolt with which a cruel man sent a child .newly to its last leng sleep, and that showed that some men and women did not consider the little child of any great valwi. No one could estimate it child's value. There was not a father worthy of the name who would take all the wealth that the Ch mcellor of the Exchequer, was going ta have, for his little child. Tee Band of Hope movement was 'one for the protection of the nation. *And the boy, what was he worth? He cost a great deal for food and clothing, but from a little English boy they got all sorts of fun, and out of a little boy's pocket, they got all sorts of things. (Laugh- ter.) A little boy was worth a great deal. In conclusion the Chairman said there were children pacing the streets of Warrington, because there was no happiness for them at home, all through drink. He sometimes wondered how it was that they did not burst from their environ- ment. That movement was to give health, brightness and joy to the young life of the world. (Applause.) During the evening Miss Jackson of the ".Y" branch of the 13.W.T.A. presented the Queen Elect with a bouquet. M r.THomas DALE said they were very fortunate to get Mr. Saiith there that night. Mr. Smith instructed their Honorary Secretary to give a brooch to each of the Qaeens, with. a suitable inscription thereon in ,memory of that event. (Applause.) They would see. that the oilier was executed.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The Macnaghten Circuit is to be congratulated upon obtaining such high-class turns as are provided for Warrington patrons this week. Vasco, termed the "mad musician," tops the bill. He is said to be the most versatile instrumentalist in the world. Hardly a musical instrument can be named that Vasco cannot play and the question is asked " what cannot • Vasco . play ?" and .not "what can he play ? " From the proverbial tin whistle to the trombone he played all manner of instruments, now producing. the most sweet music and then making the most unearthly din. He presents the most interesting musical item ever seen on the -local variety stage. Alexandra and Bertie give an rerial act entitled "After the ball," which show some remarkable feats, on the trapeze also on a heavy iron ladder put across this audbalanced on one end by Alexandra, while Bertie performed some Muscular eats on the other. A turn which requires much pluck, daring and presence of mind is that of the Alms termed the lightning equilbrists and tumblers. The male Alma, revels in head balancing. He builds a pinnacle of eight chairs, one upon the other and having placed a water bottle on the topmost one he .balances himself upon this and drinks a glass of wine the while. Another trick is to balance himself on the corner of an ordinary chair and play a guitar. These . artists received a great ovation. A most amusing and clever turn in the way of tumbling is presented by the Bros. Redmond and much laughter is caused by the two dressed as guardians of the peace looking out for juvenile smokers, and children under age frequenting the "gin palace." A laughable part of the sketch is when one of the -artists tries to catch the moon (a home made moon of course namely, the limelight) and is unsuccessful awl the other comes to his rescue with a hammer and a 12-inch nail and then nails it to the boards. The first one thereupon asks if the nail is one of "Lloyd-George's tacks." The pair also excel in tumbling and acrobatic feats. Tom Lloyd, the popular eccentric comedian, an artist who in our opinion deserved a better place on the bill, sings three songs. -namely "When the wintry winds do blow," "Half way, half way" and 'a paradv, Votes for women" to the tune of " Madaline Rossiter proves an excellent dancer in high step and clogs. John Macauley an artist with a good baritone voice sings " To-morrow will be Friday," dressed in the garb of. an Abbot, and "I'm only a poor old soldier," he proves a great favourite. Excellent pictures are shown on the biograph of the recent distruction by flood in India and "The Suffregette's dream." The orchestra under the conductorship of MX. Widdup leaves nothing to be desired.

div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Judging from the bill, next week's programme will ,be quite in keeping with the high reputation of the Palace. Other artistes will be :—Webb and Branston,. opera duettists; The Olmars, Roman statuary acrobats; Pete and Juno, coloured vocalists and dancers. div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The Lighthouse Robbery. 7
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The Lighthouse Robbery. 7

Mr. E. H. Knight, famous in theatrical Circles as the producer of that old favourite " The Grip of Iron" presents his No. 1 Company in an exciting drama The Lighthouse Robbery" at the Royal Court Theatre this week. The play has been enthusiasti- cally received for the plot is of one of intense gild thrillinc, interest, while the staging is on an elaborate scale and includes some novel mechanical effects. There is a real lighthouse and:a fine peal of bells. The Company is. a highly capable one, Miss Hilda Baynton as Rose Prescott and Mr. Fred Garrett as Tom Manley being prime favourites. The unpopular parts of William Farrell. and James Hammond are realistically portrayed by Mr. William Annesley and Mr. Percy Berresford, while little Ethel Lovatt, as little Nellie, the ocean waif,- wins all hearts by her touching presentment.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Next week Mr. Tom Watts' Company (by arrange- ment with Mr. J. Pitt Hardacre) will present the renowned play "East Lynne "—an adaptation of Mrs. Henry Woods' popular novel. The version is the same as produced by the late Mr. Wilson Barrett, and is the only one containing the character of P.C. Bullock. Mr. Edmund Kennedy will appear as Archibald Carlyle and Miss Julie Kennard will take the dual role of Lady Isabel and Madame Vine

div.head: BILLIARDS AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: BILLIARDS AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

Local Literal billiard enthusiasts entertained a team of Territorials on Wednesday evening to a hot-pot supper and a game of billiards in the Liberal Club. Some little time ago tho Territorials invited the Liberals to a similar gathering at their headquarters,and the result was a highly enjoyable evening, and a fine match, in wbich the visiting team was victorious.—On Wedne3day evening the Territorials again lost, as will be seen by the following scores : . _ _

div.head: • Mr. J. Howes and £5. To THE EDITOR OF TIM WOIRINGTON EXAMINER.
div.p: • Mr. J. Howes and £5. To THE EDITOR OF TIM WOIRINGTON EXAMINER.

Sir,—Your correspondent Mr. J. Howes is trying to evade the offer of £5 by describing it as a complete fable. Does he mean by the word fable that it is a "Lie.", If so, I make this suggestion to you Mr. Editor, that Mr. Howes and myself along with some gentlemen nominated by you go to the works where the meeting was held, and ascertain from the work- people whether the statement I have made and described by Mr. Howes as a_fable, is true or false...

My -suggestion to Mr. Homes in answer to his challenge was that we debate Tariff Reform the same evening or the 'following evening at the place where the meeting was being held, and Mr. Howes could select his own chairman, or I would meet Lim any- where else convenient to both of us.
Now hurry up with your .15, Mr. Howes, for five families can do with it. - After that I am-sure I can make arrangements for you and I to debate Tariff Reform,—Yours truly, J. MITE.
7G, Broughton-road, Pendleton, . May sth, 1909.
PRINTER'S PIE, 1909. A GREAT ISSUE.

The fact that ,the Prince of Wales is personally show- ing his interest in printing and its allied arts this year by graciously accepting the Presidency of the Printers' Pension Corporation Festival, mates the issue of "Printers' Pie, 1909," of exceptional value and importance. This gver-welcome annual, which is edited by Mr. W. Hugh SpottiswoOde, assisted Hy Mr. Arthur Croxton, has already been of remarkable service to the cause of charity, and it seems possible that the Prince of Wales' subscription list will this year mark a record. Other charities which benefit are the Book- sellers' Provident Institution, the Newsvenders' Benovo- lent and Provident Institution. the Newspaper Press Fund, and the Artists General Benevolent Institution "Printers' Pie, 1909," promises in every sense to make an artistic and literary record, Practically every important author and artist of the day is contributing to its pages, which Will .be produced with the fine finish which bas marked previous issues. The annual will be published on May 12th by The Sphere and Tatler.Ltd.. the price being Is. nett. Last year's edition of "Printers' Pie" was sold oat by the publisher three days after publication, so that orders for copies should be given at once to the bookstalls or newsTendors.
